<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:AS-conv-zero}
Let $\mathcal A=\mathcal L_\psi(t)|_{\mathbb{G}_{m}}$ and let
\[
\mathcal C:=\mathcal A[1]*_{\mathrm{mid}}\mathcal A[1]
\]
be the multiplicative middle convolution.  Then the underlying lisse sheaf of $\mathcal C$ is tame at the origin and its tame inertia representation consists of one unipotent Jordan block of size $2$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
We give the two-factor weight--Jordan calculation explicitly.  The sheaf $\mathcal A$ is unramified at $0$ and totally wild of rank one and Swan conductor one at $\infty$.  Hence it has no Kummer subobject or quotient.  For a tame character $\chi$, set
\[
\omega_\chi(M)=H^0\!\left(\mathbb P^1_{\bar k},j_{\infty!}Rj_{0*}(\mathcal L_\chi\otimes M)\right).
\]
For the trivial character, the unique tame block of $\mathcal A$ at $0$ has size one.  Moreover Grothendieck--Ogg--Shafarevich gives
$\chi_c(\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathcal A)=-1$, hence
$\chi_c(\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathcal A[1])=1$.  The monodromy filtration on this single block therefore gives
\[
P_{\mathcal A[1]}(T)=T^{-1},
\]
where a term $T^{-j}$ records a size-$j$ unipotent block at $0$, a term $T^j$ records such a block at $\infty$, and the constant coefficient is fixed by the Euler characteristic.

We now verify the multiplicativity needed in this special case rather than invoke it by name.  For multiplication $\mu:\mathbb{G}_{m}^2\to\mathbb{G}_{m}$, twisting the convolution by $\mathcal L_\chi$ and using
$\mu^*\mathcal L_\chi=\mathcal L_\chi\boxtimes\mathcal L_\chi$, projection formula and K\"unneth identify the compactly supported Mellin complex of the $!$-convolution with the tensor product of the two compactly supported Mellin complexes; the same holds without supports.  Taking the image of the compact-to-ordinary map therefore gives
\[
\omega_\chi(\mathcal A[1]*_{\mathrm{mid}}\mathcal A[1])
\cong\omega_\chi(\mathcal A[1])\otimes\omega_\chi(\mathcal A[1]).
\]
The monodromy filtration is strict for pure perverse sheaves, so Frobenius weights add under this tensor product.  Thus the corresponding Laurent polynomials multiply:
\[
P_{\mathcal C}(T)=P_{\mathcal A[1]}(T)^2=T^{-2}.
\]
Consequently the local tame representation of $\mathcal C$ at $0$ has exactly one size-$2$ unipotent Jordan block and no other block.  In particular it has rank two there, and no wild summand is present.  This is the two-factor case of the convolution product formula proved in full generality later in Theorem~\ref{thm:rojas-product}.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:kl-stationary-phase}
Assume $p\ne2$.  After the tame quadratic base change $t=s^2$, the two critical branches of
\[
\phi_s(x)=x+s^2/x
\]
are $x=s$ and $x=-s$.  The wild parts of the corresponding vanishing-cycle contributions are respectively $\mathcal L_\psi(2s)$ and $\mathcal L_\psi(-2s)$; the remaining factors are tame rank-one characters.  Consequently
\[
[2]^*\mathrm{Kl}_2\big|_{I_\infty}^{\mathrm{wild}}
   \cong \mathcal L_\psi(2s)\oplus\mathcal L_\psi(-2s)
\]
up to tame rank-one twists.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
The critical equation is
\[
\frac{\partial\phi_s}{\partial x}=1-\frac{s^2}{x^2}=0,
\]
so the only critical branches are $x=\varepsilon s$, $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}$.  Put
$x=\varepsilon s(1+z)$ near such a branch.  A direct identity, rather than a formal Taylor truncation, gives
\[
\phi_s(x)
 =\varepsilon s\left((1+z)+(1+z)^{-1}\right)
 =2\varepsilon s+\varepsilon s\frac{z^2}{1+z}.
\tag{\ref{lem:kl-stationary-phase}.1}
\]
Because $p\ne2$ and $1+z$ is a unit in the henselian local ring at $z=0$, Hensel's lemma gives a unique square root $(1+z)^{1/2}$ with value $1$ at the origin.  With the \(\acute{e}\)tale local coordinate
\[
y=z(1+z)^{-1/2}
\]
formula (\ref{lem:kl-stationary-phase}.1) becomes exactly
\[
\phi_s=2\varepsilon s+\varepsilon s y^2.
\tag{\ref{lem:kl-stationary-phase}.2}
\]
Thus the local vanishing-cycle complex factors as the constant Artin--Schreier character
$\mathcal L_\psi(2\varepsilon s)$ tensored with the quadratic Gauss vanishing cycle of
$\mathcal L_\psi(\varepsilon s y^2)$.  The latter has rank one.  Its wild part is trivial: after the tame quadratic change in the $y$-variable, the quadratic Gauss integral is a Kummer character times a geometrically constant Gauss factor, hence has Swan conductor zero in the parameter $s$.  Therefore the entire wild dependence on $s$ is the rank-one character $\mathcal L_\psi(2\varepsilon s)$.

The two critical branches are disjoint after passing to the strict henselization at $s=\infty$.  Vanishing cycles are additive over disjoint critical points, so the wild local module is the direct sum of the two contributions.  This proves the displayed decomposition.  Notice that the argument also fixes the sign and the normalization of the two Artin--Schreier phases; no appeal to a global monodromy formula is needed.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:kl2-local-internal}
Let $p$ be odd and let $\mathrm{Kl}_2$ be the Kloosterman sheaf whose trace function is the classical rank-two Kloosterman sum.  Then $\mathrm{Kl}_2$ is lisse of rank $2$ on $\mathbb{G}_{m}$, pure of weight $1$, its local monodromy at $0$ is tame unipotent with one Jordan block of size $2$, and its local monodromy at $\infty$ is totally wild with both breaks equal to $1/2$; in particular $\mathrm{Swan}_\infty(\mathrm{Kl}_2)=1$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Let $\mu:\mathbb{G}_{m}^2\to\mathbb{G}_{m}$ be multiplication and put
$\mathcal A=\mathcal L_\psi(x)|_{\mathbb{G}_{m}}$.  The degree-one lisse part of
$R\mu_!(\mathcal A\boxtimes\mathcal A)$ has, at $t\in\mathbb{G}_{m}$, the fibre
\[
H^1_c\!\left(\mathbb{G}_{m,x},\mathcal L_\psi(x+t/x)\right),
\]
and its Frobenius trace is the classical rank-two Kloosterman sum (up to the fixed sign convention).  We analyse this family directly.

For $t\ne0$, the rank-one coefficient $\mathcal L_\psi(x+t/x)$ has a simple pole at $x=0$ and a simple pole at $x=\infty$, hence Swan conductor $1$ at each end.  It has no geometric invariants, so $H_c^0=H_c^2=0$.  Grothendieck--Ogg--Shafarevich gives
\[
\chi_c(\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathcal L_\psi(x+t/x))=-1-1=-2,
\qquad \dim H^1_c=2.
\]
The two boundary Swan conductors are constant as $t$ varies in $\mathbb{G}_{m}$.  The conductor semicontinuity/base-change criterion, proved in the specialized relative form of Lemma~\ref{lem:relative-conductor-lisse} below, therefore shows that these $H^1_c$ form a lisse rank-two sheaf on $\mathbb{G}_{m,t}$.  Deligne's weight theorem for this nondegenerate one-dimensional exponential family makes it pure of weight $1$.  This is Deligne's $\mathrm{Kl}_2$.

We next determine the monodromy at $0$ without using a compactification heuristic.  The $!$-multiplicative convolution $\mathcal A[1]*_!\mathcal A[1]$ has underlying degree-one lisse sheaf $\mathrm{Kl}_2$ by the preceding fibre description.  The middle convolution is a quotient of the $!$-convolution.  Lemma~\ref{lem:AS-conv-zero} shows that its local module at $0$ is already a single block $J_2(1)$, hence has rank two.  Since the source $\mathrm{Kl}_2$ also has rank two, the quotient map is generically an isomorphism.  Thus $\mathrm{Kl}_2$ itself is tame at $0$ and its tame generator acts by one Jordan block $J_2(1)$.

At $t=\infty$ put $t=s^2$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:kl-stationary-phase} computes the two vanishing-cycle contributions directly and gives
\[
[2]^*\mathrm{Kl}_2\big|_{I_\infty}^{\mathrm{wild}}
\cong
\mathcal L_\psi(2s)\oplus\mathcal L_\psi(-2s)
\]
up to tame rank-one twists.  Each Artin--Schreier summand has break $1$ in the $s$-coordinate.  Under a tame extension of ramification degree $2$, upper-numbering breaks are multiplied by $2$, so before pullback both breaks are $1/2$.  The rank has already been shown to be two, hence there is no additional slope-zero summand.  Therefore $\mathrm{Kl}_2$ is totally wild at $\infty$ and $\mathrm{Swan}_\infty(\mathrm{Kl}_2)=1$.

As an independent normalization check, Katz proves for $\mathrm{Kl}_n$ that the local monodromy at $0$ is one unipotent Jordan block and the determinant is geometrically constant; at $n=2$ this is exactly the local representation obtained above \cite[Thm.~7.4.3]{Katz-Gauss}.  The citation is not carrying a missing family-specific step here: the rank, the block at $0$, and the two breaks at $\infty$ have all been derived in the preceding paragraphs.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:kl2-sl2-internal}
For every odd $p$,
\[
G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathrm{Kl}_2)=\operatorname{SL}_2.
\]
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
We derive the statement from Theorem~\ref{thm:kl2-local-internal}.  First the geometric determinant is trivial.  At $0$ the local monodromy is one regular unipotent block, hence has determinant one.  At $\infty$, after the tame quadratic pullback, the wild part is
$\mathcal L_\psi(2s)\oplus\mathcal L_\psi(-2s)$, whose determinant is trivial; consequently the determinant character has Swan conductor zero at $\infty$ as well.  Thus $\det\mathrm{Kl}_2$ is a geometrically tame rank-one sheaf on $\mathbb{G}_{m}$.  The tame geometric fundamental group of $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ is generated by the inertia loops at $0$ and $\infty$ with product one.  Since the determinant is already trivial on inertia at $0$, it is trivial on the whole tame quotient.  Hence the geometric monodromy of $\mathrm{Kl}_2$ lies in $\operatorname{SL}_2$.

Purity of $\mathrm{Kl}_2$ implies geometric semisimplicity by Lemma~\ref{lem:deligne-semisimple}; therefore its Zariski closure $G\subseteq\operatorname{SL}_2$ is reductive.  The regular unipotent inertia element $u\ne1$ at $0$ has infinite order in characteristic zero.  Since the component group $G/G^0$ is finite, some positive power $u^m$ lies in $G^0$, and $u^m$ is still a nonidentity unipotent.  Thus $G^0$ is positive-dimensional and contains a nontrivial unipotent.

A proper connected reductive subgroup of $\operatorname{SL}_2$ is a torus: indeed its derived Lie algebra is a semisimple proper subalgebra of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$, hence zero, so the group is commutative reductive and therefore a torus.  A torus has no nonidentity unipotent elements.  Hence $G^0=\operatorname{SL}_2$.  Because $G\subseteq\operatorname{SL}_2$, this forces $G=\operatorname{SL}_2$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:self-kl-factor}
Let $\mathrm{pr}:\mathbb{G}_{m,u}^n\times\mathbb{G}_{m,t}\times S\to\mathbb{G}_{m,t}\times S$ be the projection and set
\[
\mathcal N_n:=R^n\mathrm{pr}_!\mathcal L_\psi(F_n)|_{t\ne0}.
\]
Then $R^j\mathrm{pr}_!\mathcal L_\psi(F_n)=0$ for $j\ne n$, and
\[
\mathcal N_n\cong\Bigl(\bigotimes_{i=1}^n m_i^*\mathrm{Kl}_2\Bigr)\otimes\mathcal L_\psi(\lambda t),
\qquad m_i(t,h)=h_i t.
\]
In particular $\mathcal N_n$ is lisse of rank $2^n$ and pure of weight $n$ on $\mathbb{G}_{m,t}\times S$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
The phase separates as
\[
F_n=\lambda t+\sum_{i=1}^n(u_i^{-1}+h_i t u_i).
\]
For one variable, the substitution $x=u^{-1}$, $y=(h_it)u$ gives $xy=h_it$ and $x+y=u^{-1}+h_it u$.  Deligne's construction of $\mathrm{Kl}_2$ is precisely the compactly supported degree-one cohomology of this family; therefore
\[
R^j(\mathrm{pr}_i)_!\mathcal L_\psi(u_i^{-1}+h_it u_i)=0\quad(j\ne1),
\qquad
R^1(\mathrm{pr}_i)_!\mathcal L_\psi(u_i^{-1}+h_it u_i)=m_i^*\mathrm{Kl}_2.
\]
Relative K\"unneth puts the $n$-fold external tensor product in degree $n$ and nowhere else.  The projection formula contributes the rank-one factor $\mathcal L_\psi(\lambda t)$.  Rank and purity follow by tensoring $n$ rank-two sheaves of weight $1$ and a weight-zero Artin--Schreier sheaf.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:self-unequal-break}
Let $V$ and $W$ be $\ell$-adic inertia representations and suppose $V$ is isoclinic of break $a$, $W$ is isoclinic of break $b$, with $a<b$.  Then every break of $V\otimes W$ is $b$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
For $r>b$ both $V$ and $W$ are fixed by the upper ramification group $I^{(r)}$, so $V\otimes W$ is fixed.  For $a<r\le b$, $I^{(r)}$ acts trivially on $V$ and has no invariants on $W$; hence
\[
(V\otimes W)^{I^{(r)}}=V\otimes W^{I^{(r)}}=0.
\]
Thus the unique break is $b$.  Decomposing arbitrary representations into their break subspaces gives the usual rule that cancellation can occur only when the two breaks are equal.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:self-cg}
Let $V_2$ be a two-dimensional vector space over a field of characteristic zero. Assume that a tame generator acts on $V_2$ through one nontrivial unipotent Jordan block. For every $n\ge1$ one has
\[
V_2^{\otimes n}\cong\bigoplus_{k=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}m_{n,k}V_{n-2k+1},
\qquad
m_{n,k}=\binom{n}{k}-\binom{n}{k-1},
\]
where $V_j$ denotes one unipotent Jordan block of size $j$ and $\binom{n}{-1}=0$.  Consequently the number of Jordan blocks is
\[
\sum_km_{n,k}=\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The case $n=1$ is immediate.  Assume the decomposition for $n-1$.  In characteristic zero the Clebsch--Gordan rule is
\[
V_2\otimes V_j\cong V_{j+1}\oplus V_{j-1}\qquad(j\ge2),
\]
and $V_2\otimes V_1=V_2$.  Therefore the multiplicity in degree $k$ satisfies
\[
m_{n,k}=m_{n-1,k}+m_{n-1,k-1}.
\]
On the other hand
\[
\begin{aligned}
\binom{n}{k}-\binom{n}{k-1}
&=\binom{n-1}{k}-\binom{n-1}{k-2}\\
&=\Bigl(\binom{n-1}{k}-\binom{n-1}{k-1}\Bigr)
 +\Bigl(\binom{n-1}{k-1}-\binom{n-1}{k-2}\Bigr),
\end{aligned}
\]
so the claimed formula obeys the same recursion and initial condition.  Summing telescopes to the central binomial coefficient.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:self-tline}
For every $h\in S(\mathbb{F}_q)$ one has
\[
\mathrm{Swan}_0(\mathcal N_{n,h})=0,
\qquad
\mathrm{Swan}_\infty(\mathcal N_{n,h})=2^n,
\qquad
\dim H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathcal N_{n,h})=2^n.
\]
Moreover
\[
\dim \mathcal N_{n,h}^{I_0}=\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}.
\]
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
At $t=0$ every Kloosterman factor is tame and $\mathcal L_\psi(\lambda t)$ is unramified, hence $\mathrm{Swan}_0=0$.  At $t=\infty$ the tensor product of the Kloosterman factors has breaks at most $1/2$, whereas $\mathcal L_\psi(\lambda t)$ has the single break $1$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:self-unequal-break} therefore gives break $1$ on all $2^n$ dimensions, so $\mathrm{Swan}_\infty=2^n$.

Grothendieck--Ogg--Shafarevich on $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ gives
\[
\chi_c(\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathcal N_{n,h})=-\mathrm{Swan}_0-\mathrm{Swan}_\infty=-2^n.
\]
The compactly supported $H^0$ vanishes for every lisse sheaf on the nonproper connected curve $\mathbb{G}_{m}$.  The group $H^2_c$ is dual to the geometric coinvariants of the generic representation; it vanishes because the representation is totally wild at $\infty$, hence has no trivial quotient.  Therefore $\dim H^1_c=2^n$.

At $t=0$ each factor contributes one size-two unipotent block, so the inertia representation is $V_2^{\otimes n}$.  The dimension of the invariant space of a unipotent representation is the number of Jordan blocks.  Lemma~\ref{lem:self-cg} gives the asserted central binomial coefficient.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:self-tzero}
On $Z=\{t=0\}\cong\mathbb{G}_{m,u}^n$,
\[
\mathcal L_\psi(F_n)|_Z\cong\boxtimes_{i=1}^n\mathcal L_\psi(u_i^{-1}),
\]
and its compactly supported cohomology is one-dimensional in degree $n$, zero in all other degrees, with Frobenius eigenvalue $1$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
For one factor, $\mathcal L_\psi(u^{-1})$ has Swan conductor $1$ at $0$ and $0$ at $\infty$.  Hence $\chi_c=-1$.  It is nonconstant, so $H^0_c=H^2_c=0$ and $\dim H^1_c=1$.  Grothendieck--Lefschetz gives
\[
-\mathrm{Tr}(\mathrm{Frob}|H^1_c)=\sum_{u\ne0}\psi_q(u^{-1})=\sum_{v\ne0}\psi_q(v)=-1,
\]
so the eigenvalue is $1$.  K\"unneth gives the $n$-fold statement.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:self-integrate-t}
For fixed $h$, compactly supported integration in $t\in\mathbb A^1$ gives canonical isomorphisms
\[
H^i_c(X_h,\mathcal L_\psi(F_n))\cong H^{i-2}_c(Y_h,\mathcal L_h)(-1).
\]
In particular $H^i_c(X_h)=0$ for $i<n+1$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Let $q:X_h\to\mathbb{G}_{m}^n$ forget $t$.  For $a\in\mathbb{F}_q$,
\[
R\Gamma_c(\mathbb A^1,\mathcal L_\psi(at))=
\begin{cases}
0,&a\ne0,\\
\mathbb{Q}_\ell(-1)[-2],&a=0.
\end{cases}
\]
Therefore proper base change identifies $Rq_!\mathcal L_\psi(F_n)$ with the extension by zero from the hypersurface $\lambda+\langle h,u\rangle=0$ of $\mathcal L_h(-1)[-2]$.  Taking compactly supported cohomology yields the displayed formula.  The hypersurface $Y_h$ is smooth affine of dimension $n-1$ because all $h_i\ne0$; Artin vanishing gives $H^j_c(Y_h,\mathcal L_h)=0$ for $j<n-1$, hence the final assertion.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:relative-conductor-lisse}
Let $S$ be normal and connected over a finite field, let $\bar\rho:\mathbb P^1\times S\to S$, let $j:\mathbb{G}_{m}\times S\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^1\times S$, and let $\mathcal F$ be lisse on $\mathbb{G}_{m}\times S$.  Assume that on every geometric fibre: (i) $H_c^0=H_c^2=0$; (ii) the Artin conductor at each of the two boundary sections $0,\infty$ is locally constant on $S$.  Then $R^1\rho_!\mathcal F$ is lisse and commutes with arbitrary base change.  If, in addition, the inertia representations at one boundary section form a constant tame conjugacy class, their invariant spaces form a lisse subsheaf of $R^1\rho_!\mathcal F$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
We spell out the conductor argument underlying Laumon's semicontinuity theorem.  It is enough to test local acyclicity after pullback to a strictly henselian trait $T\to S$.  Write $\eta$ and $s$ for its generic and closed geometric points.  For $j_!\mathcal F$ on $\mathbb P^1\times T$, the only possible vanishing cycles are supported at the two boundary sections.  The local conductor--vanishing-cycle formula identifies the total dimension of the vanishing-cycle complex at a boundary point with the jump
\[
a_s(\mathcal F)-a_\eta(\mathcal F),\qquad
 a_x(\mathcal F)=\operatorname{rank}\mathcal F-
 \dim \mathcal F^{I_x}+\mathrm{Swan}_x(\mathcal F).
\]
The jump is nonnegative.  By hypothesis it is zero at both boundary sections, hence all vanishing cycles vanish.  Thus $j_!\mathcal F$ is universally locally acyclic over $T$.  Proper base change for $\bar\rho$ then identifies the specialization maps on compactly supported cohomology.  Since degrees $0$ and $2$ vanish on every fibre, only degree $1$ remains, and its specialization maps are isomorphisms.  This is exactly the lissit\'e and base-change criterion for $R^1\rho_!\mathcal F$.

For the last assertion, a constant tame conjugacy class means that, after an \`etale localization on $S$, a fixed tame generator acts by one fixed matrix $T$.  The invariant subspace is the kernel of the morphism $T-1$ of the corresponding lisse local system.  Its dimension is constant; hence the kernel is locally a direct summand and is itself lisse.  This is exactly the conductor-constancy mechanism needed here.  Laumon's semicontinuity theorem is cited for the general formalism of the local conductor formula; the vanishing-cycle consequence and the base-change deduction used in this article have been written out above \cite{Laumon-semicont}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:middle-extension-purity}
Let $C$ be a smooth proper geometrically connected curve over a finite field, let $j:U\hookrightarrow C$ be a nonempty open immersion, and let $\mathcal F$ be lisse and pure of weight $w$ on $U$.  Then
\[
H^1(C_{\bar k},j_*\mathcal F)
\]
is pure of weight $w+1$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
On a smooth curve the perverse middle extension of $\mathcal F[1]$ is $(j_*\mathcal F)[1]$.  Deligne's extension theorem says that the intermediate extension of a pure perverse sheaf is pure of the same perverse weight; here $\mathcal F[1]$ has perverse weight $w+1$, so $(j_*\mathcal F)[1]$ is pure of weight $w+1$.  The point of the intermediate extension is precisely that it has neither a nonzero subobject nor a nonzero quotient supported on $C\setminus U$; consequently no smaller boundary weight can enter its degree-zero proper cohomology.  Proper pushforward to $\operatorname{Spec}k$ preserves purity.  Finally
\[
H^0\bigl(C_{\bar k},(j_*\mathcal F)[1]\bigr)=H^1(C_{\bar k},j_*\mathcal F),
\]
so the latter is pure of weight $w+1$.  This is the curve case of the purity theorem for intermediate extensions in Weil II and the perverse-sheaf formalism of Beilinson--Bernstein--Deligne; the argument above records exactly how those foundational results apply here \cite{Deligne,BBD}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:self-excision}
Let $j:\mathbb{G}_{m,t}\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1_t$.  For every $h\in S(\mathbb{F}_q)$ there are exact sequences
\[
0\longrightarrow H^n_c(Z)\longrightarrow H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathcal N_{n,h})
\longrightarrow H^{n+1}_c(X_h,\mathcal L_\psi(F_n))\longrightarrow0,
\]
and
\[
0\longrightarrow \mathcal N_{n,h}^{I_0}\longrightarrow H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathcal N_{n,h})
\longrightarrow H^1(\mathbb P^1,j_*\mathcal N_{n,h})\longrightarrow0.
\]
The first left-hand term is the one-dimensional weight-zero line of Lemma~\ref{lem:self-tzero}.  The last term in the second sequence is pure of weight $n+1$, while $\mathcal N_{n,h}^{I_0}$ has weights at most $n$.  Consequently the weight-$(n+1)$ quotient of $H^{n+1}_c(X_h)$ is canonically
\[
W_{n,h}:=H^1(\mathbb P^1,j_*\mathcal N_{n,h}),
\qquad
\dim W_{n,h}=r(n):=2^n-\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}.
\]
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The open--closed triangle for $X_h=(t\ne0)\cup Z$, together with Lemma~\ref{lem:self-kl-factor}, identifies
\[
H^{n+1}_c(t\ne0,\mathcal L_\psi(F_n))=H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathcal N_{n,h}).
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:self-integrate-t} gives $H^n_c(X_h)=0$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:self-tzero} says that $Z$ contributes only in degree $n$.  The long exact sequence therefore collapses to the first displayed short exact sequence; it also shows that $X_h$ is concentrated in degree $n+1$.

For the second sequence, compare $j_!\mathcal N_{n,h}$ and $j_*\mathcal N_{n,h}$ on $\mathbb P^1$.  The quotient is supported at $0$ and $\infty$ with stalks the inertia invariants.  There are no invariants at $\infty$ because $\mathcal N_{n,h}$ is totally wild there.  Taking cohomology yields
\[
0\to \mathcal N_{n,h}^{I_0}\to H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathcal N_{n,h})
\to H^1(\mathbb P^1,j_*\mathcal N_{n,h})\to0.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:middle-extension-purity}, applied with $w=n$, shows that $H^1(\mathbb P^1,j_*\mathcal N_{n,h})$ is pure of weight $n+1$, whereas nearby-cycle invariants have weights at most $n$.  Hence this is exactly the top-weight quotient.  Proposition~\ref{prop:self-tline} gives its dimension.  Since the weight-zero line in the first exact sequence lies inside the lower-weight term, passing from $H^1_c$ to $H^{n+1}_c(X_h)$ does not alter the top-weight quotient.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:self-cohomology-package}
Assume $n\ge2$ and $p>\max(2,n)$.  On $S=\mathbb{G}_{m}^n$ the sheaf
\[
\mathcal H_n:=R^1\rho_!\mathcal N_n,
\qquad \rho:\mathbb{G}_{m,t}\times S\to S,
\]
is lisse of rank $2^n$.  The inertia-invariant spaces at $t=0$ form a lisse subsheaf $\mathcal E_n\subset\mathcal H_n$ of rank $\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$, and
\[
\mathcal W_n:=\mathcal H_n/\mathcal E_n
\]
is lisse of rank $r(n)$ and pure of weight $n+1$.  Fibrewise it is the top-weight quotient of $H^{n+1}_c(X_h)$ and, after the Tate twist, of $H^{n-1}_c(Y_h,\mathcal L_h)$.  Moreover
\[
\Sigma_n(h)=(-1)^{n-1}\mathrm{Tr}\!\left(\mathrm{Frob}_h\mid H^{n-1}_c(Y_h,\mathcal L_h)\right),
\]
and the contribution of all weights below $n-1$ is $O_n(q^{(n-2)/2})$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
We first prove lissit\'e of $\mathcal H_n$.  Compactify the $t$-line to $\mathbb P^1_t\times S$.  At $t=0$ the inertia representation is the constant tame module $V_2^{\otimes n}$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:kl2-local-internal} and Lemma~\ref{lem:self-cg}; hence both its invariant dimension and its Artin conductor are constant.  At $t=\infty$ Proposition~\ref{prop:self-tline} gives break $1$ on all $2^n$ dimensions, so there are no inertia invariants and the Artin conductor is the constant $2^{n+1}$.  The fibre groups in degrees $0$ and $2$ vanish by Proposition~\ref{prop:self-tline}.  Lemma~\ref{lem:relative-conductor-lisse} therefore applies and makes $\mathcal H_n=R^1\rho_!\mathcal N_n$ lisse, with base change and rank $2^n$.

The tame nearby cycles at $t=0$ are locally constant in the parameter $h$: multiplying the local parameter $t$ by the unit $h_i$ does not alter the conjugacy class of tame inertia, so each factor has the same regular unipotent block.  Therefore the kernels of $T-1$ assemble to a lisse subsheaf $\mathcal E_n$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:self-cg} gives its rank.  Fibrewise Proposition~\ref{prop:self-excision} identifies the quotient with $H^1(\mathbb P^1,j_*\mathcal N_{n,h})$.  These fibrewise maps are functorial in $h$, hence define a lisse quotient $\mathcal W_n$ of the asserted rank.

Purity is also fibrewise and then global: $\mathcal N_n$ is pure of weight $n$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:middle-extension-purity} makes $H^1(\mathbb P^1,j_*\mathcal N_{n,h})$ pure of weight $n+1$.  Thus every geometric fibre of the lisse sheaf $\mathcal W_n$ is pure of weight $n+1$, which is precisely purity of $\mathcal W_n$.

Lemma~\ref{lem:self-integrate-t} identifies $H^{n+1}_c(X_h)(1)$ with $H^{n-1}_c(Y_h,\mathcal L_h)$.  The Grothendieck--Lefschetz formula on the smooth affine $(n-1)$-fold $Y_h$, together with concentration established in Proposition~\ref{prop:self-excision}, gives the trace identity with sign $(-1)^{n-1}$.  Finally all constituents of $\mathcal E_n$ have weights at most $n$ before the Tate twist, hence at most $n-2$ afterwards; there are at most $2^n$ of them.  The Weil bound therefore gives an $O_n(q^{(n-2)/2})$ lower-weight contribution.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:self-lowdim}
For fixed $r\ge1$ and nonzero coordinates one has
\[
|\Sigma_r(h)|\ll_r q^{(r-1)/2}.
\]
In particular $|\Sigma_2(h)|=O(q^{1/2})$ and $|\Sigma_3(h)|=O(q)$, with constants independent of the extension degree.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:self-cohomology-package} in dimension $r$.  The top piece has rank $r(r)$ and weight $r-1$ after the Tate twist, while the lower part has bounded rank and strictly smaller weights.  The assertion follows by summing the Weil bounds for the finitely many Frobenius eigenvalues.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:self-foundations}
No theorem from a companion manuscript is used in the preceding construction.  The rank-two Kloosterman local calculation, the relative conductor argument, and the middle-extension purity deduction have all been written out in the specialized forms used here.  The remaining background consists only of the foundational formalism explicitly invoked inside those proofs (proper and smooth base change, vanishing cycles and the conductor formula, Grothendieck--Ogg--Shafarevich, Artin vanishing, and Weil II).  Thus every family-specific input needed to construct $\mathcal W_n$, compute $r(n)$, prove its purity and lissit\'e, and control the lower-weight contribution is contained in this article.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
For $n\ge2$ let $\mathcal G_n$ denote the lisse mixed quotient of $\mathcal H_n$ obtained by dividing out the constant boundary line of Proposition~\ref{prop:self-excision}; its fibre is $H^{n+1}_c(X_h,\mathcal L_\psi(F_n))$.  We write $\mathcal G:=\mathcal G_4$ and $\mathcal W:=\mathcal W_4$.  By Theorem~\ref{thm:self-cohomology-package}, $\mathcal W$ is pure of rank $r=r(4)=10$.  We write $G_{\mathrm{geom}}$ and $G^0_{\mathrm{geom}}$ for its geometric monodromy group and identity component.
Throughout every moment limit, the parameter $\lambda\in\mathbb F_p^\times$ and the base additive character $\psi:\mathbb F_p\to\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell^\times$ are fixed. For $q=p^m$ we write $\psi_q=\psi\circ\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb F_q/\mathbb F_p}$ and form the same family after base change to $\mathbb F_q$; to lighten notation we continue to write $\psi$ and $\Sigma_n$. Thus $q\to\infty$ always means passage through finite extensions of one fixed base field and one fixed lisse family.
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:numerics}
The two moment statements of this paper admit independent numerical confirmation, which we record because they are the load-bearing quantitative inputs; the computations are verifications, not proofs, and nothing below is used in any argument.

The exact second-moment identity
\[
\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q^n}|\Sigma_n(h)|^2
=q^{n-2}\Big((q-1)^{n+1}+1-(q-2)(-1)^n\Big)
\]
was also evaluated directly for $n=2,3,4$ and all primes $p\le19$.  For completeness, the identity itself is elementary.  Expanding the square and summing first over $h$, a pair $(u,v)\in(\mathbb{F}_q^\times)^{2n}$ contributes $q^{n-1}$ when $u=v$, contributes $q^{n-2}$ when $u,v$ are linearly independent, and contributes $0$ when $v=cu$ with $c\ne1$, because the two affine equations $h\cdot u=-\lambda$ and $h\cdot v=-\lambda$ would force $c=1$.  The unrestricted phase sum over all pairs is $1$, while the sum over the excluded dependent pairs is
\[
\sum_{c\in\mathbb{F}_q^\times\setminus\{1\}}\ \sum_{u\in(\mathbb{F}_q^\times)^n}
\psi_q\!\big((1-c^{-1})\sum_i u_i^{-1}\big)
=(q-2)(-1)^n.
\]
Adding the excess $(q^{n-1}-q^{n-2})(q-1)^n$ from the diagonal gives the displayed formula.  Thus the numerical check tests an identity proved inside the present article and carries no logical weight in what follows.

For the fourth moment, Theorem~\ref{thm:fourthmoment-n} gives $\sum_h|\Sigma_q(h)|^4=2q^{10}+O(q^9)$ when $n=4$. Writing $\mathfrak M_4(p)$ for the exact numerical value, the normalised error $\big(\mathfrak M_4(p)-2p^{10}\big)/p^{9}$ takes the values
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccc}
p & 7 & 11 & 13 & 17 & 19 & 23\\\hline
\big(\mathfrak M_4(p)-2p^{10}\big)/p^{9} & -7.59 & -6.95 & -6.91 & -6.91 & -6.94 & -6.70
\end{array}
\]
The quantity is visibly bounded, and indeed nearly constant, which is the behaviour of a genuine error term of order $q^9$ with an absolute implied constant near $7$. Had the error been of order $q^{19/2}$ and no better --- the preliminary exponent of Theorem~\ref{thm:743} --- this normalised quantity would grow like $\sqrt p$, that is, through the values $2.6,3.3,3.6,4.1,4.4,4.8$; it does not. The slow approach of $\mathfrak M_4(p)/(2p^{10})$ to $1$ over this range, from $0.46$ to $0.85$, is accounted for entirely by the secondary term of size $7p^9$, which is still a substantial fraction of the main term for $p\le23$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:numerics-extra}
The corresponding small-field checks for $n=3,4$ concern the complete moments. Two further sets of values may help the reader, and here they are; as before they are checks, and no proof depends on them.

\emph{Higher $n$.} Evaluating the right-hand side of Lemma~\ref{lem:decouple} and dividing by $q^4$ gives $\sum_h|\Sigma_n(h)|^4$ for $n=5,6$ without ever forming the $n$-fold sum. Against the main term $2q^{3n-2}$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:fourthmoment-n}, with $\delta(n)=1$ for $n\ge4$, this gives the following exact table:

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{The fourth moment for $n=5,6$, against the main term of Theorem~\ref{thm:fourthmoment-n}.}\label{tab:higher-n}
\begin{tabular}{ccccc}
\toprule
$p$ & $n$ & $\sum_h|\Sigma_n(h)|^4$ & $2q^{3n-2}$ & $\big(\mathfrak M_4-2q^{3n-2}\big)/q^{3n-3}$\\
\midrule
$7$ & $5$ & $1.170\times10^{11}$ & $1.938\times10^{11}$ & $-5.55$\\
$11$ & $5$ & $5.800\times10^{13}$ & $6.905\times10^{13}$ & $-3.52$\\
$13$ & $5$ & $5.470\times10^{14}$ & $6.058\times10^{14}$ & $-2.52$\\
$7$ & $6$ & $5.388\times10^{13}$ & $6.647\times10^{13}$ & $-2.65$\\
$11$ & $6$ & $1.139\times10^{17}$ & $9.190\times10^{16}$ & $5.26$\\
$13$ & $6$ & $1.755\times10^{18}$ & $1.331\times10^{18}$ & $8.28$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The last column is the error divided by $q^{3n-2-\delta(n)}$ with $\delta(n)=1$; it remains bounded, which is what the theorem asserts and what a larger $\delta$ would not permit.

\emph{Short boxes.} For $n=4$ and $B_H=\{|h_i|\le H\}$ the first and second moments over the box behave as follows, normalised respectively by the trivial first-moment scale $H^4p^{3/2}$ and by the natural second-moment scale $(2H+1)^4p^3$; the resulting exact values are:

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{First and second moments over short boxes for $n=4$.}\label{tab:shortbox-num}
\begin{tabular}{ccccc}
\toprule
$p$ & $H$ & $\big|\sum_{B_H}\Sigma\big|$ & $\big|\sum_{B_H}\Sigma\big|/(2H+1)^4p^{3/2}$ & $\sum_{B_H}|\Sigma|^2/(2H+1)^4p^3$\\
\midrule
$13$ & $2$ & $589$ & $0.020$ & $0.920$\\
$17$ & $2$ & $322$ & $0.007$ & $0.753$\\
$19$ & $2$ & $2664$ & $0.051$ & $0.627$\\
$23$ & $2$ & $157$ & $0.002$ & $1.004$\\
$17$ & $3$ & $7755$ & $0.046$ & $0.810$\\
$23$ & $3$ & $4380$ & $0.017$ & $0.929$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The fourth column is far below $1$, while the fifth is of order one.  These values are included only as numerical orientation: no statement or proof in this article uses a short-box theorem, and the table plays no logical role in the monodromy argument.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:711}
For every finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ of odd characteristic,
\[
q^4\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q^4}|\Sigma_q(h)|^4=\sum_{t\in\mathbb{F}_q^4}\psi(L(t))\,V(t)^4.
\]
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Additive orthogonality gives the Kloosterman factorisation directly. Indeed, inserting
\[
\frac1q\sum_{t\in\mathbb{F}_q}\psi\!\left(t\left(\lambda+\sum_{i=1}^4h_iu_i\right)\right)=\mathbf 1_{\langle h,u\rangle=-\lambda}
\]
into the constrained sum and interchanging the $u$- and $t$-sums yields
\[
q\,\Sigma_q(h)=\sum_{t\in\mathbb{F}_q}\psi(\lambda t)\prod_{i=1}^4K(th_i).
\]
Moreover $K(a)\in\mathbb R$: conjugating and substituting $x\mapsto-x$ leaves the sum unchanged. Hence $|\Sigma_q(h)|^4$ is obtained from two copies of the factorisation and two conjugate copies, with phase $\lambda(t_1+t_2-t_3-t_4)$. Summing over $h_1,\dots,h_4$ independently factors the four coordinate sums and gives exactly the displayed identity.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:diag-eval}
For $a,b\in\mathbb{F}_q^\times$ with $\rho=a/b$,
\[
\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q}K(ah)^2K(bh)^2=\begin{cases}2q^3-3q^2-3q, & \rho=1,\\ q^3-(2+\chi(\rho))q^2-3q, & \rho\ne1.\end{cases}
\]
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Expanding $K(c)^2=\sum_{x,y\ne0}\psi(x^{-1}+y^{-1}+c(x+y))$ and using orthogonality in $h$ (which, applied to a second copy of $K(c)^2$ in variables $z,w$, contributes $q$ exactly when $a(x+y)+b(z+w)=0$) gives
\[
\sum_hK(ah)^2K(bh)^2=q\sum_{s\in\mathbb{F}_q}T(s)\,T(-\rho s),\qquad T(c):=\sum_{\substack{x,y\ne0\\x+y=c}}\psi(x^{-1}+y^{-1}).
\]

\emph{Evaluation of $T$.} For $c=0$, $y=-x$ gives $x^{-1}+y^{-1}=0$, so $T(0)=q-1$. For $c\ne0$, write $y=c-x$, so $x^{-1}+y^{-1}=c/(x(c-x))$; the bijection $x=cu$ gives $T(c)=\sum_{u\ne0,1}\psi\big(\tfrac{1}{cu(1-u)}\big)$. For $m\ne0$, the equation $u^2-u+m=0$ has $1+\chi(1-4m)$ solutions, and $m=0$ corresponds to the excluded $u\in\{0,1\}$; hence, using $\sum_{n\ne0}\psi(n)=-1$ and the bijection $n=1/(cm)$,
\[
T(c)=\sum_{m\ne0}\big(1+\chi(1-4m)\big)\psi(1/(cm))=-1+E(c),\qquad E(c):=\sum_{m\ne0}\chi\big(m(m-4)\big)\psi(m/c).
\]

\emph{Auxiliary sums.} Since $m^2-4m$ has nonzero discriminant, $\sum_{m\in\mathbb{F}_q}\chi(m^2-4m)=-1$, so $\sum_{m\ne0}\chi(m^2-4m)=-1$; hence $\sum_{s\ne0}E(s)=\sum_{m\ne0}\chi(m^2-4m)\sum_{s\ne0}\psi(m/s)=1$, and likewise $\sum_{s\ne0}E(-\rho s)=1$. Using $\sum_{s\ne0}\psi(A/s)=-1+q\cdot\mathbf1_{A=0}$,
\[
\sum_{s\ne0}E(s)E(-\rho s)=-\Big(\sum_{m\ne0}\chi(m^2-4m)\Big)^2+q\sum_{m\ne0}\chi\big((m^2-4m)(\rho^2m^2-4\rho m)\big).
\]
Since $(m^2-4m)(\rho^2m^2-4\rho m)=\rho m^2(m-4)(\rho m-4)$ and $\chi(m^2)=1$ for $m\ne0$, the second sum equals $\chi(\rho)\sum_{m\ne0}\chi\big((m-4)(\rho m-4)\big)$. The quadratic $\rho m^2-4(1+\rho)m+16$ has discriminant $16(1-\rho)^2$; if $\rho\ne1$ this is nonzero, so $\sum_{m\in\mathbb{F}_q}\chi(\cdots)=-\chi(\rho)$, and subtracting the $m=0$ term ($\chi(16)=1$) gives $-\chi(\rho)-1$, whence $\sum_{s\ne0}E(s)E(-\rho s)=-1-q-q\chi(\rho)$, using $\chi(\rho)^2=1$. If $\rho=1$, the quadratic is $(m-4)^2$, and $\sum_{m\ne0}\chi((m-4)^2)=q-2$, giving $-1+q(q-2)=q^2-2q-1$.

\emph{Assembly.} From $T=-1+E$, $\sum_{s\ne0}T(s)T(-\rho s)=(q-1)-1-1+\sum_{s\ne0}E(s)E(-\rho s)$, which equals $-4-q\chi(\rho)$ for $\rho\ne1$ and $q^2-q-4$ for $\rho=1$. Adding the term $s=0$, namely $T(0)^2=(q-1)^2$, and multiplying by $q$ gives the two stated values.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:diagonal-coefficient}
Throughout the fourth-moment calculation we use the phase
\[
L(t)=\lambda(t_1+t_2-t_3-t_4)
\]
of Theorem~\ref{thm:711}. Among the three partitions of $\{1,2,3,4\}$ into two pairs, exactly two annihilate $L$ on the corresponding diagonal:
\[
(13)(24):\ t=(a,b,a,b),\qquad
(14)(23):\ t=(a,b,b,a),
\]
whereas
\[
(12)(34):\ t=(a,a,b,b),\qquad L(t)=2\lambda(a-b)
\]
is nontrivial when $a\ne b$. Equivalently, among the six arrangements of the multiset $\{a,a,b,b\}$ with $a\ne b$, four have trivial phase and two carry the phases $\psi(\pm2\lambda(a-b))$. Consequently, for fixed $n\ge2$,
\[
\sum_{t\in D}\psi(L(t))V(t)^n
=2q^{3n+2}+O_n(q^{3n+1}).
\]
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
For $t=(a,b,a,b)$ one has $t_1+t_2-t_3-t_4=a+b-a-b=0$; for $t=(a,b,b,a)$ one has $a+b-b-a=0$; and for $t=(a,a,b,b)$ one has $2(a-b)$, nonzero when $a\ne b$ because the characteristic is odd. These three patterns exhaust the pair partitions.

Write
\[
D_1=\{(a,b,a,b):ab\ne0\},\qquad D_2=\{(a,b,b,a):ab\ne0\}.
\]
On either component, by symmetry of $V$,
\[
V(t)=\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q}K(ah)^2K(bh)^2.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:diag-eval} gives $V(t)=q^3+O(q^2)$ uniformly in $a,b\ne0$, hence
$V(t)^n=q^{3n}(1+O_n(q^{-1}))$. Each component has $(q-1)^2=q^2+O(q)$ points and the phase is trivial there, so each contributes $q^{3n+2}+O_n(q^{3n+1})$. Their intersection is the line $a=b$, containing $q-1$ points, and its contribution is $O_n(q^{3n+1})$. Inclusion--exclusion proves the formula.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:why-two}
The coefficient $2$ is the number of pairings compatible with the signs in $L(t)=\lambda(t_1+t_2-t_3-t_4)$. The two variables with positive sign must be matched with the two variables with negative sign. The pairings $(13)(24)$ and $(14)(23)$ do this and give the two components of $D$; the pairing $(12)(34)$ pairs equal signs and therefore carries the nontrivial phase $2\lambda(a-b)$. This convention is used without relabelling in every subsequent stratum calculation.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:kloos4}
$\displaystyle\sum_{a\in\mathbb{F}_q^\times}K(a)^4=2q^3-3q^2-3q-1$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Take $a=b$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:diag-eval}: $\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q}K(ah)^4=2q^3-3q^2-3q$. The term $h=0$ contributes $K(0)^4=1$, and $h\mapsto ah$ permutes $\mathbb{F}_q^\times$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:P-structure}
$P=\{(a,a,b,b),(b,b,a,a):a\ne b,\ ab\ne0\}$.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
An even-multiplicity pattern on four entries is $(4)$ or $(2,2)$. Pattern $(4)$ means $t_1=t_2=t_3=t_4$, which lies in $D$. For $(2,2)$, with value $a$ at two positions and $b\ne a$ at the other two, there are $\binom{4}{2}=6$ arrangements; the condition $\{t_3,t_4\}=\{t_1,t_2\}$ holds for the four in which each of $\{1,2\}$ and $\{3,4\}$ receives one $a$ and one $b$, and fails exactly for $(a,a,b,b)$ and $(b,b,a,a)$.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:716}
$\sum_{t\in D}\psi(L(t))V(t)^4=2q^{14}+O(q^{13})$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
On $D$ the character factor is $1$. For $t_1\ne t_2$ there are exactly two diagonal tuples, $(t_3,t_4)=(t_1,t_2)$ and $(t_2,t_1)$, and by symmetry of $V$ both give $V(t_1,t_2,t_1,t_2)$; for $t_1=t_2$ there is one. By Lemma~\ref{lem:diag-eval}, $V(t_1,t_2,t_1,t_2)=q^3(1+O(1/q))$ uniformly for $t_1\ne t_2$, so $V^4=q^{12}(1+O(1/q))$; there being $(q-1)(q-2)=q^2+O(q)$ such ordered pairs, this part contributes $2q^{14}+O(q^{13})$. For $t_1=t_2$, $V=2q^3+O(q^2)$, so $V^4=16q^{12}+O(q^{11})$, and there are $q-1$ such terms, contributing $O(q^{13})$.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:constant2}
The constant $2$ here is the number of ways of matching the multiset $\{t_3,t_4\}$ to $\{t_1,t_2\}$. After division by $q^4$ it is the leading constant in Theorem~\ref{thm:743}; Proposition~\ref{prop:755} then identifies the same constant with $M_4(G_{\mathrm{geom}},W)$. This is the character-sum shadow of the decomposition $W^{\otimes2}=\operatorname{Sym}^2W\oplus\Lambda^2W$ into its two non-isomorphic irreducible $\operatorname{GL}(W)$-constituents: by Schur's lemma, $\dim(W^{\otimes2}\otimes(W^\vee)^{\otimes2})^{\operatorname{GL}(W)}$ equals the number of such constituents, namely $2$. The count above, however, is obtained by pure combinatorics with no representation theory, and its agreement with Proposition~\ref{prop:755} is a nontrivial consistency check on the whole computation.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:721}
$\sum_{t\in Z}\psi(L(t))V(t)^4=O(q^{11})$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Let $t\in Z$ have exactly $r$ nonzero entries. Since $K(0)=-1$,
\[
V(t)=(-1)^{4-r}\sum_h\prod_{i:\,t_i\ne0}K(t_ih).
\]

If $r=0$: $V=q$; one tuple, contributing $q^4$.

If $r=1$: $\sum_hK(th)=K(0)+\sum_{h\ne0}K(th)=-1+\sum_{a\ne0}K(a)$, and $\sum_{a\ne0}K(a)=\sum_{x\ne0}\psi(x^{-1})\sum_{a\ne0}\psi(ax)=\sum_{x\ne0}\psi(x^{-1})\cdot(-1)=1$, so $V=0$ and the contribution vanishes.

If $r=2$ with nonzero entries $a,b$: if $a=b$, $\sum_{h\ne0}K(ah)^2=\sum_{c\ne0}K(c)^2=q^2-q-1$, so $|V|\le q^2$.  Each fourth power is therefore $O(q^8)$, and there are $O(q)$ such tuples; hence this subcase contributes $O(q^9)$. If $a\ne b$, the sheaf $\mathrm{Kl}_2(ah)\otimes\mathrm{Kl}_2(bh)$ on $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ has rank $4$, is pure of weight $2$, is tame at $0$, has $\mathrm{Swan}_\infty\le2$, and has no trivial constituent (the same invariant argument as in Lemma~\ref{lem:ninelines-bound}(ii), applied with two factors); hence $h^0_c=h^2_c=0$, $\dim H^1_c\le2$, and $|V|\le2q^{3/2}+1$. There are $O(q^2)$ such tuples, contributing $O(q^8)$.

If $r=3$: the sheaf has rank $8$, weight $3$, $\mathrm{Swan}_\infty\le4$, and no trivial constituent (three factors cannot all have even multiplicity); so $|V|\le4q^2+1$, and $O(q^3)$ tuples contribute $O(q^{11})$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:722}
\begin{multline*}
\sum_{t\in P}\psi(L(t))V(t)^4=-q^{13}+10q^{12}-38q^{11}+44q^{10}+101q^9\\
-226q^8-210q^7+324q^6+459q^5+162q^4\;=\;-q^{13}+O(q^{12}).
\end{multline*}
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:P-structure}, the sum runs over ordered pairs $(a,b)$, $a\ne b$, $ab\ne0$, of the tuple $(a,a,b,b)$; there $\psi(L(t))=\psi(2\lambda(a-b))$ and, by symmetry of $V$ together with Lemma~\ref{lem:diag-eval}, $V(a,a,b,b)=V(a,b,a,b)=q^3-(2+u)q^2-3q$ with $u=\chi(a/b)$. Since $u^2=1$, write $\big(q^3-(2+u)q^2-3q\big)^4=A+Bu$ with
\[
A=\tfrac12\big[(q^3-3q^2-3q)^4+(q^3-q^2-3q)^4\big],\qquad B=\tfrac12\big[(q^3-3q^2-3q)^4-(q^3-q^2-3q)^4\big].
\]
Then the sum equals $A\,S_1+B\,S_2$, where
\[
S_1=\sum_{\substack{a,b\ne0\\a\ne b}}\psi(2\lambda(a-b))=\Big|\sum_{a\ne0}\psi(2\lambda a)\Big|^2-(q-1)=1-(q-1)=2-q,
\]
and, writing $a=\rho b$ with $\rho\in\mathbb{F}_q^\times\setminus\{1\}$,
\[
S_2=\sum_{\substack{a,b\ne0\\a\ne b}}\chi(a/b)\psi(2\lambda(a-b))=\sum_{\rho\ne0,1}\chi(\rho)\sum_{b\ne0}\psi\big(2\lambda b(\rho-1)\big)=\sum_{\rho\ne0,1}\chi(\rho)\cdot(-1)=1.
\]
Expanding the polynomial $A(2-q)+B$ gives the stated identity.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:pair-general}
For every fixed integer $n\ge2$,
\[
\sum_{t\in P}\psi(L(t))V(t)^n=O_n(q^{3n+1}).
\]
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
For $t=(a,a,b,b)\in P$ with $a,b\ne0$ and $a\ne b$, Lemma~\ref{lem:diag-eval} gives
\[
V(t)=q^3-(2+u)q^2-3q,\qquad u=\chi(a/b)\in\{\pm1\}.
\]
Put
\[
X_-:=q^3-3q^2-3q,\qquad X_+:=q^3-q^2-3q.
\]
Because $u=1$ gives $X_-$ and $u=-1$ gives $X_+$, for every fixed $n$ there are scalars
\[
A_n=\frac{X_-^n+X_+^n}{2},\qquad B_n=\frac{X_-^n-X_+^n}{2}
\]
such that $V(t)^n=A_n+B_nu$. The phase on $P$ is $\psi(2\lambda(a-b))$, and the two character sums computed in Theorem~\ref{thm:722} are
\[
S_1=\sum_{a,b\ne0,\ a\ne b}\psi(2\lambda(a-b))=2-q,\qquad
S_2=\sum_{a,b\ne0,\ a\ne b}\chi(a/b)\psi(2\lambda(a-b))=1.
\]
Hence the required sum is $A_nS_1+B_nS_2$. Since $A_n,B_n=O_n(q^{3n})$, this is $O_n(q^{3n+1})$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:sigma0}
Let $\Sigma_0(t)=\sum_{u\in T(\mathbb{F}_q),\ \langle t,u\rangle=0}\psi(f(u))$ denote the sum of the same family with $\lambda$ replaced by $0$. Then $V(t)=q\,\Sigma_0(t)$.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
By orthogonality, $q\Sigma_0(t)=\sum_{s\in\mathbb{F}_q}\sum_{u\in T}\psi(f(u)+s\langle t,u\rangle)=\sum_sK(st_1)\cdots K(st_4)=V(t)$.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:sigma0-planecubic}
Let all $t_i\ne0$, let $H_t=\{\sum t_iu_i=0\}\subset\mathbb P^3$, $S=\{e_3=0\}$ with $e_3=\sum_{i<j<k}u_iu_ju_k$, $C_t=H_t\cap S$, and $a_t=q+1-\#C_t(\mathbb{F}_q)$. Then $\Sigma_0(t)=-qa_t-2q-3$.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
The set $\{u\in T:\langle t,u\rangle=0\}$ is stable under $u\mapsto\mu u$ ($\mu\in\mathbb{F}_q^\times$), and $f(\mu u)=f(u)/\mu$, so $f(u)=0$ is constant on orbits; on an orbit, $\sum_{\mu\ne0}\psi(f(u)/\mu)$ equals $-1$ if $f(u)\ne0$ (substitute $\nu=f(u)/\mu$) and $q-1$ if $f(u)=0$. Hence $\Sigma_0=-N+qN_0$, where $N$ is the number of orbits and $N_0$ the number with $f=0$.

Now $N=\#\{u\in\mathbb P^3:\text{all }u_i\ne0,\ u\in H_t\}$. The plane $H_t$ has $q^2+q+1$ points; each $H_t\cap\{u_i=0\}$ is a line with $q+1$ points, since $(t_j)_{j\ne i}\ne0$; each $H_t\cap\{u_i=u_j=0\}$ is a single point; and $H_t\cap\{u_i=u_j=u_k=0\}$ is empty because $t_l\ne0$. Inclusion--exclusion gives $N=(q^2+q+1)-4(q+1)+6=q^2-3q+3$.

Since all $u_i\ne0$, the condition $f(u)=0$ is equivalent to $e_3(u)=0$, so $N_0=\#C_t^\circ(\mathbb{F}_q)$, where $C_t^\circ$ is $C_t$ minus the coordinate hyperplanes. If $u\in C_t$ has $u_1=0$ then $e_3(u)=u_2u_3u_4=0$, so at least two coordinates vanish; three cannot, as above; and each of the six choices of a vanishing pair determines exactly one point of $H_t$, which lies on $S$. Hence $N_0=\#C_t(\mathbb{F}_q)-6=q-5-a_t$, and $\Sigma_0=-(q^2-3q+3)+q(q-5-a_t)=-qa_t-2q-3$.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:ninelines}
The surface $S=\{e_3=0\}\subset\mathbb P^3$, the Cayley nodal cubic, is singular exactly at the four coordinate points and contains exactly nine lines: the six coordinate edges $\{u_i=u_j=0\}$ and the three lines
\[
\lambda_{ij|kl}=\{u_i+u_j=0,\ u_k+u_l=0\},\qquad \{i,j\}\sqcup\{k,l\}=\{1,2,3,4\}.
\]
Consequently, if all $t_i\ne0$, $C_t$ contains a line if and only if $t_a=t_b$ and $t_c=t_d$ for some partition $\{a,b\}\sqcup\{c,d\}=\{1,2,3,4\}$, that is, if and only if $t\in D\cup P$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
\emph{Singular points.} One has $\partial e_3/\partial u_1=u_2u_3+u_2u_4+u_3u_4$, and cyclically. If $u$ is singular with $u_1=0$, then $\partial/\partial u_2=u_3u_4=0$, say $u_3=0$; then $\partial/\partial u_1=u_2u_4=0$, so $u_2=0$ or $u_4=0$, and in either case $u$ is a coordinate point. Each coordinate point is singular.

\emph{Lines through a node.} At $e_1$ set $u_1=1$, so $e_3=e_2(u_2,u_3,u_4)+u_2u_3u_4$. A line through $e_1$ is $\{(1:su_2:su_3:su_4)\}$, on which $e_3=s^2e_2(u_2,u_3,u_4)+s^3u_2u_3u_4$; this vanishes identically in $s$ if and only if $e_2(u_2,u_3,u_4)=0$ and $u_2u_3u_4=0$, i.e.\ if and only if two of $u_2,u_3,u_4$ vanish. These give the three coordinate edges through $e_1$.

\emph{Lines avoiding all nodes.} Such a line $\lambda$ lies in no coordinate plane, since $S\cap\{u_1=0\}=\{u_2u_3u_4=0\}$ is a union of edges. So $\lambda$ meets $\{u_i=0\}$ in one point, which lies on $S$ and therefore has a second vanishing coordinate; not being a node, it has exactly two. Hence the four intersection points coincide in pairs and $\lambda$ is spanned by $q_2=(A,B,0,0)$ and $q_1=(0,0,C,D)$ in some ordering of the coordinates, with $ABCD\ne0$. Writing a point of $\lambda$ as $(sA,sB,rC,rD)$, $e_3=rs\big[AB(C+D)s+CD(A+B)r\big]$, which vanishes identically in $r,s$ if and only if $A+B=0$ and $C+D=0$; that is, $\lambda=\lambda_{ij|kl}$.

\emph{Which planes.} If $H_t\supseteq\{u_i=u_j=0\}$ then $t_k=t_l=0$. On $\lambda_{ij|kl}$, parametrised as above with $A=-B$, $C=-D$, one has $\sum_mt_mu_m=s(t_i-t_j)+r(t_k-t_l)$, which vanishes identically iff $t_i=t_j$ and $t_k=t_l$. The three partitions give $t_1=t_2,\ t_3=t_4$, which is $P$ or $D$; and $t_1=t_3,t_2=t_4$ and $t_1=t_4,t_2=t_3$, both in $D$.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lem:ninelines-bound}
Let $t\in G$ and $\mathcal F_t=\bigotimes_{i=1}^4\mathrm{Kl}_2(t_ih)$ on $\mathbb{G}_{m,h}$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $C_t$ is irreducible and $|a_t|\le2\sqrt q$;
\item $\mathcal F_t$ is tame at $0$, has $\mathrm{Swan}_\infty=\tfrac12\#\{\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}^4:L_\varepsilon\ne0\}\le8$ where $L_\varepsilon=\sum_i\varepsilon_i\sqrt{t_i}$, has no trivial geometric constituent, and $\dim H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathcal F_t)=\mathrm{Swan}_\infty\le8$;
\item $|V(t)|\le8q^{5/2}+1$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
(i) By Proposition~\ref{prop:ninelines}, $C_t$ contains no line, hence is geometrically irreducible. If $C_t$ is smooth, it is a smooth plane cubic with an $\mathbb{F}_q$-rational point, hence an elliptic curve, and Hasse's bound gives $|a_t|\le2\sqrt q$ \cite{Weil}.

Suppose that $C_t$ is singular. Its normalization has genus zero. We verify that the six coordinate-boundary points counted in Lemma~\ref{lem:sigma0-planecubic} are smooth points of the plane section. Consider, for example, the point with $u_3=u_4=0$ and $u_1u_2\ne0$. Since every $t_i$ is nonzero, the equation of $H_t$ determines the unique point
\[
(u_1:u_2:0:0)=(t_2:-t_1:0:0).
\]
At this point
\[
\nabla e_3=(0,0,u_1u_2,u_1u_2),\qquad
\nabla H_t=(t_1,t_2,t_3,t_4).
\]
The two gradients are linearly independent because $t_1,t_2\ne0$ while the first two coordinates of $\nabla e_3$ vanish. Thus the complete intersection $C_t=H_t\cap S$ is smooth at this point. Permuting the coordinates treats the other five boundary points. Therefore every one of the six boundary points is smooth on $C_t$ and lifts to an $\mathbb{F}_q$-rational point of the normalization. The normalization is consequently a smooth projective genus-zero curve with an $\mathbb{F}_q$-point, hence isomorphic to $\mathbb P^1_{\mathbb{F}_q}$. An irreducible singular plane cubic has one singular point, and replacing it by the one or two points above it changes the rational point count by at most one. Hence $|a_t|\le1$ in the singular case, which is stronger than the claimed bound.

(ii) Each $\mathrm{Kl}_2$ is tame at $0$ with unipotent monodromy, and a tensor product of tame representations is tame. At $\infty$, $\mathrm{Kl}_2(t_ih)|_{I_\infty}\cong[2]_*\big(\mathcal{L}_\psi(2\sqrt{t_i}x)\otimes\mathcal L_{\chi_2}\big)$ with $x^2=h$; pulling back along $[2]$ and using $[2]_*[2]^*\mathcal L\cong\mathcal L\oplus\mathcal L^\sigma$ gives $[2]^*\mathcal F_t|_{I_\infty}\cong\bigoplus_{\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}^4}\mathcal{L}_\psi(2L_\varepsilon x)\otimes(\mathrm{tame})$, and the break of $\mathcal{L}_\psi(cx)$ at $x=\infty$ is $1$ for $c\ne0$ and $0$ otherwise, Swan conductors dividing by the degree of the cover. For the trivial constituent: since $t\in G$, some value among the $t_i$ occurs with odd multiplicity; grouping by value, $\mathcal F_t=\bigotimes_v\mathrm{Kl}_2(vh)^{\otimes m_v}$, and the sheaves $\mathrm{Kl}_2(vh)$ for distinct $v$ are pairwise non-isomorphic even up to rank-one twist by Lemma~\ref{lem:kl-nonisom}. Proposition~\ref{prop:kl-independence} then gives the geometric monodromy group of the tuple as $\prod_v\operatorname{SL}_2$ acting through the standard representation in each factor, and the invariants are $\bigotimes_v(\mathrm{std}^{\otimes m_v})^{\operatorname{SL}_2}$, which vanishes because $-I\in\operatorname{SL}_2$ acts on $\mathrm{std}^{\otimes m}$ by $(-1)^m$ and some $m_v$ is odd. Dually the coinvariants vanish, so $h^0_c=h^2_c=0$ and $\chi_c=-\mathrm{Swan}_\infty$ gives $\dim H^1_c=\mathrm{Swan}_\infty$.

(iii) $V(t)=K(0)^4+\sum_{h\ne0}\mathrm{Tr}(\mathrm{Frob}_h|\mathcal F_t)=1-\mathrm{Tr}(\mathrm{Frob}|H^1_c)$ by Grothendieck--Lefschetz and (ii). As $\mathcal F_t$ is pure of weight $4$, $H^1_c$ has weights $\le5$, so $|\mathrm{Tr}|\le\dim H^1_c\cdot q^{5/2}\le8q^{5/2}$.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lem:elliptic-family}
Let $G^\circ\subseteq G$ be the locus where $C_t$ is smooth, $\pi:\mathcal C\to G^\circ$ the resulting family of elliptic curves with section the point $u_1=u_2=0$ of $C_t$, and $R=R^1\pi_*\mathbb{Q}_\ell$: lisse of rank $2$, pure of weight $1$, with $\Lambda^2R\cong\mathbb{Q}_\ell(-1)$ by the Weil pairing and $\mathrm{Tr}(\mathrm{Frob}_t|R)=a_t$. Then $G\setminus G^\circ$ has $O(q^3)$ points; and for $p\ge5$, $R$ is tamely ramified, so $\mathrm{Swan}_\infty(R|_\lambda)=0$ for a generic line $\lambda\subset\mathbb A^4$.
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
$C_t$ is singular if and only if $H_t$ passes through a node of $S$, which forces some $t_i=0$ and is excluded on $G$, or is tangent to $S$, i.e.\ $[t]$ lies on the dual surface $S^\vee\subset(\mathbb P^3)^\vee$. The latter is a proper closed subvariety of dimension $2$, $S$ not being a plane, so it has $O(q^2)$ points of $\mathbb P^3$ and $O(q^3)$ points of the affine cone.

After restricting to a generic affine line, the generic fibre is an elliptic curve over the function field of that line. At every missing point of its smooth locus, the inertia action on $H^1$ is tame when the residue characteristic is $p\ge5$: for multiplicative reduction the action is unipotent and tame, while for potentially good reduction the wild inertia is trivial in residue characteristic at least $5$ (the only possible wild elliptic-curve inertia occurs in characteristics $2$ and $3$). Thus the pullback of $R$ to a generic line has Swan conductor $0$ at infinity.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:coinvariants}
For $k\ge1$ the sheaf $\operatorname{Sym}^kR\otimes\mathcal{L}_\psi(L)$ has no nonzero geometric coinvariants on $G^\circ$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Nonvanishing of the coinvariants is equivalent to $\operatorname{Hom}(\operatorname{Sym}^kR,\mathcal{L}_\psi(-L))\ne0$. A nonzero such morphism is nonzero on a dense open set, hence restricts to a nonzero morphism on a generic line $\lambda=\{t^0+sv\}$ chosen with $L(v)\ne0$ and $[v]\in G^\circ$. On $\lambda$ the sheaf $\mathcal{L}_\psi(-L)$ equals $\mathcal{L}_\psi(-L(t^0)-sL(v))$, which has $\mathrm{Swan}_\infty=1$ since $L(v)\ne0$, whereas $\operatorname{Sym}^kR|_\lambda$ has $\mathrm{Swan}_\infty=0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:elliptic-family}. Swan conductors are additive in short exact sequences and nonnegative, so a quotient of a sheaf with vanishing Swan conductor has vanishing Swan conductor, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{lem:power-sums}
With $\alpha\beta=q$, $\alpha+\beta=a_t$, and $s_k=\sum_{j=0}^k\alpha^j\beta^{k-j}=\mathrm{Tr}(\mathrm{Frob}|\operatorname{Sym}^kR)$: $a_t^2=s_2+q$, $a_t^3=s_3+2qs_1$, $a_t^4=s_4+3qs_2+2q^2$.
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Direct expansion in $\alpha,\beta$ gives $s_2=a_t^2-q$, $s_3=a_t^3-2a_tq$, $s_4=a_t^4-3a_t^2q+q^2$; substituting yields the three identities.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:739}
For $p\ge5$,
\[
\sum_{t\in G}\psi(L(t))V(t)^4=O(q^{13}).
\]
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
On $G$, Lemma~\ref{lem:sigma0-planecubic} gives
\[
V(t)=-q^2(a_t+2+3/q).
\]
Both $G$ and $a_t$ depend only on the projective class $[t]\in\mathbb P^3$: replacing $t$ by $ct$ does not change the plane $H_t$, hence does not change $C_t$ or $a_t$.  For every integer $0\le k\le4$, decompose $G$ into projective rays.  On a ray represented by $[t]$,
\[
\sum_{c\in\mathbb F_q^\times}\psi(cL(t))=
\begin{cases}
q-1,&L(t)=0,\\
-1,&L(t)\ne0.
\end{cases}
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_{t\in G}\psi(L(t))a_t^k
=q\sum_{[t]\in\bar G\cap\{L=0\}}a_{[t]}^k
 -\sum_{[t]\in\bar G}a_{[t]}^k.
\]
The hyperplane $L=0$ has at most $q^2+q+1\le3q^2$ projective points, while $\mathbb P^3(\mathbb F_q)$ has at most $4q^3$ points.  Lemma~\ref{lem:ninelines-bound}(i) gives $|a_t|\le2q^{1/2}$ on $G$, so
\[
\left|\sum_{t\in G}\psi(L(t))a_t^k\right|
\le q(3q^2)(2q^{1/2})^k+(4q^3)(2q^{1/2})^k
\le7\cdot2^kq^{3+k/2}.
\]
Expanding
\[
V(t)^4=q^8(a_t+2+3/q)^4
\]
and applying the preceding estimate term by term, the largest exponent occurs at $k=4$ and is $8+3+2=13$.  This proves the theorem.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:generic-cohomological-check}
Under the same hypotheses one also has the weaker, independent estimate
\[
\sum_{t\in G}\psi(L(t))V(t)^4=O(q^{27/2}).
\]
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
We retain the original cohomological proof as an independent check.  By Lemmas~\ref{lem:sigma0} and~\ref{lem:sigma0-planecubic}, on $G$ we have
\[
V(t)=-q^2a_t-2q^2-3q,
\]
so
\[
V(t)^4=q^8\big(a_t+2+3/q\big)^4=q^8\sum_{k=0}^4\binom{4}{k}(2+3/q)^{4-k}a_t^k,
\]
and it suffices to prove $\sum_{t\in G}\psi(L(t))a_t^k=O(q^{11/2})$ for $0\le k\le4$.

On $G\setminus G^\circ$ we have $|a_t|\le1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:ninelines-bound}(i) and $O(q^3)$ points by Lemma~\ref{lem:elliptic-family}, contributing $O(q^3)$.

On $G^\circ$, expand $a_t^k$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:power-sums} as $\sum_jc_jq^{m_j}s_{k_j}$ with $k_j+2m_j=k$.  For $k_j=0$, the same additive-orthogonality argument as before gives $O(q^{k/2+3})=O(q^5)$.  For $k_j\ge1$ put $\mathcal K_j=\operatorname{Sym}^{k_j}R\otimes\mathcal{L}_\psi(L)$.  Proposition~\ref{prop:coinvariants} kills the top group $H_c^8(G^\circ,\mathcal K_j)$.  Weil II gives weights at most $k_j+i$ on $H_c^i$ for $i\le7$, hence a trace bound $O(q^{(k_j+7)/2})$.  Multiplying by $q^{m_j}=q^{(k-k_j)/2}$ gives
\[
O\!\left(q^{(k+7)/2}\right)\le O(q^{11/2})
\]
for $k\le4$.  The geometric cohomology groups are fixed as $q=p^m$ varies, so the implied constants are independent of $m$.  Thus the required $O(q^{11/2})$ bound follows, and multiplication by $q^8$ gives $O(q^{27/2})$.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{lem:uniformity}
Every step of Theorem~\ref{thm:711} and Lemmas~\ref{lem:diag-eval}--\ref{lem:elliptic-family} is valid over an arbitrary finite extension $\mathbb F_q/\mathbb F_p$ of fixed odd characteristic $p\ge5$, with implied constants independent of $q$.
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
The Kloosterman factorisation and reality of $K$ are orthogonality identities over $\mathbb F_q$. Lemma~\ref{lem:diag-eval} uses only bijective changes of variables in $\mathbb F_q^\times$ and the standard quadratic-character evaluations, valid over every finite field of odd characteristic. The diagonal, degenerate and two-pair estimates use the same identities and exact point counts. Lemma~\ref{lem:sigma0-planecubic} is inclusion--exclusion on $\mathbb P^3(\mathbb F_q)$; Proposition~\ref{prop:ninelines} is geometric and independent of the extension degree; the Hasse bound and the classification of an irreducible singular cubic hold over every $\mathbb F_q$. Finally, in Theorem~\ref{thm:739} the scheme $G^\circ$ and each sheaf $\mathcal K_j$ are defined once over the fixed field $\mathbb F_p$; replacing $q=p^m$ merely replaces the arithmetic Frobenius by its $m$-th power.  The geometric groups $H_c^i(G^\circ_{\overline{\mathbb F}_p},\mathcal K_j)$, and hence their dimensions, do not change with $m$.  The implied constant is therefore literally independent of $q$, with no separate uniform-Betti theorem required.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{lem:complement}
Let $r(h):=\#\{i:h_i\ne0\}$. For $h\in\mathbb{F}_q^4$ with $r=r(h)\le3$, write $h''$ for the tuple of nonzero coordinates. Then $\Sigma_q(h)=(-1)^{4-r}\Sigma_r(h'')$, where $\Sigma_r$ is the $r$-variable member of the same family, and
\[
\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q^4\setminus\mathbb{G}_{m}^4(\mathbb{F}_q)}|\Sigma_q(h)|^4=O(q^7).
\]
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
\emph{The identity.} If $h_{i_1},\dots,h_{i_r}\ne0$ and $h_j=0$ otherwise, the constraint $\sum_ih_iu_i=-\lambda$ involves only $u_{i_1},\dots,u_{i_r}$, so the remaining $4-r$ variables range freely over $\mathbb{F}_q^\times$ and the phase splits; hence
\[
\Sigma_q(h)=\Big(\prod_{j\notin\{i_k\}}\sum_{u_j\ne0}\psi(u_j^{-1})\Big)\cdot\Sigma_r(h'')=(-1)^{4-r}\Sigma_r(h''),
\]
using $\sum_{u\ne0}\psi(u^{-1})=\sum_{v\ne0}\psi(v)=-1$.

\emph{The four cases.} For $r=0$ the constraint reads $0=-\lambda$ with $\lambda\ne0$, so the sum is empty and $\Sigma_q(h)=0$. For $r=1$, say $h_1\ne0$, the constraint forces $u_1=-\lambda/h_1$, a single admissible value, so $|\Sigma_q(h)|=1$; there are $4(q-1)$ such $h$, contributing $O(q)$. For $r=2$, Corollary~\ref{cor:self-lowdim} gives $|\Sigma_2|\ll q^{1/2}$; there are $O(q^2)$ such $h$, contributing $O(q^4)$. For $r=3$, the same corollary gives $|\Sigma_3|\ll q$; there are $O(q^3)$ such $h$, contributing $O(q^7)$.

Adding the four cases gives $O(q^7)$.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:743}
For every finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ of characteristic $p\ge5$, with an implied constant independent of $q$,
\[
\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q^4}|\Sigma_q(h)|^4=2q^{10}+O(q^{9}).
\]
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Theorem~\ref{thm:711} decomposes $q^4\sum_h|\Sigma_q(h)|^4$ over $D\sqcup Z\sqcup P\sqcup G$. Theorems~\ref{thm:716}, \ref{thm:721}, \ref{thm:722}, and~\ref{thm:739} give
\[
2q^{14}+O(q^{13})+O(q^{11})+\big(-q^{13}+O(q^{12})\big)+O(q^{13})
=2q^{14}+O(q^{13}).
\]
Dividing by $q^4$ gives
\[
\sum_{h\in\mathbb F_q^4}|\Sigma_q(h)|^4=2q^{10}+O(q^9),
\]
as asserted. Uniformity is Lemma~\ref{lem:uniformity}; the contribution from $\mathbb{F}_q^4\setminus\mathbb{G}_{m}^4$ is $O(q^7)=o(q^{10})$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:complement}.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:743-sharpened}
The sharp $O(q^9)$ error now comes directly from the projective-ray estimate in Theorem~\ref{thm:739}.  Proposition~\ref{prop:generic-cohomological-check} records the former cohomological argument, which gives the weaker $O(q^{19/2})$ error after normalization and is retained only as an independent check.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:751}
Let $k$ be a finite field of characteristic $p$, let $\ell\ne p$, and let $S/k$ be smooth and geometrically connected of dimension $D\ge1$. Let $\mathcal F$ be a lisse $\mathbb{Q}_\ell$-sheaf on $S$, of rank $r\ge1$ and pure of integer weight $w$. Put $V=\mathcal F_{\bar s}$, and let $G\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be the Zariski closure of the image of $\pi_1^{\mathrm{geom}}(S)$. Then
\[
M_{2n}(G,V)=\limsup_{E/k}S_{2n}(E,\mathcal F),
\qquad
S_{2n}(E,\mathcal F):=(\#E)^{-D-nw}\sum_{x\in S(E)}|\mathrm{Tr}(\mathrm{Frob}_{E,x}|\mathcal F)|^{2n}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
We give the argument in the form used later. Fix an embedding of the coefficient field into $\mathbb C$ and put
\[
\mathcal T_n:=\mathcal F^{\otimes n}\otimes(\mathcal F^\vee)^{\otimes n}.
\]
The sheaf $\mathcal T_n$ is lisse and pure of weight $0$. If $x\in S(E)$ and $q_E=\#E$, purity of $\mathcal F$ gives, for every Frobenius eigenvalue $\alpha$, the identity $\overline\alpha=q_E^w\alpha^{-1}$. Hence
\[
|\mathrm{Tr}(\mathrm{Frob}_x|\mathcal F)|^{2n}
=q_E^{nw}\mathrm{Tr}(\mathrm{Frob}_x|\mathcal T_n),
\]
and therefore
\[
S_{2n}(E,\mathcal F)
=q_E^{-D}\sum_{x\in S(E)}\mathrm{Tr}(\mathrm{Frob}_x|\mathcal T_n).
\tag{\ref{thm:751}.1}
\]
Apply Grothendieck--Lefschetz to the right-hand side. Deligne's weight theorem gives weights at most $i$ on $H_c^i(S_{\bar k},\mathcal T_n)$ because $\mathcal T_n$ has weight $0$. Thus every term with $i<2D$, after multiplication by $q_E^{-D}$, is $O(q_E^{-1/2})$; the implied constant is fixed because the cohomology groups are fixed while $E/k$ varies through finite extensions.

For the top group, Poincar\'e duality gives
\[
H_c^{2D}(S_{\bar k},\mathcal T_n)
\cong (\mathcal T_{n,\bar s})_{\pi_1^{\rm geom}(S)}(-D).
\]
The representation of $\pi_1^{\rm geom}(S)$ on a pure lisse sheaf is semisimple (Lemma~\ref{lem:deligne-semisimple} below), so geometric coinvariants and geometric invariants have the same dimension. Zariski density then gives
\[
\dim(\mathcal T_{n,\bar s})_{\pi_1^{\rm geom}}
=\dim(\mathcal T_{n,\bar s})^{\pi_1^{\rm geom}}
=\dim(V^{\otimes n}\otimes(V^\vee)^{\otimes n})^G
=M_{2n}(G,V).
\]
After the factor $q_E^{-D}$ in (\ref{thm:751}.1), the Tate twist $(-D)$ disappears. Consequently
\[
S_{2n}(E,\mathcal F)=\mathrm{Tr}(F_E|Q)+O(q_E^{-1/2}),
\qquad
Q:=(\mathcal T_{n,\bar s})_{\pi_1^{\rm geom}(S)},
\tag{\ref{thm:751}.2}
\]
where $F_E$ is the arithmetic Frobenius induced on $Q$.

All eigenvalues $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m$ of $F_k$ on $Q$ have complex absolute value $1$: this is the weight-zero assertion for the top quotient. For $E=\mathbb F_{q^a}$, the main term in (\ref{thm:751}.2) is $\sum_j\beta_j^a$. Its absolute value is at most $m=\dim Q$. Conversely, simultaneous Diophantine approximation on the compact torus $(S^1)^m$ supplies integers $a_\nu\to\infty$ for which $\beta_j^{a_\nu}\to1$ for every $j$. Along this subsequence the trace tends to $m$, while the error tends to zero. Hence the limsup is $m=M_{2n}(G,V)$, as claimed. This is the standard proof of Katz's moment principle from the trace formula and Weil II; no additional equidistribution theorem is needed in the present application.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:753}
Let $V$ be a $\mathbb{Q}_\ell$-vector space of dimension $N\ge2$ and $G\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ Zariski-closed reductive.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
\item If $M_4(G,V)\le5$ then $V$ is $G$-irreducible.
\item If $M_4(G,V)=2$ then either $G\supseteq \operatorname{SL}(V)$, or $G/(G\cap\text{scalars})$ is finite.
\item If $V$ is self-dual as a $G$-module and $N\ge3$, then $M_4(G,V)\ge3$. Equivalently, $M_4(G,V)=2$ with $N\ge3$ forces $V\not\cong V^\vee$, and in particular forbids $G\subseteq\mathrm O(V)$ and $G\subseteq\operatorname{Sp}(V)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
We reproduce the group-theoretic argument of Katz's formulation of Larsen's alternative \cite[Thm.~1.1.6]{Katz-Larsen}, together with the elementary self-duality consequence used here.
Extend scalars from $\mathbb{Q}_\ell$ to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$; the moments, irreducibility questions, identity components, and inclusions of algebraic subgroups are unchanged by this extension, so we may work over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero.

For any decomposition $V^{\otimes2}=\bigoplus_i m_iV_i$ into nonzero $G$-modules, complete reducibility and Schur's lemma give
\[
M_4(G,V)=\dim\operatorname{End}_G(V^{\otimes2})\ge\sum_i m_i^2,
\]
with equality exactly when the displayed $V_i$ are pairwise nonisomorphic irreducibles.

For (1), if $V=V_1\oplus V_2$ with both summands nonzero, then
\[
V^{\otimes2}=V_1^{\otimes2}\oplus V_2^{\otimes2}\oplus2(V_1\otimes V_2),
\]
so $M_4(G,V)\ge1+1+2^2=6$, a contradiction.

Assume now $M_4(G,V)=2$. By (1), $V$ is irreducible. The $G$-module
\[
\operatorname{End}(V)=\mathbf1\oplus\operatorname{End}_0(V)=\mathbf1\oplus\operatorname{Lie}(\operatorname{SL}(V))
\]
has two nonzero $G$-stable summands. Since
\[
M_4(G,V)=\dim\operatorname{End}_G(\operatorname{End}(V))=2,
\]
these two summands must be distinct irreducible $G$-modules. Let $G^{\rm der}$ be the derived algebraic subgroup. It lies in $\operatorname{SL}(V)$ and is normal in $G$, hence $\operatorname{Lie}(G^{\rm der})$ is a $G$-stable subspace of the irreducible module $\operatorname{Lie}(\operatorname{SL}(V))$. Thus either
\[
\operatorname{Lie}(G^{\rm der})=\operatorname{Lie}(\operatorname{SL}(V))
\quad\text{or}\quad
\operatorname{Lie}(G^{\rm der})=0.
\]
In the first case $(G^{\rm der})^0=\operatorname{SL}(V)$ and therefore $G\supseteq\operatorname{SL}(V)$. In the second case $G^{\rm der}$ is finite. For fixed $\gamma\in G$, the commutator morphism
\[
G^0\longrightarrow G^{\rm der},\qquad g\longmapsto g\gamma g^{-1}\gamma^{-1},
\]
has connected source and finite target, hence is constant; at $g=1$ it equals $1$. Therefore $G^0\subseteq Z(G)$. Because $V$ is irreducible, Schur's lemma puts $Z(G)$ inside the scalar torus, and so $G^0\subseteq G\cap\{\text{scalars}\}$. The quotient $G/(G\cap\text{scalars})$ consequently has trivial identity component and is a zero-dimensional algebraic group, hence finite. This proves (2).

For (3), $M_4=2$ would first make $V$ irreducible by (1). A nonzero $G$-equivariant isomorphism $V\simeq V^\vee$ is represented, up to scalar, by a nondegenerate bilinear form; transposition and Schur's lemma show that the form is either symmetric or alternating. In the symmetric case
\[
\operatorname{Sym}^2V=\mathbf1\oplus\operatorname{Sym}^2_0V,
\]
with $\operatorname{Sym}^2_0V\ne0$ for $N\ge3$, while $\Lambda^2V\ne0$. Hence $V^{\otimes2}=\operatorname{Sym}^2V\oplus\Lambda^2V$ already contains at least three nonzero $G$-submodules. In the alternating case $N$ is even and at least $4$, and similarly
\[
\Lambda^2V=\mathbf1\oplus\Lambda^2_0V,
\]
with $\Lambda^2_0V\ne0$, while $\operatorname{Sym}^2V\ne0$. Complete reducibility then gives $M_4\ge3$ in either case. Thus $M_4=2$ forbids self-duality.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{lem:deligne-semisimple}
Let $S$ be smooth and geometrically connected over a finite field $k$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a lisse $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$-sheaf, pure of one weight. Then the representation of $\pi_1^{\rm geom}(S)$ on a geometric fibre of $\mathcal F$ is completely reducible. Equivalently, the geometric monodromy group is reductive.
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
We reproduce Deligne's extension-splitting argument in the form recorded by Katz in his Weil~II lectures.  A standard space-filling-curve reduction replaces $S$, after a finite extension of $k$, by a smooth geometrically connected curve $C\to S$ whose pullback of $\mathcal F$ has the same geometric monodromy group.  Thus it is enough to prove semisimplicity on a curve.  We now give that proof in full.

Proceed by induction on the length of a Jordan--H\"older series of $\mathcal F$ as a representation of the arithmetic fundamental group $\pi_1(C)$.  If $\mathcal F$ is arithmetically irreducible, then its restriction to the normal subgroup $\pi_1^{\rm geom}(C)$ is semisimple (the usual Clifford-theoretic normal-subgroup argument), so there is nothing to prove.

Otherwise choose a nonzero arithmetically irreducible lisse subsheaf $\mathcal A\subset\mathcal F$ and put $\mathcal B=\mathcal F/\mathcal A$.  Both $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$ are pure of the same weight as $\mathcal F$: at each closed point their Frobenius eigenvalues occur among those of $\mathcal F$.  By induction their geometric restrictions are semisimple.  It remains to split geometrically
\[
0\longrightarrow\mathcal A\longrightarrow\mathcal F\longrightarrow\mathcal B\longrightarrow0.
\tag{\ref{lem:deligne-semisimple}.1}
\]
Tensor (\ref{lem:deligne-semisimple}.1) with $\mathcal B^\vee$.  The identity of $\mathcal B$ gives a Frobenius-fixed element
\[
\mathbf 1_{\mathcal B}\in
H^0(C_{\bar k},\mathcal B\otimes\mathcal B^\vee).
\]
A geometric splitting of (\ref{lem:deligne-semisimple}.1) is exactly a lift of this element to
$H^0(C_{\bar k},\mathcal F\otimes\mathcal B^\vee)$.  In the long exact cohomology sequence the only obstruction is therefore
\[
\partial(\mathbf 1_{\mathcal B})
 \in H^1(C_{\bar k},\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B^\vee).
\]
The connecting morphism is Frobenius-equivariant, hence this obstruction is Frobenius-fixed.  But $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B^\vee$ is pure of weight $0$, and Weil~II gives weights at least $1$ on its $H^1$ over the smooth curve.  Thus $1$ is not an eigenvalue of Frobenius on that $H^1$, so the fixed obstruction must vanish.  The identity lifts, (\ref{lem:deligne-semisimple}.1) splits geometrically, and the induction closes.

The space-filling-curve reduction and the preceding splitting argument are precisely Deligne's geometric-semisimplicity theorem, in Katz's formulation \cite[pp.~37--38]{Katz-WeilII}.  Notice that the only weight input used after reduction is the strict inequality ``weight $\ge1$'' for $H^1$ of a weight-zero lisse sheaf; no monodromy classification enters.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{rem:selfdual-noncircular}
Part (3) is Katz's \cite[Thm.~1.1.6]{Katz-Larsen}; the mechanism is elementary and worth recalling, since the whole non-circularity of Section~\ref{sec:monodromy} turns on it. There is a $\operatorname{GL}(V)$-invariant, hence $G$-invariant, decomposition $V^{\otimes2}=\operatorname{Sym}^2V\oplus\Lambda^2V$ into two nonzero summands, of dimension $\ge2$ each when $N\ge3$. If $V$ is self-dual, one of the two summands contains a $G$-invariant line (the invariant form), so $V\otimes V^\vee\cong V^{\otimes2}$ acquires a third constituent beyond the two, and $M_4=\dim\mathrm{End}_G(V^{\otimes2})\ge3$.

The consequence used below is that \emph{non-self-duality of $W_n$ is a formal consequence of $M_4(G_{\mathrm{geom}},W_n)=2$ alone}, for every $n$ with $r(n)\ge3$. It requires no classification theorem and, in particular, no prior inclusion $\operatorname{SL}_{r(n)}\subseteqG_{\mathrm{geom}}$. Corollary~\ref{cor:notselfdual-uncond} records this unconditional form. The later Proposition~\ref{prop:7510} is intentionally placed after the $n=4$ monodromy theorem and gives the familiar dimension argument only once the inclusion of $\operatorname{SL}_{10}$ is already known.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:757-general}
Let $n\ge2$ and $p>\max(2,n)$. Then $G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)$ is a reductive algebraic subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}(W_n)$.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Theorem~\ref{thm:self-cohomology-package} proves that $\mathcal W_n$ is lisse and pure on the smooth, geometrically connected torus $\mathbb{G}_{m}^n$. Lemma~\ref{lem:deligne-semisimple} therefore makes the geometric representation semisimple. The Zariski closure of a semisimple representation in characteristic zero is reductive: if its unipotent radical were nontrivial, Lie--Kolchin would produce a nontrivial invariant filtration on some faithful representation, contradicting complete reducibility. This proves the assertion. Finiteness of the determinant and of the scalar intersection is proved separately, and directly from the boundary monodromy, in Proposition~\ref{prop:finite-det-internal}; no such finiteness is needed for the present reductivity statement.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:notselfdual-uncond}
Let $n\ge3$, so that $r(n)\ge5\ge3$, and let $p>\max(2,n)$. Then $W_n\not\cong W_n^\vee$ as a $G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)$-module; in particular $G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)$ is contained in no orthogonal and no symplectic group on $W_n$. The same holds for $n\ge4$ with $r(n)\ge10$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
$G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)$ is reductive by Proposition~\ref{prop:757-general}, and Theorem~\ref{thm:fourthmoment-n} together with Katz's moment theorem, Theorem~\ref{thm:751}, gives $M_4(G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n),W_n)=2$. Since $r(n)\ge3$, Theorem~\ref{thm:753}(3) applies and gives $W_n\not\cong W_n^\vee$. No step uses the Guralnick--Tiep classification or any prior inclusion $\operatorname{SL}_{r(n)}\subseteqG_{\mathrm{geom}}$.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:754}
Let $V$ be as above with $\dim V\ge5$, and let $G\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a closed subgroup whose identity component $G^\circ$ is \emph{reductive}. Then $M_4(G,V)=2$ if and only if one of:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\Alph*)]
\item $G\supseteq\operatorname{SL}(V)$;
\item (\emph{Lie-type case}) $\bar S:=S/Z(S)$ for $S:=F^*(G)$ is $\mathrm{PSp}_{2k}(3)$ or $\mathrm{PSp}_{2k}(5)$ ($k\ge2$) with $V|_S$ a Weil module of dimension $(q^k\pm1)/2$, or $\mathrm{PSU}_k(2)$ ($k\ge4$) with $V|_S$ a Weil module of dimension $(2^k+2(-1)^k)/3$ or $(2^k-(-1)^k)/3$;
\item (\emph{extraspecial case}) $\dim V=\pi^a$ for an odd prime $\pi$, and $F^*(G)=Z(G)E$ for $E$ extraspecial of order $\pi^{1+2a}$;
\item $G$ is finite with $(\dim V,G)$ one of the pairs listed in \cite[Table~I]{GT}.
\end{enumerate}
None of (B)--(D) is confined to $\dim V\le6$: they are dimension-specific finite lists, and must be checked against $r(n)$ directly, not dismissed by a growth-rate heuristic.
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{rem:GT-idea}
Two points require care, and both are easy to get wrong.

\emph{The citation.} It is tempting to assert that Guralnick--Tiep leaves no finite exceptions once $\dim V>6$. That would conflate \cite[Thm.~1.4]{GT}, an $M_8$-matching statement with essentially one exception overall, with \cite[Thm.~1.5]{GT}, the $M_4$-only statement actually available here (the paper computes $M_4=2$ and no more); matching $M_4$ alone is far weaker and Table~I's exceptions are not confined to small dimensions.

\emph{The exclusion mechanism.} One might try to exclude case~(B) by \emph{primitivity} of $W_4$, citing Proposition~\ref{prop:759}. That is circular: the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:759} uses that $\operatorname{SL}_{10}\subseteqG_{\mathrm{geom}}$ is already known (it argues that a $G_{\mathrm{geom}}$-stable decomposition would be stabilized by the connected subgroup $\operatorname{SL}_{10}$, contradicting irreducibility of the \emph{standard representation of $\operatorname{SL}_{10}$}) --- so primitivity is a \emph{consequence} of case~(A) already holding, not an independently available fact that could rule out cases (B)--(D) beforehand. Nothing in this paper establishes primitivity of $W_n$ without first knowing $\operatorname{SL}_{r(n)}\subseteqG_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)$.

The correct mechanism, used from here on, does not need primitivity at all: cases (B), (C), (D) are excluded by \emph{matching the dimension $r(n)$ against their explicit numerical description}, and, where a numerical coincidence survives, by a \emph{determinant-order} argument using only $G_{\mathrm{geom}}$'s definition as a Zariski-closed subgroup and the independent ray-determinant obstruction proved in Proposition~\ref{prop:ray-det-p} --- neither of which presupposes $\operatorname{SL}_{r(n)}\subseteqG_{\mathrm{geom}}$.
