Irreducibility (needed throughout) comes from Larsen's alternative alone, Theorem~\ref{thm:753}(1), since $M_4=2\le5$; this uses no classification and so is available before Theorem~\ref{thm:754} is invoked. Primitivity is derived only \emph{after} the $\operatorname{SL}$-inclusion is known; in rank $10$ this is Proposition~\ref{prop:759}.

What is established below: all three non-$\operatorname{SL}$ cases force \emph{finite} monodromy by Proposition~\ref{prop:BCD-finite}, so the classification step reduces to excluding finite $G_{\mathrm{geom}}$; Corollary~\ref{cor:infinite-suffices} records this reduction. Case (D) is then confined to $n=4,5$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:caseD-complete}, and those two dimensions are excluded by Propositions~\ref{prop:gt-dim10-exclusion} and~\ref{prop:caseD-n5}; the unitary half of case (B) is reduced by Proposition~\ref{prop:caseB-unitary} and the surviving collisions are excluded by Proposition~\ref{prop:caseB-selfdual}; case (C) is reduced by Proposition~\ref{prop:extraspecial-exclusion}, with the prime-rank value $n=127$ closed by Corollary~\ref{cor:n127-closed}; and the symplectic $q=3$ half of case (B) is controlled by Proposition~\ref{prop:caseB-2adic} and Remark~\ref{rem:caseB-residual}. The resulting optional range is stated in Theorem~\ref{thm:monodromy-n-status}.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:BCD-finite}
Let $G\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be closed with $M_4(G,V)=2$ and $\dim V\ge5$, and suppose $G\cap\{\mathrm{scalars}\}$ is finite. If $G$ falls under case \emph{(B)}, \emph{(C)} or \emph{(D)} of Theorem~\ref{thm:754}, then $G$ is finite.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
In case (D), $G$ is finite by definition. In case (B), $F^*(G)=S$ is a finite quasisimple group and $G/Z(G)$ embeds in $\mathrm{Aut}(S/Z(S))$, so $G$ is an extension of a finite group by $Z(G)\subseteq G\cap\{\mathrm{scalars}\}$, which is finite by hypothesis; hence $G$ is finite. In case (C), $F^*(G)=Z(G)E$ with $E$ extraspecial of order $\pi^{1+2a}$, and $G$ lies in the normaliser $N=(EZ)\!:\!\operatorname{Sp}_{2a}(\pi)$ of \cite[\S5]{GT}, so $G/(G\cap\{\mathrm{scalars}\})$ embeds in the finite group $\pi^{2a}\rtimes\operatorname{Sp}_{2a}(\pi)$; again $G$ is finite.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:infinite-suffices}
For every $n$ and every $p>\max(2,n)$ for which $M_4(G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n),W_n)=2$ holds and $r(n)\ge5$: if $G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)$ is infinite, then $G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)\supseteq\operatorname{SL}_{r(n)}$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
Proposition~\ref{prop:finite-det-internal} gives a finite scalar intersection. By Theorem~\ref{thm:754} one of (A)--(D) holds, and Proposition~\ref{prop:BCD-finite} makes each of (B), (C), (D) finite. So an infinite $G_{\mathrm{geom}}$ must satisfy (A).
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:caseD-complete}
Case \emph{(D)} of Theorem~\ref{thm:754} can occur only for $n\in\{4,5\}$.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
The finite groups listed in \cite[Table~I]{GT} occur only in dimensions
\[
6,7,8,10,12,14,18,22,23,24,26,28,45,52,78,133,248,342,1333,
\]
the largest being $1333$.  The sequence
$r(n)=2^n-\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ is strictly increasing for $n\ge2$.  To see this, write $C_n=\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$.  If $n=2m$, then
\[
C_{2m+1}=\frac{2m+1}{m+1}C_{2m},
\qquad
r(2m+1)-r(2m)=2^{2m}-\frac{m}{m+1}C_{2m}>0,
\]
because $C_{2m}\le2^{2m-1}$.  If $n=2m+1$, then
\[
C_{2m+2}=2C_{2m+1},
\qquad
r(2m+2)-r(2m+1)=2^{2m+1}-C_{2m+1}>0,
\]
since $C_{2m+1}<2^{2m+1}$.  In particular
$r(10)=772$ and $r(11)=1586>1333$, so case~(D) can occur only for $4\le n\le10$ within the range relevant here.  Direct evaluation gives
\[
r(4),\ldots,r(10)=10,22,44,93,186,386,772.
\]
Comparing this list with the dimensions in Table~I leaves only $10$ and $22$, i.e. only $n=4$ and $n=5$.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:caseB-unitary}
Let $d$ be the dimension of a Weil module of $\mathrm{PSU}_k(2)$ occurring in case~(B) of Theorem~\ref{thm:754}, so that $3d=2^k+2(-1)^k$ or $3d=2^k-(-1)^k$; in both cases $3d=2^k+e$ with $e\in\{-2,-1,1,2\}$. Then $d=r(n)$ is possible only for $n\in\{2,3,4,5\}$.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
For $n\ge2$ one has $\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\le2^{n-1}$, so $2^{n-1}\le r(n)<2^n$ and therefore
\[
3\cdot2^{n-1}\;\le\;3r(n)\;<\;3\cdot2^n .
\]
If $3r(n)=2^k+e$ with $|e|\le2$ then $2^k\in(3\cdot2^{n-1}-2,\ 3\cdot2^n+2)$. The only power of two in that interval is $2^{n+1}$: indeed $2^n<\tfrac32\cdot2^n$ and $2^{n+2}=4\cdot2^n>3\cdot2^n+2$ for $n\ge2$, while $\tfrac32\cdot2^n<2^{n+1}<3\cdot2^n$. So $k=n+1$, and
\[
3\big(2^n-\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\big)=2^{n+1}+e
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
2^n-3\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}=e\in\{-2,-1,1,2\}.
\]
Write $C_n:=\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ and $f(n):=2^n-3C_n$.  We prove the required monotonicity rather than infer it from the central-binomial ratio.  The exact recurrences
\[
C_{2m+1}=C_{2m}\frac{2m+1}{m+1},\qquad C_{2m+2}=2C_{2m+1}
\]
give
\[
f(2m+2)=2f(2m+1).
\]
Moreover
\[
f(2m+1)-f(2m)
 =4^m-3C_{2m}\frac{m}{m+1}.
\]
For $m=2$ this difference is $16-12=4$.  For $m\ge3$, the sequence
$C_{2m}/4^m$ is decreasing in $m$ and begins at $C_6/4^3=5/16$, whence
\[
3\frac{C_{2m}}{4^m}\frac{m}{m+1}
 \le 3\cdot\frac5{16}\cdot\frac{m}{m+1}<1.
\]
Thus $f(2m+1)>f(2m)$ for every $m\ge2$; together with
$f(2m+2)=2f(2m+1)$ and $f(5)=2>0$, this shows that $f$ is strictly increasing for $n\ge4$.  Its initial values are
\[
f(2)=-2,\quad f(3)=-1,\quad f(4)=-2,\quad f(5)=2,\quad f(6)=4,\quad f(7)=23.
\]
Hence $f(n)\in\{-2,-1,1,2\}$ exactly for $n\in\{2,3,4,5\}$.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:caseB-selfdual}
The two unitary collisions left by Proposition~\ref{prop:caseB-unitary}, at $n=4$ and $n=5$, cannot occur.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
By \cite[Table~II]{GT}, a Weil module of $\mathrm{SU}_k(q)$ of dimension $(q^k+q(-1)^k)/(q+1)$ carries an invariant symplectic form when $k$ is odd and an invariant quadratic form when $k$ is even, i.e.\ its ambient classical group $\mathcal G$ is $\operatorname{Sp}(V)$ resp.\ $\mathrm O(V)$. At $n=4$ the collision is $r(4)=10=(2^5+2(-1)^5)/3$, so $k=5$ is odd and $\mathcal G=\operatorname{Sp}_{10}$; at $n=5$ it is $r(5)=22=(2^6+2(-1)^6)/3$, so $k=6$ is even and $\mathcal G=\mathrm O_{22}$. In both cases $G\subseteq\mathcal G$ forces $W_n\cong W_n^\vee$, contradicting Corollary~\ref{cor:notselfdual-uncond}. Likewise the symplectic family in case~(B) of Theorem~\ref{thm:754} with $q=5$ is excluded outright, since by \cite[Table~II]{GT} a Weil module of $\mathrm{Sp}_{2k}(q)$ with $q\equiv1\!\pmod4$ is self-dual (ambient $\operatorname{Sp}(V)$ or $\mathrm O(V)$).
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{prop:caseB-2adic}
Suppose $r(n)=(3^k\pm1)/2$ for some $k\ge1$, and write $s(\cdot)$ for the binary digit sum and $v_2$ for the $2$-adic valuation. Then, with $C_n:=\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $v_2\big(2r(n)\big)=1+v_2(C_n)$, and by Kummer's theorem $v_2(C_n)=s(n/2)$ for $n$ even and $v_2(C_n)=s\big(\tfrac{n+1}2\big)-1$ for $n$ odd.
\item If $r(n)=(3^k+1)/2$, then $v_2(C_n)\in\{0,1\}$; equivalently $n$ lies in the set
\[
\mathcal E:=\{2^a:a\ge1\}\ \cup\ \{2^a-1:a\ge2\}\ \cup\ \{2^a+2^b-1:a>b\ge1\},
\]
which has density zero, with $O\big((\log N)^2\big)$ elements below $N$.
\item If $r(n)=(3^k-1)/2$ with $k$ odd, then $v_2(C_n)=0$, i.e.\ $n=2^a-1$ for some $a$.
\item If $r(n)=(3^k-1)/2$ with $k$ even, then $v_2(C_n)=1+v_2(k)$.
\end{enumerate}
Moreover $2^n-1\le3^k\le2^{n+1}$ in every case, so $k$ is uniquely determined by $n$; for $n\ge3$ the left inequality is strict, and the endpoint is attained only at $n=2$, where $2r(2)=4=3^1+1$.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
(i) Since $0<C_n<2^n$ we have $v_2(C_n)\le n-1<n$, so $v_2(2^n-C_n)=v_2(C_n)$ and $v_2(2r(n))=1+v_2(C_n)$. The Kummer evaluation follows directly from Kummer's theorem: for $n=2m$, $v_2\binom{2m}{m}$ is the number of carries in $m+m$ base $2$, which is $s(m)$; for $n=2m+1$, $\binom{2m+1}{m}=\tfrac12\binom{2m+2}{m+1}$, so $v_2=s(m+1)-1$.

(ii) The hypothesis is $3^k+1=2r(n)$. Now $3\equiv3\pmod 8$ and $3^2\equiv1\pmod 8$, so $3^k\equiv3$ or $1\pmod8$ according as $k$ is odd or even, whence $v_2(3^k+1)=2$ or $1$ respectively. Comparing with (i), $1+v_2(C_n)\in\{1,2\}$, i.e.\ $v_2(C_n)\le1$. For $n=2m$ even this reads $s(m)\le1$, i.e.\ $m=2^{a-1}$, i.e.\ $n=2^a$; for $n$ odd it reads $s\big(\tfrac{n+1}2\big)\le2$, i.e.\ $\tfrac{n+1}2=2^{a-1}$ or $2^{a-1}+2^{b-1}$, i.e.\ $n=2^a-1$ or $n=2^a+2^b-1$. The counting statement is immediate, since $\mathcal E\cap[1,N]$ is indexed by pairs $(a,b)$ with $2^b<2^a\le2N$.

(iii)--(iv) The hypothesis is $3^k-1=2r(n)$. For $k$ odd, $3^k-1\equiv2\pmod 8$, so $v_2(3^k-1)=1$ and (i) gives $v_2(C_n)=0$, which by (ii)'s dictionary means $s\big(\tfrac{n+1}2\big)=1$, i.e.\ $n=2^a-1$. For $k$ even, the lifting-the-exponent identity at the prime $2$ gives $v_2(3^k-1)=v_2(3-1)+v_2(3+1)+v_2(k)-1=2+v_2(k)$, and (i) gives $v_2(C_n)=1+v_2(k)$.

For the final assertion, $2^{n-1}\le r(n)<2^n$ (the elementary bound used in Proposition~\ref{prop:caseB-unitary}) gives $2^n\le 2r(n)<2^{n+1}$, hence $2^n-1\le3^k\le2^{n+1}$ after subtracting or adding $1$. That window contains at most one power of $3$, since $2^{n+1}/(2^n-1)<3$ for every $n\ge2$; so $k$ is unique. For $n\ge3$ the lower endpoint cannot be attained: $2^n-1\equiv7\pmod8$, whereas $3^k\equiv3$ or $1\pmod 8$ according as $k$ is odd or even. At $n=2$ it is attained, $3^1=2^2-1$, and indeed $r(2)=2=(3^1+1)/2$ is a genuine collision; this endpoint lies outside the range $n\ge4$ of the optional classification theorem proved here.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
\label{rem:caseB-residual}
By \cite[Table~II]{GT}, $3\equiv3\pmod4$ gives ambient $\operatorname{GL}(V)$, so the self-duality obstruction of Corollary~\ref{cor:notselfdual-uncond} does not by itself eliminate this family. Proposition~\ref{prop:caseB-2adic} reduces each fixed $n$ to at most one candidate exponent $k$ in the equations $2r(n)=3^k\pm1$.

For the range actually used in Theorem~\ref{thm:monodromy-n-status}, namely $4\le n\le2{,}097{,}150$, Appendix~\ref{app:computations} gives a direct exact modular verification: the single prime $\pi=2^{61}-1$ rejects every candidate. Thus the optional theorem does not depend on a computation beyond its stated range.

An earlier draft also contained a much broader exploratory sweep.  Because that range is irrelevant to Theorem~\ref{thm:monodromy-n-status}, no numerical claim from the broader sweep is used or retained as evidence here; Appendix~\ref{app:computations} records exactly the finite verification needed for the stated theorem and nothing more.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{prop:ray-det-p}
Let $n\ge2$ and $p>\max(2,n)$.  Write $d$ for the order of the image of the geometric determinant character
\[
\det\mathcal W_n:\pi_1^{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathbb{G}_{m}^n)\longrightarrow\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell^{\,\times}.
\]
Then $p\mid d$.  More precisely, there is a ray
\[
\Delta_a:\mathbb{G}_{m,h}\longrightarrow\mathbb{G}_{m}^n,\qquad
h\longmapsto(a_1h,\ldots,a_nh),
\]
for which the wild part of $\det(\mathcal W_n|_{\Delta_a})$ is a nontrivial Artin--Schreier character of exact order $p$.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
We give the ray calculation because only this divisibility, rather than the full determinant formula, is needed in the optional finite-group check below.

\emph{Step 1: Fourier realization on a ray.}
Put
\[
\mathcal K_a(s):=\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mathrm{Kl}_2(a_is).
\]
The stalk of $\mathcal H_n|_{\Delta_a}$ at $h$ is
\[
H^1_c\!\left(\mathbb{G}_{m,t},\bigotimes_i\mathrm{Kl}_2(a_iht)\otimes\mathcal{L}_\psi(\lambda t)\right).
\]
After the change of variable $s=ht$ this becomes
\[
H^1_c\!\left(\mathbb{G}_{m,s},\mathcal K_a(s)\otimes
\mathcal{L}_\psi((\lambda/h)s)\right).
\]
Thus, with dual coordinate $z=\lambda/h$, the family is the Fourier--Deligne transform of $\mathcal K_a$, followed by the inversion $h=\lambda/z$.  In particular its wild local monodromy at $h=\infty$ is the local Fourier transform from $s=\infty$ to $z=0$ of $\mathcal K_a|_{I_\infty}$.

\emph{Step 2: the slope-$1/2$ summands.}
Choose square roots $b_i^2=a_i$ over $\overline{\mathbb F}_p$ and put
\[
L_\varepsilon=\sum_{i=1}^n\varepsilon_i b_i,
\qquad \varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}^n.
\]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:kl2-local-internal}, after the tame quadratic pullback $s=x^2$ one has, up to tame rank-one factors,
\[
[2]^*\mathcal K_a|_{I_\infty}
 \cong\bigoplus_{\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}^n}
 \mathcal L_\psi(2L_\varepsilon x).
\]
The two terms indexed by $\varepsilon$ and $-\varepsilon$ descend together to a rank-two inertia module $M_{L_\varepsilon}$ of slope $1/2$ and Swan conductor $1$.  We choose $a$ in the nonempty Zariski-open set on which all $L_\varepsilon$ and $\sum_i a_i$ are nonzero.  Then
\[
\mathcal K_a|_{I_\infty}
 \cong\bigoplus_{\{\varepsilon,-\varepsilon\}}M_{L_\varepsilon}
\]
up to tame factors, with $2^{n-1}$ summands.

\emph{Step 3: the local Fourier transform of one summand.}
Theorem~\ref{thm:laumon-local-special} gives
\[
\operatorname{rank}\operatorname{FT}^{(\infty,0)}(M_b)=1,
\qquad
\mathrm{Swan}\operatorname{FT}^{(\infty,0)}(M_b)=1.
\]
Hence its wild part is a rank-one Artin--Schreier character.  We now record the dependence on $b$, which is the only further point needed here.  Let $\pi$ be a uniformizer at $s=\infty$ and write $\pi=u^2$ on the tame quadratic cover.  The wild character is represented by the phase $b/u$ (the harmless factor $2$ is absorbed into $b$).  In local Fourier coordinates the kernel has phase $1/(\pi z)$, so the total phase is
\[
\Phi(u,z)=\frac bu+\frac1{u^2z}.
\]
Its critical equation is
\[
\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial u}
=-\frac b{u^2}-\frac2{u^3z}=0,
\qquad	ext{hence}\qquad
u(z):=u=-\frac2{bz}.
\]
Because $p\ne2$, this critical point is nondegenerate: substituting the critical relation into $\partial^2\Phi/\partial u^2$ gives a nonzero multiple of $b^4z^3$.  The one-dimensional stationary-phase/vanishing-cycle calculation therefore identifies the wild rank-one output with the Artin--Schreier character whose phase is the critical value
\[
\Phi(\nu(z),z)=-\frac{b^2}{4}\,z.
\]
A different normalization of the Fourier kernel multiplies the coefficient by one fixed nonzero scalar $c\in\overline{\mathbb F}_p^\times$, independent of $b$; the crucial facts are that the dependence is $cb^2z$ and that $c\ne0$.  This is also forced by the Swan-$1$ conclusion above: $c=0$ would make the output tame.

\emph{Step 4: determinant of the wild part.}
The determinant of a direct sum is the tensor product of the determinants.  Therefore the wild Artin--Schreier parameter in the determinant of the ray Fourier transform is
\[
c\sum_{\{\varepsilon,-\varepsilon\}}L_\varepsilon^2\,z.
\]
Since $L_{-\varepsilon}^2=L_\varepsilon^2$,
\[
\sum_{\{\varepsilon,-\varepsilon\}}L_\varepsilon^2
=\frac12\sum_{\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}^n}
 \left(\sum_i\varepsilon_i b_i\right)^2
=2^{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2
=2^{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n a_i;
\]
the mixed terms vanish because $\sum_\varepsilon\varepsilon_i\varepsilon_j=0$ for $i\ne j$.  By the choice of $a$ this coefficient is nonzero.

Finally, the lower-weight subsheaf $\mathcal E_n$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:self-cohomology-package} comes from the tame $t=0$ inertia invariants.  Along the ray, rescaling the local parameter $t$ by the units $a_i h$ changes only tame local data; hence $\mathcal E_n|_{\Delta_a}$ has no wild monodromy at $h=\infty$.  Passing from $\mathcal H_n$ to the quotient $\mathcal W_n$ therefore leaves the nontrivial wild determinant character just computed unchanged.  A nontrivial Artin--Schreier rank-one character has image of exact order $p$.  Thus the restriction of $\det\mathcal W_n$ to $\pi_1^{\mathrm{geom}}(\Delta_a)$ has order divisible by $p$, and so does its global image.  Hence $p\mid d$.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{prop:gt-dim10-exclusion}
Let $n=4$, $p\ge5$. Then $G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_4)$ is not (conjugate to) $2.M_{12}$ or $2.M_{22}$ in the representations of \cite[Table~I]{GT} --- the only case-(D) candidates at dimension $10$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:caseD-complete}.
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
Both $2.M_{12}$ and $2.M_{22}$ are quasisimple: $M_{12}$, $M_{22}$ are non-abelian finite simple groups and $2.M_{12}$, $2.M_{22}$ their perfect double covers, listed in \cite[Table~I]{GT} as the full group $G$ itself, so $[2.M_{12},2.M_{12}]=2.M_{12}$ and likewise for $2.M_{22}$. Every homomorphism from a perfect group to an abelian group is trivial; in particular, if $G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_4)$ equalled one of them, the determinant character $\delta=\det\circ\rho$ would be trivial, i.e.\ $d=\mathrm{ord}(\delta)=1$. Proposition~\ref{prop:ray-det-p} proves internally that $p\mid d$. Since $p\ge5>1$, this contradicts $d=1$.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{prop:caseD-n5}
Case \emph{(D)} cannot occur at $n=5$.
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:caseD-complete}, the only Table~I entry in dimension $r(5)=22$ is $\bar S=\mathrm{McL}$ with ambient group $\mathcal G=\mathrm O_{22}$. That forces $W_5\cong W_5^\vee$, contradicting Corollary~\ref{cor:notselfdual-uncond}.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{lem:r127-cert}
The integer
\[
N:=r(127)=158165610439505190298619509827693829853
\]
is prime.
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
We record a complete Pocklington chain.  Set
\[
q=264457377389337124878141757615577.
\]
Then
\[
N-1=2^2\cdot149519\cdot q,\qquad q^2>N.
\]
For each row of the following table, the displayed integer $F$ is a completely factored divisor of $M-1$, satisfies $F^2>M$, and the base $a=2$ satisfies
\[
2^{M-1}\equiv1\pmod M,
\qquad
\gcd\!\bigl(2^{(M-1)/\ell}-1,M\bigr)=1
\quad\text{for every prime }\ell\mid F.
\]
\begin{gather*}
52963-1=2\cdot3\cdot7\cdot13\cdot97,
\qquad F_{52963}=13\cdot97=1261,\\
138445283-1=2\cdot1307\cdot52963,
\qquad F_{138445283}=52963,\\
192366951822841-1=2^3\cdot3\cdot5\cdot11579\cdot138445283,\\
F_{192366951822841}=138445283,\\
1676641-1=2^5\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot499,
\qquad F_{1676641}=7\cdot499=3493,\\
q-1=2^3\cdot7\cdot11\cdot29\cdot953\cdot48163\cdot1676641\cdot192366951822841,\\
F_q=1676641\cdot192366951822841,\\
N-1=2^2\cdot149519\cdot q,
\qquad F_N=q.
\end{gather*}
The primes $7,13,97,499$ are verified directly by trial division up to their square roots.  Starting with the first and fourth rows and proceeding upward through the table, Pocklington's criterion therefore proves successively that
$52963$, $138445283$, $192366951822841$, $1676641$, $q$, and finally $N$ are prime.  Every congruence and gcd displayed above is an exact integer calculation; no probable-prime test is used.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
\label{prop:extraspecial-exclusion}
Case \emph{(C)} of Theorem~\ref{thm:754} requires $r(n)$ to be a power of an odd prime. For $n\ge2$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $r(n)$ is odd if and only if $n=2^s-1$ for some integer $s\ge1$; for every other $n$, $r(n)$ is even and case \emph{(C)} is excluded.
\item Among $n=2^s-1$ with $2\le s\le20$ (that is, $n\le1048575$), $r(n)$ is a prime power exactly for $n=3$ (where $r(3)=5$) and $n=127$ (where $r(127)$ is the prime of Lemma~\ref{lem:r127-cert}). For $s\in\{3,4,5,6\}$ one has the explicit factorisations
\[
\begin{aligned}
r(7)&=3\cdot31, & r(15)&=17\cdot1549,\\
r(31)&=9419\cdot196087, & r(63)&=185849\cdot404009\cdot110635901.
\end{aligned}
\]
For $8\le s\le20$, $r(n)$ is not a prime power; exact witnesses are listed below.
\item Consequently case \emph{(C)} is excluded for every $n\le2097150$ except $n\in\{3,127\}$; $n=3$ lies outside the stated range $n\ge4$ of this split article. The least value of the form $2^s-1$ not covered by (ii) is $2^{21}-1=2097151$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
For (i), if $n=2m$ is even, Kummer's theorem gives
$v_2\binom{2m}{m}\ge1$ for every $m\ge1$ (adding $m+m$ in base two always produces a carry), so $r(2m)$ is even.  If $n=2m+1$ is odd, Kummer's theorem identifies
$v_2\binom{2m+1}{m}$ with the number of carries in the binary addition $m+(m+1)$.  This addition is carry-free exactly when $m=2^t-1$ for some $t\ge0$, equivalently $n=2^{t+1}-1$.  Since $2^n$ is even, $r(n)=2^n-\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ is odd exactly in that case.

For (ii), the cases $s=2$ and $s=7$ give respectively the primes $r(3)=5$ and $r(127)$, the latter by Lemma~\ref{lem:r127-cert}.  The displayed factorizations settle $3\le s\le6$.  For
$s\in\{8,9,12,13,15,16,17,19,20\}$ the table exhibits a prime $q$ with
$q^e\Vert r(n)$ for an exponent $e$ strictly smaller than the exponent that a pure prime power with base $q$ would require: in the rows written $q\mid r(n)$ but $q^2\nmid r(n)$ one has $e=1$ and $r(n)>q$, while at $s=9$ one has $3^2\Vert r(n)$ and $r(n)>3^2$.  Thus $r(n)$ cannot be a power of a single prime.

For $s\in\{10,11,14,18\}$ the displayed Fermat congruence fails.  Hence $r(n)$ is composite.  To exclude a composite perfect prime power, one performs the finite exact test
\[
 a=2,3,\ldots,\lfloor\log_2 r(n)\rfloor:
 \qquad u=\lfloor r(n)^{1/a}\rfloor,
 \quad u^a\ne r(n),\ (u+1)^a\ne r(n).
\]
Integer roots are computed by monotone integer arithmetic (for example, binary search), so this is a deterministic certificate rather than a floating-point test.  No equality occurs in any of the four rows.  This proves (ii).

Finally, if $n\le2097150$ and $r(n)$ is odd, part (i) forces $n=2^s-1$; then necessarily $s\le20$, since $2^{21}-1=2097151$.  Part (ii) therefore leaves only $n=3,127$, proving (iii).
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- proposition-17: body_md -->
\label{prop:kummer-obstruction}
Let $n=2^s-1$ and $q$ an odd prime. If $q$ divides $\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ --- equivalently, by Kummer's theorem, if adding $2^{s-1}-1$ and $2^{s-1}$ in base $q$ produces at least one carry --- then $q\nmid r(n)$.
<!-- end proposition-17 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
$r(n)=2^n-\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\equiv2^n\pmod q$, and $q\nmid2^n$ since $q$ is odd.
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
\label{rem:kummer-ceiling}
Proposition~\ref{prop:kummer-obstruction} explains why the range in Theorem~\ref{thm:monodromy-n-status} cannot be extended by the obvious device of looking for a small prime factor of $r(n)$, and it is the reason we state a ceiling rather than a theorem. The carry condition is satisfied by more and more primes as $s$ grows: among the $45$ odd primes below $200$, the number that divide $\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$, hence cannot divide $r(n)$, is $30$ at $s=8$, $39$ at $s=20$, $44$ at $s=40$, and all $45$ for every $s$ with $54\le s\le400$, the range we checked; below $54$ the count is not monotone in $s$, the last shortfall occurring at $s=53$. So for large $s$ the integer $r(2^s-1)$ is coprime to every small prime for a structural reason, and exhibiting two distinct prime divisors --- the cheapest way to rule out a prime power --- requires factoring a number with more than $10^4$ digits whose factors are all large. Deciding whether $r(2^s-1)$ is a prime power for all $s$ therefore appears to be a genuine Diophantine question, of the same character as deciding primality in a sparse exponential family, and not one this paper's methods reach. By Corollary~\ref{cor:infinite-suffices} it can be bypassed entirely: a proof that $G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)$ is infinite removes the need to know anything about the arithmetic of $r(n)$.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- proposition-18: body_md -->
\label{prop:tame-abelian}
Let $U=\mathbb{G}_{m}^n$ over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$ and let $G$ be a finite quotient of $\pi_1^{\mathrm{geom}}(U)$. Then every quotient of $G$ of order prime to $p$ is abelian.
<!-- end proposition-18 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
A connected finite \'etale cover of a torus over an algebraically closed field, of degree prime to the characteristic, is an isogeny of tori; equivalently, all such covers are Kummer covers $x\mapsto x^m$ with $\gcd(m,p)=1$. Hence the maximal prime-to-$p$ quotient of $\pi_1^{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathbb{G}_{m}^n)$ is $\big(\widehat{\mathbb Z}^{(p')}\big)^n$, which is abelian. A quotient of $G$ of order prime to $p$ is in particular a prime-to-$p$ quotient of $\pi_1^{\mathrm{geom}}(U)$, hence a quotient of that abelian group.
<!-- end proof-54 -->
<!-- proposition-19: body_md -->
\label{prop:wild-criterion}
Let $n\ge2$, $p>\max(2,n)$, and suppose $G:=G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)$ is finite. Let $P$ denote the image in $G$ of the wild inertia group at $h=\infty$ along a coordinate line on which $\mathcal W_n$ has positive Swan conductor and a nonzero slope-$0$ part. Then
\[
p\ \big|\ \big[G:G\cap\{\mathrm{scalars}\}\big].
\]
<!-- end proposition-19 -->
<!-- proof-55: body_md -->
The argument is elementary once the local break decomposition is known. The group $P$ is a nontrivial finite $p$-group: it is the image of wild inertia, hence of a pro-$p$ group, and it is nontrivial because the chosen line has positive Swan conductor. For the coordinate lines used later, positivity follows internally from Theorem~\ref{thm:swan-total}. Write $W_n|_P=\mathbf1^{\oplus a_0}\oplus\bigoplus_j\xi_j$ with $a_0\ge1$ the dimension of the slope-$0$ part and the $\xi_j$ the nontrivial characters occurring there. We do not need $W_n|_P$ to decompose into characters: it suffices that the slope-$0$ part contributes the eigenvalue $1$ and that some element acts with an eigenvalue $\ne1$. Choose $g\in P$ acting nontrivially on $W_n$ and let $\zeta\ne1$ be an eigenvalue of $g$; such $g$ and $\zeta$ exist since $P\ne1$ acts faithfully on the wild part.

Then $g$ has the eigenvalue $1$ on $W_n$, coming from the slope-$0$ part, and also the eigenvalue $\zeta\ne1$; in particular $g$ is not scalar. Let $k\ge1$ be the order of the image of $g$ in $\bar G:=G/(G\cap\{\mathrm{scalars}\})$, i.e.\ the least $k$ with $g^k$ scalar. Comparing the two eigenvalues of $g^k$, which must agree since $g^k$ is scalar, gives $\zeta^k=1$. As $P$ is a $p$-group, $\zeta$ is a root of unity of $p$-power order and is $\ne1$, so its order is divisible by $p$; hence $p\mid k$. Since $k$ divides $|\bar G|$, the claim follows.
<!-- end proof-55 -->
<!-- proposition-20: body_md -->
\label{prop:caseC-dickson}
In case \emph{(C)} of Theorem~\ref{thm:754} with $a=1$ and $\pi\ge7$, the image $H$ of $\bar G$ in $\operatorname{Sp}_2(\pi)=\operatorname{SL}_2(\pi)$ is all of $\operatorname{SL}_2(\pi)$; equivalently $\bar G=(\mathbb Z/\pi)^2\rtimes\operatorname{SL}_2(\pi)$.
<!-- end proposition-20 -->
<!-- proof-56: body_md -->
Restricted to the extraspecial subgroup $E$, the module $W_n\otimes W_n^\vee$ is the direct sum of the $\pi^2$ characters of $E/Z(E)$, each with multiplicity one. The quotient $H$ permutes these characters and fixes the trivial one. Therefore $M_4=2$ says that $H$ has exactly two orbits on the character group, so it is transitive on the $\pi^2-1$ nonzero characters. Hence $(\pi^2-1)\mid|H|$; and $|H|$ divides $|\operatorname{SL}_2(\pi)|=\pi(\pi^2-1)$. Hence $|H|=\pi^2-1$ or $\pi(\pi^2-1)$. Suppose $|H|=\pi^2-1$. Then $\pi\nmid|H|$, so by Dickson's classification of the subgroups of $\operatorname{SL}_2(\pi)$ \cite{Dickson} a subgroup of order prime to $\pi$ is cyclic, binary dihedral of order dividing $2(\pi\pm1)$, or one of $\operatorname{SL}_2(3)$, $2.S_4$, $\operatorname{SL}_2(5)$, of order at most $120$. All of these have order at most $\max\big(120,\,2(\pi+1)\big)$, which is less than $\pi^2-1$ for $\pi\ge7$. So $|H|=\pi(\pi^2-1)$ and $H=\operatorname{SL}_2(\pi)$.
<!-- end proof-56 -->
<!-- proposition-21: body_md -->
\label{prop:caseC-congruence}
Suppose $r(n)=\pi^a$ with $\pi$ an odd prime, and suppose $G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)$ falls under case \emph{(C)} of Theorem~\ref{thm:754}. Then
\[
p\ \big|\ \pi\cdot\big|\operatorname{Sp}_{2a}(\pi)\big| .
\]
In particular, for $a=1$ this reads $p=\pi$ or $p\mid\pi^2-1$.
<!-- end proposition-21 -->
<!-- proof-57: body_md -->
Write $G=G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)$, which is finite by Proposition~\ref{prop:BCD-finite}, and $\bar G:=G/(G\cap\{\mathrm{scalars}\})$. By case (C), $F^*(G)=Z(G)E$ with $E$ extraspecial of order $\pi^{1+2a}$, so $\bar G$ contains $\bar E:=E/Z(E)\cong(\mathbb Z/\pi)^{2a}$ as a normal subgroup, and $\bar G/\bar E$ embeds in $\operatorname{Sp}_{2a}(\pi)$; call its image $H$. Thus $|\bar G|$ divides $\pi^{2a}\big|\operatorname{Sp}_{2a}(\pi)\big|$.

Restricted to $E$, the module $W_n\otimes W_n^\vee$ is the direct sum of the $\pi^{2a}$ characters of $\bar E$, each occurring exactly once; this is the standard decomposition for the unique faithful irreducible module of an extraspecial group. The group $G$ permutes these characters through $H$, fixing the trivial one, so
\[
M_4(G,W_n)=\dim\mathrm{End}_G\big(W_n\otimes W_n^\vee\big)=\#\{\text{$H$-orbits on the $\pi^{2a}$ characters}\}.
\]
Since $M_4(G,W_n)=2$, the group $H$ is transitive on the $\pi^{2a}-1$ nontrivial characters. A group acting transitively on the nonzero vectors of a nonzero $\mathbb F_\pi$-space has no nonzero fixed vector there, so the coinvariants $(\bar E)_H$ vanish and $[\bar G,\bar G]\supseteq\bar E\ne1$. Hence $\bar G$ is non-abelian.

Now $\bar G$ is a finite quotient of $G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)$, hence of $\pi_1^{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathbb{G}_{m}^n)$. If $p$ did not divide $\pi^{2a}|\operatorname{Sp}_{2a}(\pi)|$ it would not divide $|\bar G|$, and Proposition~\ref{prop:tame-abelian} would force $\bar G$ abelian, a contradiction. So $p\mid\pi^{2a}|\operatorname{Sp}_{2a}(\pi)|$, and since $p\mid\pi^{2a}$ only when $p=\pi$, the stated divisibility follows.
<!-- end proof-57 -->
<!-- proposition-22: body_md -->
\label{prop:weil-fixed}
Assume case \emph{(C)} of Theorem~\ref{thm:754} with $a=1$, so $r(n)=\pi$ and $\bar G=(\mathbb Z/\pi)^2\rtimes\operatorname{SL}_2(\pi)$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:caseC-dickson}. Let $g\in G$ be any non-scalar element and let $k\ge2$ be the order of its image in $\bar G$. Then every eigenvalue of $g$ on $W_n$ occurs with multiplicity at most
\[
\frac\pi k+\sqrt\pi .
\]
If, moreover, $g$ is supplied by wild inertia as in Proposition~\ref{prop:wild-criterion}, then $p\mid k$ and $\dim W_n^{\,g}\le \pi/p+\sqrt\pi$.
<!-- end proposition-22 -->
<!-- proof-58: body_md -->
Let $\chi$ be the character of $W_n$ and $N$ the order of $g$. For $x\in G$ we bound $|\chi(x)|$ by cases on the image $\bar x$. If $x$ is scalar, $|\chi(x)|=\pi$. If $\bar x$ lies in $\bar E=E/Z(E)$ and is nontrivial, then $x\in EZ\setminus Z$ and $\chi(x)=0$, since the character of the unique faithful irreducible module of an extraspecial group vanishes off the centre. Otherwise $\bar x$ has nontrivial image $\bar h\ne1$ in $\operatorname{Sp}_2(\pi)$, and the standard character formula for the Weil module of the extraspecial normaliser (the setting of \cite[\S5]{GT}) gives $|\chi(x)|^2=\#\{v\in\mathbb F_\pi^2:\bar hv=v\}$. As $\bar h\in\operatorname{SL}_2(\pi)$ is nontrivial, its fixed space in $\mathbb F_\pi^2$ has dimension at most $1$, so $|\chi(x)|\le\sqrt\pi$.

Now $g^i$ is scalar exactly when $k\mid i$, so among $i=0,\dots,N-1$ there are $N/k$ indices with $|\chi(g^i)|=\pi$ and $N-N/k$ with $|\chi(g^i)|\le\sqrt\pi$. For an eigenvalue $\zeta$ of $g$,
\[
m_\zeta=\frac1N\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\chi(g^i)\zeta^{-i},
\qquad
|m_\zeta|\le\frac1N\Big(\frac Nk\pi+\Big(N-\frac Nk\Big)\sqrt\pi\Big)=\frac\pi k+\Big(1-\frac1k\Big)\sqrt\pi\le\frac\pi k+\sqrt\pi .
\]
<!-- end proof-58 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:caseC-criterion}
Assume that case \emph{(C)} of Theorem~\ref{thm:754} holds with $a=1$, and suppose that for some line $\ell$ the tame \emph{(}slope-$0$\emph{)} part of $W_n|_\ell$ at $\infty$ has dimension
\[
\dim\big(W_n|_\ell\big)^{P}\;>\;\frac{r(n)}p+\sqrt{r(n)} ,
\]
where $P$ is the image of wild inertia. Then case \emph{(C)} is impossible. Consequently, whenever cases \emph{(B)} and \emph{(D)} have already been excluded, one must be in case \emph{(A)}, and $G^0_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)=\operatorname{SL}_{r(n)}$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-59: body_md -->
Proposition~\ref{prop:wild-criterion} produces a non-scalar $g\in P$ whose image in $\bar G$ has order divisible by $p$, and $\big(W_n|_\ell\big)^{P}\subseteq W_n^{\,g}$. Proposition~\ref{prop:weil-fixed} then gives $\dim W_n^{\,g}\le r(n)/p+\sqrt{r(n)}$, contradicting the displayed strict inequality. Thus case \emph{(C)} is impossible. The final assertion follows from the exhaustive alternatives in Theorem~\ref{thm:754}.
<!-- end proof-59 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{lem:tame-from-break}
Let $V$ be a representation of the inertia group at $\infty$, of dimension $N$, and let $\beta_{\min}$ denote the smallest nonzero break of $V$ and $S=\mathrm{Swan}_\infty(V)$. Then the wild part has $\dim V^{\mathrm{wild}}\le S/\beta_{\min}$, and hence
\[
\dim V^{P}\ \ge\ N-\frac{S}{\beta_{\min}} .
\]
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-60: body_md -->
Write the break decomposition $V=\bigoplus_\alpha V(\alpha)$. Then $S=\sum_{\alpha>0}\alpha\dim V(\alpha)\ge\beta_{\min}\sum_{\alpha>0}\dim V(\alpha)=\beta_{\min}\dim V^{\mathrm{wild}}$, and $V^{P}=V(0)$ has dimension $N-\dim V^{\mathrm{wild}}$.
<!-- end proof-60 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:n127-criterion}
Let $\ell$ be a coordinate line and let $\beta_{\min}$ and $S=\mathrm{Swan}_\infty(\mathcal W_{127}|_\ell)$ be as above, so that $S=2^{126}$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:swan-total}. If
\begin{equation}\label{eq:n127-criterion}
\frac{S}{\beta_{\min}}\ <\ r(127)-\frac{r(127)}p-\sqrt{r(127)},
\end{equation}
then $G^0_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_{127})=\operatorname{SL}_{r(127)}$. In particular, for every prime $p>127$ the right-hand side of~\eqref{eq:n127-criterion} exceeds $1.569\cdot10^{38}$, so:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item if every nonzero break of $\mathcal W_{127}|_\ell$ at $\infty$ is at least $1$, the criterion holds, since then $S/\beta_{\min}\le2^{126}<8.51\cdot10^{37}$, and $n=127$ is closed for every $p>127$;
\item if the smallest nonzero break is $\tfrac12$, the criterion holds precisely when $S<7.84\cdot10^{37}$, that is when $\mathrm{Swan}_\infty<0.922\cdot2^{126}$, equivalently $\mathrm{Swan}_0>0.078\cdot2^{126}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-61: body_md -->
Combine Lemma~\ref{lem:tame-from-break} with Corollary~\ref{cor:caseC-criterion}: the former gives $\dim\big(\mathcal W_{127}|_\ell\big)^{P}\ge r(127)-S/\beta_{\min}$, and hypothesis~\eqref{eq:n127-criterion} makes this exceed $r(127)/p+\sqrt{r(127)}$, which excludes case (C). At $n=127$, case (D) is excluded by Proposition~\ref{prop:caseD-complete}, while the unitary case-(B) alternatives are excluded by Propositions~\ref{prop:caseB-unitary}--\ref{prop:caseB-selfdual}; the $q=3$ symplectic alternative is covered by the exact finite verification in Appendix~\ref{app:computations}. The numerical statements are exact integer computations with $r(127)=2^{127}-\binom{127}{63}$ and $p\ge131$.
<!-- end proof-61 -->
<!-- proposition-23: body_md -->
\label{prop:higher-moments}
Let $G\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be finite with $V$ irreducible of dimension $N$, and set $\bar G=G/(G\cap\{\mathrm{scalars}\})$. Then for every $k\ge1$
\[
M_{2k}(G,V)\ \ge\ \frac{N^{2k}}{|\bar G|}.
\]
If moreover $G$ falls under case \emph{(C)} of Theorem~\ref{thm:754} with $a=1$, so that $N=\pi$ is prime and $\bar G=(\mathbb Z/\pi)^2\rtimes\operatorname{SL}_2(\pi)$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:caseC-dickson}, then $|\bar G|=\pi^3(\pi^2-1)$ and
\[
M_6(G,V)\ \ge\ \frac{\pi^3}{\pi^2-1}\ >\ \pi,
\qquad
M_8(G,V)\ \ge\ \frac{\pi^5}{\pi^2-1}\ >\ \pi^3 .
\]
<!-- end proposition-23 -->
<!-- proof-62: body_md -->
For finite $G$ one has $M_{2k}(G,V)=\dim\big(V^{\otimes k}\otimes\overline V^{\otimes k}\big)^G=\frac1{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}|\chi(g)|^{2k}$, where $\chi$ is the character of $V$. Discarding all terms except the scalar ones, and noting that a scalar $g=\lambda\cdot\mathrm{id}$ has $|\chi(g)|=N$, the $|G\cap\{\mathrm{scalars}\}|$ scalar elements contribute
\[
\frac{|G\cap\{\mathrm{scalars}\}|\cdot N^{2k}}{|G|}=\frac{N^{2k}}{|\bar G|},
\]
which gives the first inequality since every term is non-negative. The two displayed consequences follow by substituting $|\bar G|=\pi^2\cdot|\operatorname{SL}_2(\pi)|=\pi^2\cdot\pi(\pi^2-1)$ and $N=\pi$.
<!-- end proof-62 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:n127-moment}
Suppose
\[
M_6\big(G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_{127}),W_{127}\big)\ <\ r(127)=158165610439505190298619509827693829853 .
\]
Then $G^0_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_{127})=\operatorname{SL}_{r(127)}$ for \emph{every} prime $p>127$, with no residual set of characteristics.
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- proof-63: body_md -->
At $n=127$, case (D) is excluded by Proposition~\ref{prop:caseD-complete}, while the unitary case-(B) alternatives are excluded by Propositions~\ref{prop:caseB-unitary}--\ref{prop:caseB-selfdual}; the $q=3$ symplectic alternative is covered by the exact finite verification in Appendix~\ref{app:computations}. If case (C) held, then $G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_{127})$ would be finite by Proposition~\ref{prop:BCD-finite}, with $W_{127}$ irreducible of prime dimension $\pi=r(127)$, and Proposition~\ref{prop:higher-moments} would give $M_6>\pi$, contrary to hypothesis. Hence case (A) holds in Theorem~\ref{thm:754}, giving the stated special-linear identity component. No step refers to $p$.
<!-- end proof-63 -->
<!-- proposition-24: body_md -->
\label{prop:no-interpolation}
Within Larsen--Guralnick--Tiep's alternatives, the value $M_4=2$ does not distinguish the special-linear branch from the extraspecial branch. More precisely, at $N=r(127)$ the special-linear branch has $M_6=6$, whereas case \emph{(C)}, if it occurred, would satisfy $M_6>N$. Thus a sixth-moment input carries genuinely new information not contained in the equality $M_4=2$.
<!-- end proposition-24 -->
<!-- proof-64: body_md -->
Give $G$ the uniform measure and set $X(g)=|\chi(g)|^2$, so that $M_{2k}=\mathbb E[X^k]$ and $M_2=\mathbb E[X]=1$ by irreducibility. In case (C) the scalars form an atom of mass $1/|\bar G|=1/\big(\pi^3(\pi^2-1)\big)$ carrying the value $X=\pi^2$. Its contribution to $M_{2k}$ is $\pi^{2k}/|\bar G|$, namely
\[
6.3\cdot10^{-39}\ \ (k=2),\qquad 1.58\cdot10^{38}\ \ (k=3).
\]
So a single atom, of mass $\pi^{-5}$, is invisible in the fourth moment and dominant in the sixth. Case (A) has $M_4=2$, $M_6=6$; case (C) has $M_4=2$ (by hypothesis) and $M_6>\pi$. Hence $M_4$ does not determine $M_6$.
<!-- end proof-64 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
\label{rem:moment-route}
Proposition~\ref{prop:no-interpolation} explains the situation exactly: the fourth moment cannot exclude case (C) for a structural reason, not for want of effort, and the sixth is the first moment used here in which the scalar atom becomes visible. It also shows that no soft inequality will substitute for computing $M_6$.

The computation itself is the six-variable analogue of Section~\ref{sec:monodromy}, and the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:decouple} extends verbatim to every even moment: with $L_6(t)=\lambda(t_1-t_2+t_3-t_4+t_5-t_6)$ and $V_6(t)=\sum_hK(t_1h)\cdots K(t_6h)$,
\[
q^6\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q^n}\big|\Sigma_n(h)\big|^6=\sum_{t\in\mathbb{F}_q^6}\psi\big(L_6(t)\big)\,V_6(t)^n .
\]
Two features make this more tractable than one might expect, and they determine where the remaining work lies.

\emph{The main term is forced by a matching count.} Write $\mathcal K_t=\bigotimes_{j=1}^6[\times t_j]^*\mathrm{Kl}_2$, of rank $64$ and weight $6$ on $\mathbb{G}_{m}$, whose trace function is the integrand of $V_6$. Then $V_6(t)=m(t)q^4+O(q^{7/2})$, where $m(t)=\dim(\mathcal K_t)_{\pi_1^{\mathrm{geom}}}$ is the dimension of geometric coinvariants, by the Grothendieck--Lefschetz trace formula; the term $m(t)q^4$ is the contribution of $H^2_c$ and the error is the Weil bound on $H^1_c$. Since $\mathrm{Kl}_2$ is self-dual, $[\times a]^*\mathrm{Kl}_2\otimes[\times b]^*\mathrm{Kl}_2$ has invariants precisely when $a=b$, and a pairing $i\sim j$ with $t_i=t_j$ annihilates $L_6$ precisely when the positions $i,j$ carry opposite signs in $L_6$. The perfect matchings between $\{1,3,5\}$ and $\{2,4,6\}$ number $3!=6$, each contributing a three-dimensional stratum, which agrees with Lemma~\ref{lem:m6-SL}: $M_6(\operatorname{SL}(V),V)=6$.

\emph{The error is amplified favourably by $n$.} On the strata where $m(t)=0$ one has $|V_6(t)|\ll q^{7/2}$, so their total contribution after normalisation is $O\big(C^nq^{7n/2-4n+3}\big)=O\big(C^nq^{3-n/2}\big)$, which tends to $0$ for every $n\ge7$; the gap between $q^4$ and $q^{7/2}$ is raised to the $n$-th power. Strata of lower dimension with $m(t)\ge2$ --- for instance $t_1=\cdots=t_6$, where $m=5$ --- carry factors $m(t)^n$, but they are of dimension $1$ or $2$ against the three-dimensional main stratum, so they contribute $O(m^nq^{-1})$ and vanish in the limit $q\to\infty$ at fixed $n$. This is the opposite of the situation at $M_4$, where the saving $\delta(n)=\min(1,(n-2)/2)$ has to be extracted with care.

The classification of the strata with $m(t)\ge1$ is supplied by Proposition~\ref{prop:kl-independence} and the Temperley--Lieb invariant count. If the distinct nonzero dilation values have even multiplicities $\mu_i$, then
\[
m(t)=\prod_i\mathrm{Cat}(\mu_i/2).
\]
On degenerate strata no such classification is needed: the bound $|V_6(t)|\ll q^{(8-s)/2}$ for $s$ vanishing coordinates already makes their normalized contribution tend to zero. This is substantially lighter than the four-factor coinvariant analysis of Section~\ref{sec:monodromy}, where the Cayley cubic, its nine lines, and the elliptic family $C_t$ enter. The complete assembly is Theorem~\ref{thm:m6}, and Corollary~\ref{cor:n127-closed} closes $n=127$ for every $p>127$.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{lem:kl-nonisom}
Let $p>2$ and $a,b\in\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p^\times$. If $[\times a]^*\mathrm{Kl}_2\cong[\times b]^*\mathrm{Kl}_2\otimes\mathcal L$ as $\pi_1^{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathbb{G}_{m})$-representations for some rank-one $\mathcal L$ of finite order, then $a=b$.
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-65: body_md -->
Both sides are lisse of rank $2$ on $\mathbb{G}_{m}$, so compare their local representations at $\infty$. The local calculation of Theorem~\ref{thm:kl2-local-internal} gives
\[
\mathrm{Kl}_2|_{I_\infty}\cong[2]_*\bigl(\mathcal L_\psi(2y)\otimes\mathcal L_{\chi_2}(y)\bigr),\qquad y^2=x,
\]
with both breaks equal to $\tfrac12$ and $\mathrm{Swan}_\infty(\mathrm{Kl}_2)=1$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:kl2-local-internal}. Pulling back by $[\times c]$ replaces the two Artin--Schreier parameters after the tame quadratic cover by $\pm2c^{1/2}$.

We first show that the finite-order rank-one twist $\mathcal L$ is tame at $\infty$. By Hasse--Arf, a wild rank-one character has an integral positive break $b\ge1$. Since $b\ne\tfrac12$, the unequal-break tensor lemma implies that every break of $[\times b]^*\mathrm{Kl}_2\otimes\mathcal L$ would then equal $b$, and its Swan conductor would be $2b\ge2$, contradicting the Swan conductor $1$ of $[\times a]^*\mathrm{Kl}_2$. Thus $\mathcal L$ is tame.

After pullback by the tame double cover $[2]$, tensoring by $\mathcal L$ changes only the tame factor and cannot change the wild Artin--Schreier parameters. Hence the unordered parameter sets
\[
\{2a^{1/2},-2a^{1/2}\}\quad\text{and}\quad\{2b^{1/2},-2b^{1/2}\}
\]
must coincide. Therefore $a^{1/2}=\pm b^{1/2}$ and hence $a=b$.
<!-- end proof-65 -->
<!-- proposition-25: body_md -->
\label{prop:kl-independence}
Let $p>2$ and let $a_1,\dots,a_r\in\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p^\times$ be pairwise distinct. Then
\[
G_{\mathrm{geom}}\Big(\bigoplus_{i=1}^r[\times a_i]^*\mathrm{Kl}_2\Big)=\operatorname{SL}_2^{\,r}.
\]
Consequently, for multiplicities $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_r\ge1$,
\[
\dim\Big(\bigotimes_{i=1}^r\big([\times a_i]^*\mathrm{Kl}_2\big)^{\otimes\mu_i}\Big)^{\pi_1^{\mathrm{geom}}}=\prod_{i=1}^r\dim\big(V_2^{\otimes\mu_i}\big)^{\operatorname{SL}_2}=\prod_{i=1}^rc(\mu_i),
\]
where $c(\mu)=0$ for $\mu$ odd and $c(\mu)=\mathrm{Cat}(\mu/2)$ for $\mu$ even.
<!-- end proposition-25 -->
<!-- proof-66: body_md -->
Let $G\subseteq\operatorname{SL}_2^{\,r}$ be the Zariski closure of the image. Each projection $G\to\operatorname{SL}_2$ is surjective by Proposition~\ref{prop:kl2-sl2-internal}, since $[\times a_i]$ is an automorphism of $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ and therefore does not change the geometric monodromy image. Suppose $G\ne\operatorname{SL}_2^{\,r}$. Since $\operatorname{SL}_2$ is quasi-simple, Goursat's lemma applied to the projection of $G$ to a pair of factors $i\ne j$ produces, for some such pair, a common nontrivial quotient of the two copies of $\operatorname{SL}_2$ and hence an isomorphism identifying them; as $\operatorname{SL}_2$ has no outer automorphisms as an algebraic group and its standard representation is unique up to isomorphism, this forces $[\times a_i]^*\mathrm{Kl}_2\cong[\times a_j]^*\mathrm{Kl}_2\otimes\mathcal L$ for some rank-one $\mathcal L$ of finite order, the twist accounting for the case in which the common quotient is $\mathrm{PSL}_2$ rather than $\operatorname{SL}_2$. Lemma~\ref{lem:kl-nonisom} then gives $a_i=a_j$, a contradiction. Hence $G=\operatorname{SL}_2^{\,r}$.

For the second statement, $\bigotimes_i\big([\times a_i]^*\mathrm{Kl}_2\big)^{\otimes\mu_i}$ is $\bigotimes_iV_2^{\otimes\mu_i}$ as a representation of $\operatorname{SL}_2^{\,r}$, with the $i$-th factor acting through the $i$-th copy, so the invariants factor. Finally $\dim(V_2^{\otimes\mu})^{\operatorname{SL}_2}$ is the multiplicity of the trivial representation in $V_2^{\otimes\mu}$.  It is $0$ for $\mu$ odd because the central element $-I$ acts by $(-1)^\mu$.  If $\mu=2m$, Lemma~\ref{lem:self-cg} shows that the trivial block $V_1$ occurs with multiplicity
\[
\binom{2m}{m}-\binom{2m}{m-1}
=\frac1{m+1}\binom{2m}{m}=\mathrm{Cat}(m).
\] Since $\operatorname{SL}_2$ is reductive, invariants and coinvariants have the same dimension.
<!-- end proof-66 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{lem:m6-SL}
For $N\ge3$ and $V$ the standard representation, $M_6(\operatorname{SL}_N,V)=\dim\mathrm{End}_{\operatorname{SL}_N}(V^{\otimes3})=3!=6$.
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-67: body_md -->
The centre of $\operatorname{GL}_N$ acts on $V^{\otimes3}$ by scalars, hence commutes with every endomorphism, so $\mathrm{End}_{\operatorname{SL}_N}(V^{\otimes3})=\mathrm{End}_{\operatorname{GL}_N}(V^{\otimes3})$. By Schur--Weyl duality the latter is the image of the group algebra $\mathbb{Q}_\ell[S_3]$ acting by permutation of the tensor factors, and that action is faithful as soon as $N\ge3$; hence the dimension is $|S_3|=6$.
<!-- end proof-67 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{lem:offtorus-general}
Let $n\ge2$, $m\ge1$, and for $h\in\mathbb{F}_q^n$ let $r(h):=\#\{i:h_i\ne0\}$. Then $\Sigma_n(h)=(-1)^{n-r(h)}\Sigma_{r(h)}(h'')$, where $h''$ is the tuple of nonzero coordinates and $\Sigma_0:=0$, and
\[
\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q^n\setminus\mathbb{G}_{m}^n(\mathbb{F}_q)}\big|\Sigma_n(h)\big|^{2m}\;=\;O_{n,m}\big(q^{(n-1)(m+1)-m}\big)\;=\;O_{n,m}\big(q^{-(m+1)}\cdot q^{(m+1)n-m}\big).
\]
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- proof-68: body_md -->
The degeneration identity follows directly, exactly as in Lemma~\ref{lem:complement}: if $h_j=0$ then $u_j$ does not occur in the constraint $\langle h,u\rangle=-\lambda$, so it ranges freely over $\mathbb{F}_q^\times$ and contributes the factor $\sum_{u_j\ne0}\psi(u_j^{-1})=-1$; iterating over the $n-r$ vanishing coordinates gives the sign, and for $r=0$ the constraint reads $0=-\lambda$ with $\lambda\ne0$, so the sum is empty. By Corollary~\ref{cor:self-lowdim} applied in $r$ variables, $|\Sigma_r|\le C_rq^{(r-1)/2}$ with $C_r$ depending on $r$ alone. There are $\binom{n}{r}(q-1)^r=O(q^r)$ tuples with $r(h)=r$, so the stratum $r$ contributes
\[
O\big(q^{r}\cdot q^{m(r-1)}\big)=O\big(q^{\,r(m+1)-m}\big),
\]
which is increasing in $r$; the maximum over $0\le r\le n-1$ is attained at $r=n-1$ and equals $q^{(n-1)(m+1)-m}=q^{-(m+1)}\cdot q^{(m+1)n-m}$.
<!-- end proof-68 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
For $n=4$ and $m=2$ the exponent is $(n-1)(m+1)-m=7$, recovering the bound $O(q^7)$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:complement}; the normalising factor there is $q^{(m+1)n-m}=q^{10}$.
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{thm:m6}
Let $n\ge7$ and $p>\max(2,n)$. Then
\[
M_6\big(G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n),W_n\big)=3!=6 .
\]
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- proof-69: body_md -->
\emph{Decoupling.} Exactly as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:decouple}, writing three copies of $\Sigma_n$ and three conjugates and using that $K$ is real,
\[
q^6\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q^n}\big|\Sigma_n(h)\big|^6=\sum_{t\in\mathbb{F}_q^6}\psi\big(L_6(t)\big)V_6(t)^n,
\qquad
L_6(t)=\lambda\sum_{j=1}^6(-1)^{j+1}t_j,
\]
with $V_6(t)=\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q}\prod_{j=1}^6K(t_jh)$; each $h_i$ occurs in exactly one bracket, so the $h$-sum factors into $n$ identical copies.

\emph{The local sum.} Let $\mathcal K_t=\bigotimes_{j=1}^6[\times t_j]^*\mathrm{Kl}_2$ on $\mathbb{G}_{m}$, lisse of rank $64$, pure of weight $6$, with conductor bounded by an absolute constant. Its trace function is the integrand of $V_6$, so by the Grothendieck trace formula, the vanishing of $H^0_c$, and Weil~II,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:V6}
V_6(t)=m(t)\,q^4+O\big(q^{7/2}\big),\qquad m(t):=\dim(\mathcal K_t)_{\pi_1^{\mathrm{geom}}},
\end{equation}
the term $m(t)q^4$ being $H^2_c=(\mathcal K_t)_{\pi_1^{\mathrm{geom}}}(-1)$ of weight $8$, the error being $H^1_c$ of weight $\le7$, and the implied constant absolute, and in particular uniform in $t$: $\mathcal K_t$ has rank $64$, is tame at $0$, and has all breaks at $\infty$ at most $\tfrac12$, so $\mathrm{Swan}_\infty(\mathcal K_t)\le32$ and its conductor is bounded independently of $t$ and of $q$; the sum of the Betti numbers is then bounded in terms of the rank and conductor alone.

\emph{Vanishing coordinates.} Suppose first that exactly $s\ge1$ of the $t_j$ vanish, so that $\mathcal K_t$ as written is undefined. Since $K(0)=\sum_{y\ne0}\psi(y)=-1$, one has $\prod_jK(t_jh)=(-1)^s\prod_{t_j\ne0}K(t_jh)$, and the remaining product is the trace function of $\bigotimes_{t_j\ne0}[\times t_j]^*\mathrm{Kl}_2$, of rank $2^{6-s}$ and weight $6-s$; as above $|V_6(t)|\ll q^{(8-s)/2}$ with an absolute implied constant. There are $O(q^{6-s})$ such $t$, so after dividing by $q^6$ and normalising by $q^{-(4n-3)}$ their total contribution is
\[
O\big(C^nq^{-s+n(8-s)/2-(4n-3)}\big)=O\big(C^nq^{\,3-s-sn/2}\big),
\]
and $3-s-sn/2\le2-n/2<0$ for $n\ge7$. So these strata contribute $o(1)$ and we may assume every $t_j\ne0$.

\emph{The coinvariants.} Let $a_1,\dots,a_r$ be the distinct values among the $t_j$, with multiplicities $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_r$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:kl-independence}, $G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal K_t)=\operatorname{SL}_2^{\,r}$ acting through $\bigotimes_iV_2^{\otimes\mu_i}$, so
\[
m(t)=\prod_{i=1}^r\dim\big(V_2^{\otimes\mu_i}\big)^{\operatorname{SL}_2}=\prod_{i=1}^rc(\mu_i),
\qquad
c(\mu)=\begin{cases}0,&\mu\text{ odd},\\ \mathrm{Cat}(\mu/2),&\mu\text{ even},\end{cases}
\]
with $\mathrm{Cat}(1)=1$, $\mathrm{Cat}(2)=2$, $\mathrm{Cat}(3)=5$. Hence $m(t)=0$ unless every multiplicity is even, and the partitions of $6$ into even parts give exactly three families:
\[
(2,2,2):\ \dim=3,\ m=1;\qquad (4,2):\ \dim=2,\ m=2;\qquad (6):\ \dim=1,\ m=5 .
\]

\emph{Bookkeeping.} Normalize by $q^{-(4n-3)}$ after dividing the decoupling identity above by $q^6$. Strata with $m(t)=0$ obey $|V_6|\ll q^{7/2}$ and contribute $O\big(C^nq^{7n/2-4n+3}\big)=O\big(C^nq^{3-n/2}\big)\to0$ for $n\ge7$. The stratum $(4,2)$ contributes $O\big(2^nq^{2-3}\big)=O(2^nq^{-1})\to0$, and $(6)$ contributes $O\big(5^nq^{1-3}\big)=O(5^nq^{-2})\to0$; the constants $2^n,5^n$ are harmless because $M_6$ is a limit as $q\to\infty$ with $n$ fixed: no uniformity in $n$ is claimed or needed, and the number of strata of $\mathbb{F}_q^6$ does not depend on $n$. For the same reason the expansion $V_6(t)^n=m(t)^nq^{4n}\big(1+O_n(q^{-1/2})\big)$ is legitimate once $q$ is large in terms of $n$. Finally, on the $(2,2,2)$ stratum $m=1$, and the six positions carry the signs $+,-,+,-,+,-$ of $L_6$. Fix one of the $\frac{6!}{2^3 3!}=15$ perfect matchings of the six positions. If every pair occupies one $+$ and one $-$ position, the two occurrences of each value cancel in $L_6$, so $L_6\equiv0$ on that configuration and its $q^3(1+o(1))$ points each contribute $\psi(0)=1$; the pairings of this kind are the bijections $\{1,3,5\}\to\{2,4,6\}$, and there are $3!=6$ of them. Otherwise some pair occupies two positions of the same sign, and then $L_6$ restricted to that configuration is a nonzero linear form in the three distinct values $a_1,a_2,a_3$; summing $\psi(L_6)$ over $a\in(\mathbb{F}_q^\times)^3$ gives $O(q^2)$ by orthogonality, which after the normalisation above is $O(q^{-1})$. So only the six sign-alternating pairings survive, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:m6-analytic}
\lim_{q\to\infty}\;q^{-(4n-3)}\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q^n}\big|\Sigma_n(h)\big|^6\;=\;6 .
\end{equation}

\emph{From the analytic limit to the group-theoretic moment.} Apply Katz's moment theorem, Theorem~\ref{thm:751}, with moment index $3$. Here $S=\mathbb{G}_{m}^n$ has dimension $D=n$ and $\mathcal W_n$ is pure of weight $w=n+1$, so the Katz normalisation is $q^{-D-3w}=q^{-(4n+3)}$. Put
\[
T_q(h)=\mathrm{Tr}(\mathrm{Frob}_h|\mathcal W_n),\qquad \Phi_q(h)=-q\Sigma_n(h).
\]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:self-cohomology-package}, after the integral Tate twist relating $X_h$ and $Y_h$, the trace of the full cohomology differs from the top-weight trace only by the lower-weight contribution; hence
\[
\Phi_q(h)=T_q(h)+B_q(h),\qquad |B_q(h)|\ll_n q^{n/2},\qquad |T_q(h)|+|\Phi_q(h)|\ll_n q^{(n+1)/2}.
\]
The elementary inequality $||x+y|^6-|x|^6|\ll |x|^5|y|+|x|^4|y|^2+\cdots+|y|^6$ therefore gives a pointwise difference $O_n(q^{3n+5/2})$. After summing over $O(q^n)$ points and multiplying by $q^{-(4n+3)}$, the normalized error is $O_n(q^{-1/2})$. Thus
\[
q^{-(4n+3)}\sum_{h\in\mathbb{G}_{m}^n(\mathbb{F}_q)}|T_q(h)|^6
=q^{-(4n-3)}\sum_{h\in\mathbb{G}_{m}^n(\mathbb{F}_q)}|\Sigma_n(h)|^6+O_n(q^{-1/2}).
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:offtorus-general} with $m=3$, replacing $\mathbb{G}_{m}^n(\mathbb{F}_q)$ by $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ changes the right-hand side by $O_n(q^{-4})$. Equation~\eqref{eq:m6-analytic} therefore gives $S_6(\mathbb F_q,\mathcal W_n)=6+O_n(q^{-1/2})$. Letting $q$ run through the finite extensions of the fixed base field and invoking Theorem~\ref{thm:751} yields
\[
M_6\big(G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n),W_n\big)=6.
\]
<!-- end proof-69 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:n127-closed}
$G^0_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_{127})=\operatorname{SL}_{r(127)}$ for every prime $p>127$.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-70: body_md -->
Theorem~\ref{thm:m6} gives $M_6=6<r(127)$. Theorem~\ref{thm:n127-moment} then gives $G^0_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_{127})=\operatorname{SL}_{r(127)}$ for every $p>127$.
<!-- end proof-70 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
\label{rem:m6-numeric}
Equation~\eqref{eq:V6} together with the table for $m(t)$ was tested by exact computation of $V_6(t)$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$ for $p=11,13,17,19$ and representatives of each configuration type. In every case the residual $\big(V_6(t)-m(t)q^4\big)/q^{7/2}$ was of absolute value at most $4.2$, consistent with an absolute implied constant, and in particular $m=0$ was confirmed both for six distinct parameters and for configurations with an odd multiplicity. This is a check on the statement, not a substitute for its proof.
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- proposition-26: body_md -->
\label{prop:m6-second}
In case \emph{(C)} at $n=127$, with $\pi=r(127)$, one has $M_6(G,W_{127})>\pi-1$, by an argument that does not use the scalar elements. This is not logically independent of Proposition~\ref{prop:higher-moments}: whereas Proposition~\ref{prop:higher-moments} needs only the upper bound $|\bar G|\le\pi^2|\operatorname{Sp}_2(\pi)|$ supplied by case \emph{(C)} itself, the argument below uses $H=\operatorname{SL}_2(\pi)$ in full, to bound the dimensions of the irreducible constituents. It is a consistency check on the first bound, not a second proof from independent hypotheses.
<!-- end proposition-26 -->
<!-- proof-71: body_md -->
Restricted to $E$, the module $W_{127}^{\otimes3}$ has central character $\omega^3$, where $\omega$ is the faithful character by which $Z(E)\cong\mu_\pi$ acts on $W_{127}$. Since $\pi$ is an odd prime greater than $3$, $\omega^3\ne1$, so every $E$-constituent of $W_{127}^{\otimes3}$ is one of the faithful irreducibles of dimension $\pi$ with central character $\omega^3$; comparing dimensions, $W_{127}^{\otimes3}\cong\pi^2\cdot V_{\omega^3}$, and the multiplicity space $M_3$ has dimension $\pi^2$ and carries a projective action of $H=\operatorname{SL}_2(\pi)$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:caseC-dickson}. Hence
\[
M_6=\dim\mathrm{End}_G\big(W_{127}^{\otimes3}\big)=\dim\mathrm{End}_H(M_3)\ \ge\ \#\{\text{irreducible constituents of }M_3\}.
\]
Since $\pi\ge5$ the Schur multiplier of $\operatorname{SL}_2(\pi)$ is trivial, so projective representations are ordinary, and every irreducible representation of $\operatorname{SL}_2(\pi)$ has dimension $\pi-1$, $\pi$ or $\pi+1$. Write $M_3=\bigoplus_im_iS_i$ with the $S_i$ pairwise non-isomorphic irreducibles; this is legitimate because $H$ is finite and the coefficients have characteristic $0$, so $M_3$ is semisimple. Then $\sum_im_i\dim S_i=\pi^2$ with $\dim S_i\le\pi+1$ gives $\sum_im_i\ge\pi^2/(\pi+1)$, and since $m_i^2\ge m_i$,
\[
M_6=\dim\mathrm{End}_H(M_3)=\sum_im_i^2\ \ge\ \sum_im_i\ \ge\ \frac{\pi^2}{\pi+1}\ >\ \pi-1,
\]
the last step because $\pi^2>(\pi-1)(\pi+1)$.
<!-- end proof-71 -->
<!-- proposition-27: body_md -->
\label{prop:holder-fails}
The inequality
\[
M_6\le\big(\sup\nolimits_h|\widehat\Sigma_n(h)|^2\big)\,M_4,
\qquad
\widehat\Sigma_n:=\Sigma_n/q^{(n-1)/2},
\]
in which $\widehat\Sigma_n$ is the weight-$0$ normalised trace, cannot yield $M_6<\pi$ at $n=127$.
<!-- end proposition-27 -->
<!-- proof-72: body_md -->
The inequality itself is H\"older, and with $M_4=2$ it gives $M_6\le2\sup_h|\widehat\Sigma_n|^2$; to conclude $M_6<\pi$ one would need $\sup_h|\widehat\Sigma_n|<\sqrt{\pi/2}=8.9\cdot10^{18}$. But $\sup_h|\widehat\Sigma_n|\to\pi=1.58\cdot10^{38}$ in both cases under consideration. In case (C) the scalar elements of $G$ have $|\mathrm{tr}|=\pi$ exactly. In case (A), $G_{\mathrm{geom}}\supseteq\operatorname{SL}_\pi$ and the normalized traces equidistribute, by Katz's equidistribution theorem for the connected special-linear monodromy group, in the conjugacy classes of a maximal compact subgroup; on that compact group the supremum of $|\mathrm{tr}|$ is $\pi$, attained at the scalars; so values arbitrarily close to $\pi$ occur. Hence the bound available is $M_6\le2\pi^2$, never $M_6<\pi$.
<!-- end proof-72 -->
<!-- remark-14: body_md -->
\label{rem:three-routes}
Corollary~\ref{cor:n127-closed} settles $n=127$ unconditionally, for every $p>127$, by the sixth-moment computation of Theorem~\ref{thm:m6}. The proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:decouple} extends verbatim to every even moment, and the resulting six-variable local sum $V_6(t)=\sum_h\prod_{j=1}^6K(t_jh)$ is a sum over a curve, computed via Proposition~\ref{prop:kl-independence} and a Temperley--Lieb count, without the surface geometry --- the Cayley cubic, its nine lines, the elliptic family $C_t$ --- that the fourth-moment analysis of Section~\ref{sec:monodromy} required. Nothing is left outstanding at this value of $n$.
<!-- end remark-14 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
\label{thm:n127-tame}
Assume case \emph{(C)} of Theorem~\ref{thm:754} at $n=127$.  Let $\tau$ be a topological generator of the image in $G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_{127})$ of tame inertia at the divisor $D=\{h_{127}=0\}$.  If
\begin{equation}\label{eq:n127-tame}
0<\operatorname{rank}(\tau-1)
<\frac{r(127)}2-\sqrt{r(127)},
\end{equation}
then case \emph{(C)} is impossible, and $G^0_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_{127})=\operatorname{SL}_{r(127)}$ for every prime $p>127$.
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- proof-73: body_md -->
The first bound of Proposition~\ref{prop:weil-fixed} is characteristic-free: for any non-scalar element $x$ in the extraspecial normalizer whose image in the projective quotient has order $k\ge2$, every eigenvalue of $x$ has multiplicity at most
\[
\frac{\pi}{k}+\sqrt\pi\le\frac\pi2+\sqrt\pi,
\qquad \pi=r(127).
\]
Because tame inertia is procyclic, $\tau$ fixes a space of dimension
\[
\dim\ker(\tau-1)=r(127)-\operatorname{rank}(\tau-1).
\]
The two strict inequalities in~\eqref{eq:n127-tame} imply that $\tau$ is neither the identity nor a nontrivial scalar: a nontrivial scalar has $\operatorname{rank}(\tau-1)=r(127)$.  Thus Proposition~\ref{prop:weil-fixed} applies and gives
\[
r(127)-\operatorname{rank}(\tau-1)
\le\frac{r(127)}2+\sqrt{r(127)},
\]
whereas~\eqref{eq:n127-tame} gives the strict reverse inequality.  This contradiction excludes case~(C).  The remaining finite alternatives at $n=127$ are excluded by Proposition~\ref{prop:caseD-complete}, Propositions~\ref{prop:caseB-unitary}--\ref{prop:caseB-selfdual}, and the exact modular verification in Appendix~\ref{app:computations}; hence the $\operatorname{SL}$ branch remains.
<!-- end proof-73 -->
<!-- remark-15: body_md -->
\label{rem:two-criteria}
Theorems~\ref{thm:n127-criterion} and~\ref{thm:n127-tame} are two local criteria, while Corollary~\ref{cor:n127-closed} resolves $n=127$ unconditionally by the sixth moment.  The second criterion is deliberately stated directly in terms of the actual tame-inertia operator on $\mathcal W_{127}$; no vanishing-cycle module from another manuscript is imported.  Its numerical margin is enormous: any independently established bound
$0<\operatorname{rank}(\tau-1)<r(127)/2-\sqrt{r(127)}$
would immediately exclude the extraspecial alternative.
<!-- end remark-15 -->
<!-- theorem-16: body_md -->
\label{thm:n127}
Let
\[
\pi:=r(127)=2^{127}-\binom{127}{63}=158165610439505190298619509827693829853,
\]
a prime. For every prime $p>127$ with
\[
p\ne\pi\qquad\text{and}\qquad p\nmid\pi^2-1,
\]
one has $G^0_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_{127})=\operatorname{SL}_{r(127)}$.
<!-- end theorem-16 -->
<!-- proof-74: body_md -->
At $n=127$, case (D) is excluded by Proposition~\ref{prop:caseD-complete}; the unitary case-(B) alternatives are excluded by Propositions~\ref{prop:caseB-unitary}--\ref{prop:caseB-selfdual}, and the $q=3$ symplectic alternative is covered by the exact finite verification in Appendix~\ref{app:computations}. Thus only case (C) remains. Since $\pi$ is prime, case (C) has $a=1$, and Proposition~\ref{prop:caseC-congruence} forces $p=\pi$ or $p\mid\pi^2-1$. Under the stated hypothesis neither holds, so case (C) is excluded and case (A) of Theorem~\ref{thm:754} applies.
<!-- end proof-74 -->
<!-- remark-16: body_md -->
\label{rem:n127}
$r(127)$ is prime, so a group of the shape $Z(G)\cdot E$ with $E$ extraspecial of order $r(127)^3$ is not excluded by dimension alone, and neither the determinant exclusion used in Proposition~\ref{prop:gt-dim10-exclusion} nor the self-duality exclusion of Corollary~\ref{cor:notselfdual-uncond} applies: case (C) permits a scalar subgroup of order divisible by $p$, so $\det$ need not be trivial, and nothing forces an invariant form. What does apply is Proposition~\ref{prop:caseC-congruence}, which reduces the case to the congruence $p=\pi$ or $p\mid\pi^2-1$; Theorem~\ref{thm:n127} is the resulting statement. Since $\pi(\pi^2-1)$ is a fixed integer of $115$ decimal digits, that argument alone leaves a \emph{finite and explicit} set of exceptional characteristics rather than all $p>127$, though one cannot list it without factoring $\pi^2-1$. Those characteristics are removed by the sixth moment: Corollary~\ref{cor:n127-closed} excludes case (C) at $n=127$ for every $p>127$, by a bound on $M_6$ in case (C) that never mentions the characteristic. The case $n=127$ is therefore closed, and what the present remark records is why the congruence route could not close it and what had to replace it.
<!-- end remark-16 -->
<!-- theorem-17: body_md -->
\label{thm:monodromy-n-status}
Let $4\le n\le 2097150$ and $p>n$. Then the direct fourth-moment/Guralnick--Tiep route, using the exact finite certificates recorded in Appendix~\ref{app:computations}, gives
\[
G^0_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)=\operatorname{SL}_{r(n)}.
\]
This theorem is retained as an independent route; it is not used in the principal proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:monodromy-n}.
<!-- end theorem-17 -->
<!-- proof-75: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:757-general} the geometric monodromy group is reductive, and Proposition~\ref{prop:finite-det-internal} gives a finite scalar intersection. The fourth-moment theorem below, Theorem~\ref{thm:fourthmoment-n}, together with Katz's moment theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:751}), gives $M_4(G_{\mathrm{geom}},W_n)=2$. Hence Theorem~\ref{thm:754} leaves cases (A)--(D) of Guralnick--Tiep.

Case (D) is confined by Proposition~\ref{prop:caseD-complete} to $n\in\{4,5\}$ and is excluded there by Propositions~\ref{prop:gt-dim10-exclusion} and~\ref{prop:caseD-n5}. Case (C) is excluded by Proposition~\ref{prop:extraspecial-exclusion}; its exceptional prime-rank value $n=127$ is closed by Corollary~\ref{cor:n127-closed}. In case (B), the unitary possibilities are reduced by Proposition~\ref{prop:caseB-unitary} and the surviving collisions are excluded by Proposition~\ref{prop:caseB-selfdual}. The $q=3$ symplectic family is reduced by Proposition~\ref{prop:caseB-2adic} to the finite sweep whose exact deterministic certificate is described in Appendix~\ref{app:computations}; within the stated range the only genuine collisions are $n=2,3$, outside the present theorem. Thus cases (B)--(D) are impossible and case (A) gives $\operatorname{SL}_{r(n)}\subseteqG_{\mathrm{geom}}$. Finiteness of the scalar intersection then gives $G^0_{\mathrm{geom}}=\operatorname{SL}_{r(n)}$ by Larsen's alternative, Theorem~\ref{thm:753}.
<!-- end proof-75 -->
<!-- remark-17: body_md -->
\label{rem:residual-range}
The upper bound $2097150$ belongs only to the optional direct-classification route: it is the last value before the first untested prime-power instance $n=2^{21}-1$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:extraspecial-exclusion}. The principal boundary-unipotent route below has no such Diophantine range and proves the main theorem for every $n\ge4$. No assertion about $n=2,3$ is made in this split article; those low ranks require separate arguments and are outside its stated scope.
<!-- end remark-17 -->
<!-- proposition-28: body_md -->
\label{prop:755}
$M_4(G_{\mathrm{geom}},W)=2$.
<!-- end proposition-28 -->
<!-- proof-76: body_md -->
Everything needed here is now internal.  Theorem~\ref{thm:self-cohomology-package} gives that $\mathcal W=\mathcal W_4$ is lisse of rank $r(4)=10$ and pure of weight $5$ on $S=\mathbb{G}_{m}^4$.  It also identifies $\mathcal W_h$ with the weight-$5$ quotient of $H_c^5(X_h)$ and shows, after the Tate twist $H_c^3(Y_h)\cong H_c^5(X_h)(1)$, that all lower-weight terms in the trace of $H_c^3(Y_h)$ contribute $O(q)$.  Since
\[
\Sigma_q(h)=-\mathrm{Tr}(\mathrm{Frob}_h|H_c^3(Y_h)),
\]
we therefore have, uniformly in the finite extensions $E/\mathbb F_p$,
\[
\mathrm{Tr}(\mathrm{Frob}_{E,h}|\mathcal W)=-q\Sigma_q(h)+B_h,
\qquad |B_h|\ll q^2.
\tag{\ref{prop:755}.1}
\]
Purity gives $|\mathrm{Tr}(\mathrm{Frob}_{E,h}|\mathcal W)|\le10q^{5/2}$, and (\ref{prop:755}.1) then also gives $q|\Sigma_q(h)|\ll q^{5/2}$.  Put $A_h=-q\Sigma_q(h)$.  The elementary inequality
\[
\big||A+B|^4-|A|^4\big|
\ll |A|^3|B|+|A|^2|B|^2+|A||B|^3+|B|^4
\]
therefore gives a pointwise difference $O(q^{19/2})$ between $|\mathrm{Tr}(\mathrm{Frob}_h|\mathcal W)|^4$ and $q^4|\Sigma_q(h)|^4$.  Summing over $O(q^4)$ points and applying the Katz normalization $q^{-14}$ gives an $O(q^{-1/2})$ error.  Hence
\[
S_4(E,\mathcal W)=q^{-10}\sum_{h\in S(E)}|\Sigma_q(h)|^4+O(q^{-1/2}).
\]
The points outside $\mathbb{G}_{m}^4$ contribute $O(q^7)=o(q^{10})$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:complement}; Theorem~\ref{thm:743} therefore gives
\[
S_4(E,\mathcal W)=2+O(q^{-1/2}).
\]
The parameter $\lambda$ and the base sheaf are fixed while $E$ runs through finite extensions, as stipulated at the start of the section.  Theorem~\ref{thm:751} now gives $M_4(G_{\mathrm{geom}},W)=2$.
<!-- end proof-76 -->
<!-- proposition-29: body_md -->
\label{prop:756}
$W$ is $G_{\mathrm{geom}}$-irreducible.
<!-- end proposition-29 -->
<!-- proof-77: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:753}(1) it suffices that $M_4\le5$, which holds by Proposition~\ref{prop:755}. Concretely, if $V=V_1\oplus V_2$ with both nonzero, $V^{\otimes2}\cong V_1^{\otimes2}\oplus V_2^{\otimes2}\oplus2(V_1\otimes V_2)$, whence $M_4(G,V)\ge1+1+2^2=6$.
<!-- end proof-77 -->
<!-- proposition-30: body_md -->
\label{prop:757}
The rank-$10$ group $G_{\mathrm{geom}}=G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_4)$ is reductive.
<!-- end proposition-30 -->
<!-- proof-78: body_md -->
This is Proposition~\ref{prop:757-general} with $n=4$.
<!-- end proof-78 -->
<!-- theorem-18: body_md -->
\label{thm:758}
Let $p\ge5$. Then
\[
G^0_{\mathrm{geom}}=\operatorname{SL}_{10},\qquad \operatorname{SL}_{10}\subseteq G_{\mathrm{geom}}=\mu\cdot\operatorname{SL}_{10}\subseteq\operatorname{GL}_{10},
\]
with $\mu=G_{\mathrm{geom}}\cap\{\text{scalars}\}$ finite cyclic; in particular $(G_{\mathrm{geom}})^{\mathrm{der}}=\operatorname{SL}_{10}$. Writing $D:=\det(G_{\mathrm{geom}})$, one has $D=\mu_d$ for some $d\ge1$, $\mu=\mu_{10d}$, and $G_{\mathrm{geom}}=\{g\in\operatorname{GL}_{10}:\det g\in\mu_d\}$.
<!-- end theorem-18 -->
<!-- proof-79: body_md -->
$G_{\mathrm{geom}}$ is Zariski closed by definition, reductive by Proposition~\ref{prop:757}, acts irreducibly by Proposition~\ref{prop:756}, has $\dim W=r(4)=10>6$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:self-cohomology-package}, and satisfies $M_4(G_{\mathrm{geom}},W)=2$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:755}. Theorem~\ref{thm:754} therefore gives $G_{\mathrm{geom}}\supseteq\operatorname{SL}_{10}$. Proposition~\ref{prop:finite-det-internal} gives a finite scalar intersection, and Theorem~\ref{thm:753}(2) then gives $G^0_{\mathrm{geom}}=\operatorname{SL}_{10}$.

For the structure, $D=\det(G_{\mathrm{geom}})$ is a closed subgroup of $\mathbb{G}_{m}$, hence finite or all of $\mathbb{G}_{m}$; if $D=\mathbb{G}_{m}$ then, since $\operatorname{SL}_{10}=\ker(\det)\subseteqG_{\mathrm{geom}}$, we would get $G_{\mathrm{geom}}=\operatorname{GL}_{10}$, contradicting Proposition~\ref{prop:finite-det-internal}, which gives finite determinant image. So $D=\mu_d$ and $G_{\mathrm{geom}}=\det^{-1}(\mu_d)$; given $g$ with $\det g=\zeta\in\mu_d$, choosing $\lambda$ with $\lambda^{10}=\zeta$ gives $\lambda^{-1}g\in\operatorname{SL}_{10}$, so $g\in\mu_{10d}\cdot\operatorname{SL}_{10}$, and a scalar $\lambda I$ lies in $G_{\mathrm{geom}}$ iff $\lambda\in\mu_{10d}$.
<!-- end proof-79 -->
<!-- proposition-31: body_md -->
\label{prop:759}
$W$ is a primitive $G_{\mathrm{geom}}$-module.
<!-- end proposition-31 -->
<!-- proof-80: body_md -->
The standard representation of $\operatorname{SL}_{10}$ is irreducible: given nonzero $v,w$, extend each to a basis and adjust the final vector by $(\det g)^{-1}$ to find $g\in\operatorname{SL}_{10}$ with $gv=w$. If $W=\bigoplus_{i=1}^mW_i$, $m\ge2$, is a $G_{\mathrm{geom}}$-stable decomposition permuted via $\sigma:G_{\mathrm{geom}}\to S_m$, then since $\operatorname{SL}_{10}\subseteqG_{\mathrm{geom}}$ is connected, $\sigma(\operatorname{SL}_{10})$ is trivial, so $\operatorname{SL}_{10}$ stabilizes each $W_i$, contradicting irreducibility of the standard representation.
<!-- end proof-80 -->
<!-- proposition-32: body_md -->
\label{prop:7510}
$W\not\cong W^\vee$ as $G_{\mathrm{geom}}$-modules.
<!-- end proposition-32 -->
<!-- proof-81: body_md -->
If $W\cong W^\vee$, $W$ carries a nondegenerate $\operatorname{SL}_{10}$-invariant bilinear form $B=B_++B_-$ (symmetric plus alternating), with the nonzero summand $B_\varepsilon$ nondegenerate by irreducibility of $W$ under $\operatorname{SL}_{10}$, forcing $\operatorname{SL}_{10}$ into $\mathrm O_{10}$ or $\operatorname{Sp}_{10}$. But $\dim\operatorname{SL}_{10}=99$ while $\dim\mathrm O_{10}=45$, $\dim\operatorname{Sp}_{10}=55$, and a $99$-dimensional group admits no injective homomorphism into a group of dimension $45$ or $55$.
<!-- end proof-81 -->
<!-- proposition-33: body_md -->
\label{prop:twisted-selfdual}
Let $n\ge4$ and $p>n$. Then there is no lisse rank-one sheaf $\mathcal L$ on $\mathbb{G}_{m}^n$ with
\[
\mathcal W_n\;\cong\;\mathcal W_n^\vee\otimes\mathcal L
\]
geometrically.  Indeed $r(n)\ge r(4)=10$ in the present range, so the standard representation of $\operatorname{SL}_{r(n)}$ is not self-dual.
<!-- end proposition-33 -->
<!-- proof-82: body_md -->
Suppose such an $\mathcal L$ exists and write $r=r(n)$. Restrict the corresponding isomorphism of $\pi_1^{\mathrm{geom}}$-representations to the subgroup $\operatorname{SL}_r\subseteqG_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)$. A rank-one sheaf restricts to a one-dimensional character of that subgroup; but $\operatorname{SL}_r$ is perfect for $r\ge2$, being equal to its own commutator subgroup, so it has no nontrivial one-dimensional characters and $\mathcal L|_{\operatorname{SL}_r}$ is trivial. The isomorphism therefore reads
\[
V\;\cong\;V^\vee\qquad\text{as representations of }\operatorname{SL}_r,
\]
where $V$ is the tautological $r$-dimensional representation. The standard representation of $\operatorname{SL}_r$ is self-dual precisely when $r=2$, the highest weights of $V$ and $V^\vee$ being $\varpi_1$ and $\varpi_{r-1}$, which coincide only for $r=2$. Since $n\ge4$ and $r(n)\ge r(4)=10$, this is a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-82 -->
<!-- remark-18: body_md -->
\label{rem:no-circularity}
Corollary~\ref{cor:notselfdual-uncond} asserts only that $\mathcal W_n\not\cong\mathcal W_n^\vee$. Proposition~\ref{prop:twisted-selfdual} is stronger: in the stated range $n\ge4$, once $\operatorname{SL}_{r(n)}\subseteqG_{\mathrm{geom}}$ is known, it rules out self-duality even after an arbitrary rank-one twist.

No circularity is introduced. The chain establishing $\operatorname{SL}_r\subseteqG_{\mathrm{geom}}$ runs
\[
\text{fourth moment}\ \longrightarrow\ M_4(G_{\mathrm{geom}},W_n)=2\ \longrightarrow\ \text{classification}\ \longrightarrow\ \operatorname{SL}_r\subseteqG_{\mathrm{geom}},
\]
the classification step being Theorems~\ref{thm:753} and~\ref{thm:754},
and the hypotheses of the two classification theorems are irreducibility of $W_n$, the value $M_4=2$, and $\dim W_n>6$ --- self-duality, twisted or otherwise, appears nowhere among them. Non-self-duality is therefore a \emph{consequence} of the monodromy determination and is never used in obtaining it. The same remark applies to primitivity: in this article it is deduced only after the special-linear subgroup has been obtained and is not an input to the classification step.
<!-- end remark-18 -->
<!-- proposition-34: body_md -->
\label{prop:boundary-degen}
For $h\in\mathbb{F}_p^4$ with $h_1=0$ and $h_2,h_3,h_4\ne0$, the phase $F_4(u,t;0,h_2,h_3,h_4)$ splits as $u_1^{-1}+F_3(u_2,u_3,u_4,t;h_2,h_3,h_4)$, and consequently
\[
R^5\pi_!\mathcal{L}_\psi(F_4)\big|_{h_1=0}\ \cong\ R^4\pi'_!\mathcal{L}_\psi(F_3),
\]
of rank $2^3-1=7$ by the $n=3$ specialization of Theorem~\ref{thm:self-cohomology-package}, a strict drop from the generic mixed rank $2^4-1=15$ in the $n=4$ case.
<!-- end proposition-34 -->
<!-- proof-83: body_md -->
At $h_1=0$ the linear term $h_1u_1$ vanishes, decoupling $u_1$ from $t$; K\"unneth with the rank-$1$, weight-$0$ factor $H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_{m,u_1},\mathcal{L}_\psi(u_1^{-1}))$ (Frobenius eigenvalue $1$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:self-tzero} in one variable) identifies $R^5\pi_!\mathcal{L}_\psi(F_4)|_{h_1=0}$ with $R^4\pi'_!\mathcal{L}_\psi(F_3)$ shifted appropriately in degree, of rank $2^3-1=7$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:self-cohomology-package}.
<!-- end proof-83 -->
<!-- theorem-19: body_md -->
\label{thm:swan-H}
Let $n\ge2$, $p>\max(2,n)$, and let $c=(c_2,\dots,c_n)$ consist of nonzero elements. Put $\ell_c=\{(h_1,c_2,\dots,c_n):h_1\in\mathbb{G}_{m}\}$. For the rank-$2^n$ sheaf $\mathcal H_n:=R^1\rho_!\mathcal N_n$ one has
\[
\mathrm{Swan}_0(\mathcal H_n|_{\ell_c})+\mathrm{Swan}_\infty(\mathcal H_n|_{\ell_c})=2^{n-1}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-19 -->
<!-- proof-84: body_md -->
Put $X=\mathbb{G}_{m,h_1}\times\mathbb{G}_{m,t}$, let $m(h_1,t)=h_1t$, and set
\[
\mathcal M=\Big(\bigotimes_{i=2}^n\mathrm{Kl}_2(c_it)\Big)\otimes\mathcal{L}_\psi(\lambda t),\qquad
\mathcal N=m^*\mathrm{Kl}_2\otimes\mathrm{pr}_t^*\mathcal M.
\]
Each $\mathrm{Kl}_2(c_it)$ is tame at $0$ and has breaks $1/2$ at $\infty$, whereas $\mathcal{L}_\psi(\lambda t)$ has break $1$ at $\infty$. Lemma~\ref{lem:self-unequal-break} therefore gives $\mathrm{Swan}_0(\mathcal M)=0$ and $\mathrm{Swan}_\infty(\mathcal M)=2^{n-1}$, so $\chi_c(\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathcal M)=-2^{n-1}$.

For the first projection $\rho:X\to\mathbb{G}_{m,h_1}$, compactly supported base change and the fibre computation of Theorem~\ref{thm:self-cohomology-package} give $R^0\rho_!=R^2\rho_!=0$ and $R^1\rho_!\mathcal N=\mathcal H_n|_{\ell_c}$. Thus $\chi_c(X,\mathcal N)=-\chi_c(\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathcal H_n|_{\ell_c})$.

For the second projection $\mathrm{pr}_t:X\to\mathbb{G}_{m,t}$, the fibre over $t$ is $[\times t]^*\mathrm{Kl}_2$ tensored with the constant vector space $\mathcal M_t$. The automorphism $h_1\mapsto th_1$ identifies $H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_{m},[\times t]^*\mathrm{Kl}_2)$ with the fixed one-dimensional space $H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathrm{Kl}_2)$, while degrees $0$ and $2$ vanish. Hence $R^1\mathrm{pr}_{t!}\mathcal N\simeq\mathcal M\otimes\mathcal E$ for a geometrically constant line $\mathcal E$, so
\[
\chi_c(X,\mathcal N)=-\chi_c(\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathcal M)=2^{n-1}.
\]
Consequently $\chi_c(\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathcal H_n|_{\ell_c})=-2^{n-1}$. Since $\mathcal H_n|_{\ell_c}$ is lisse on $\mathbb{G}_{m}$, Grothendieck--Ogg--Shafarevich gives the asserted sum of Swan conductors.
<!-- end proof-84 -->
<!-- lemma-27: body_md -->
\label{lem:boundary-fibre-unipotent}
Let $n\ge2$ and $p>\max(2,n)$. Write $\mathcal N_n|_{\ell_c}=\mu^*\mathrm{Kl}_2\otimes\mathcal M$ on $\mathbb{G}_{m,t}\times\mathbb{G}_{m,h_1}$, where $\mu(h_1,t)=h_1t$ and $\mathcal M=\big(\bigotimes_{i\ge2}m_{c_i}^*\mathrm{Kl}_2\big)\otimes\mathcal{L}_\psi(\lambda t)$ does not involve $h_1$. Let $\xi$ be the generic point of the divisor $\{h_1=0\}$ in $\mathbb A^1_{h_1}\times\mathbb{G}_{m,t}$. Then the inertia group $I_\xi$ acts on $\mu^*\mathrm{Kl}_2$ through the local monodromy of $\mathrm{Kl}_2$ at the origin, hence unipotently with a single Jordan block of size $2$; and it acts trivially on $\mathcal M$.
<!-- end lemma-27 -->
<!-- proof-85: body_md -->
The map $\mu$ extends to $\mathbb A^1_{h_1}\times\mathbb{G}_{m,t}\to\mathbb A^1_s$. In the discrete valuation ring $\mathcal O_\xi$, whose uniformiser is $h_1$, the pullback of the uniformiser $s$ is $h_1t$ with $t$ a unit, so $v_\xi(\mu^\#s)=1$. Hence $\mathcal O_{\mathbb A^1_s,0}\to\mathcal O_\xi$ is a local homomorphism of discrete valuation rings with ramification index one, and $I_\xi$ maps to the inertia group at $s=0$.
