The action on $\mu^*\mathrm{Kl}_2$ therefore factors through the local monodromy of $\mathrm{Kl}_2$ at $0$, which is unipotent with a single Jordan block of size $2$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:kl2-local-internal}. Since $\mathcal M$ is pulled back from $\mathbb{G}_{m,t}$ it is unramified along $\{h_1=0\}$.
<!-- end proof-85 -->
<!-- theorem-20: body_md -->
\label{thm:laumon-local-special}
Let $V$ be a continuous $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$-representation of the inertia group at $\infty$ whose breaks lie in $[0,1)$.  Write $r(V)=\dim V$ and $s(V)=\mathrm{Swan}(V)$.  The external input is Laumon's local Fourier-transform theorem, specifically \cite[Thm.~2.4.3(ii)b, proved in \S2.5]{Laumon}: on the slope-$<1$ category the local transform from $\infty$ to $0'$ is exact and satisfies
\[
r\bigl(\operatorname{FT}^{(\infty,0')}(V)\bigr)=r(V)-s(V),
\qquad
\mathrm{Swan}\bigl(\operatorname{FT}^{(\infty,0')}(V)\bigr)=s(V).
\tag{\ref{thm:laumon-local-special}.1}
\]
More precisely, an isoclinic summand of slope $\alpha<1$ is carried to an isoclinic summand of slope $\alpha/(1-\alpha)$.  In particular a tame summand ($\alpha=0$) stays tame with the same rank, while a rank-two summand of slope $1/2$ and Swan conductor $1$ becomes rank one of slope $1$ and Swan conductor $1$.
<!-- end theorem-20 -->
<!-- proof-86: body_md -->
We extract the numerical part of Laumon's local stationary-phase theorem and spell out the passage from a single break to an arbitrary representation.  The local Fourier functor is defined by degree-one vanishing cycles of the Fourier kernel.  Laumon's concentration theorem shows that in the range of breaks $<1$ no other cohomological degree occurs; consequently the functor is exact and commutes with direct sums and with extension of the residue field.

First suppose that $V$ is isoclinic of slope $\alpha<1$, rank $d$, and Swan conductor $d\alpha$.  The local stationary-phase calculation identifies the transform with the vanishing cycles at the unique critical branch of the phase obtained by adding the Fourier kernel.  The Deligne--Laumon conductor formula computes the dimension of this vanishing-cycle space as the drop of the Artin conductor.  In this situation the drop is
\[
d-d\alpha=d(1-\alpha).
\]
Hence
\[
r\bigl(\operatorname{FT}^{(\infty,0')}(V)\bigr)=d(1-\alpha).
\tag{\ref{thm:laumon-local-special}.2}
\]
Applying Fourier involutivity to this local contribution and using Grothendieck--Ogg--Shafarevich gives equality of the Swan conductors before and after the local transform:
\[
\mathrm{Swan}\bigl(\operatorname{FT}^{(\infty,0')}(V)\bigr)=d\alpha.
\tag{\ref{thm:laumon-local-special}.3}
\]
Equations (\ref{thm:laumon-local-special}.2)--(\ref{thm:laumon-local-special}.3) force the unique output break to be
\[
\frac{d\alpha}{d(1-\alpha)}=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}.
\]
The calculation above is the slope-$<1$ specialization of Laumon's local stationary-phase argument.  Fu's explicit Legendre-transform formulation gives the same critical-branch normal form for rank-one constituents and provides an independent normalization check \cite{Fu}.

For a general $V$ with breaks in $[0,1)$, write its break decomposition
$V=\bigoplus_{\alpha<1}V(\alpha)$.  Exactness of the local Fourier functor gives the direct sum of the transforms of the $V(\alpha)$.  Summing (\ref{thm:laumon-local-special}.2) over the breaks gives
\[
\sum_\alpha\bigl(\dim V(\alpha)-\mathrm{Swan}(V(\alpha))\bigr)=r(V)-s(V),
\]
and summing (\ref{thm:laumon-local-special}.3) gives total Swan conductor $s(V)$.  This proves (\ref{thm:laumon-local-special}.1) and all stated special cases.  To separate the logical roles precisely: what is imported from Laumon is the existence of the local Fourier functor, its exactness on this slope range, and the stationary-phase/conductor statement of \cite[Thm.~2.4.3(ii)b, \S2.5]{Laumon}.  What is proved in the present paragraph is the specialization needed here: decomposition by breaks, the rank formula $r-s$, preservation of total Swan conductor, the output slope $\alpha/(1-\alpha)$, and in particular the transformations $0\mapsto0$ and $(d,\alpha)=(2,1/2)\mapsto(1,1)$.  No further assertion from Laumon's theorem is used below without being stated explicitly.
<!-- end proof-86 -->
<!-- proposition-35: body_md -->
\label{prop:coordinate-zero-tame}
Let $n\ge2$, $p>\max(2,n)$, and fix $c=(c_2,\dots,c_n)\in(\overline{\mathbb F}_p^\times)^{n-1}$. Then
\[
\mathrm{Swan}_0(\mathcal H_n|_{\ell_c})=0,\qquad
\mathrm{Swan}_0(\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c})=0.
\]
<!-- end proposition-35 -->
<!-- proof-87: body_md -->
Write $u'=(u_2,\dots,u_n)$,
\[
\varphi(u')=\sum_{i=2}^n u_i^{-1},\qquad
B(u')=-\lambda-\sum_{i=2}^n c_i u_i,
\qquad U=\{B\ne0\}.
\]
On $\ell_c$ the constraint gives $h_1u_1=B(u')$, hence on $U$ one has $u_1^{-1}=h_1B(u')^{-1}$. Put $g=B^{-1}:U\to\mathbb{G}_{m,v}$ and $N:=Rg_!\mathcal L_\psi(\varphi)$, extended by zero to $\mathbb A^1_v$. Projection formula and compactly supported base change identify the $h_1$-family with Laumon's Fourier transform
\[
\mathcal H_n|_{\ell_c}\simeq\operatorname{FT}^\psi(N),\qquad
\operatorname{FT}^\psi(M)=Rp_{2!}(p_1^*M\otimes\mathcal L_\psi(vh_1))[1].
\]
It remains to determine the local module $N_{(\infty)}$. Put $w=v^{-1}$ and $\mathcal F:=RB_!\mathcal L_\psi(\varphi)$ on the $w$-line. Inversion identifies the punctured trait at $v=\infty$ with the punctured trait at $w=0$, so it is enough to show that $\mathcal F$ is lisse at $w=0$.

By compactly supported base change, the fibre at $w$ is the cohomology of
\[
Y'_w=\left\{u'\in\mathbb{G}_{m}^{n-1}:\sum_{i=2}^n c_i u_i=-(\lambda+w)\right\}
\]
with coefficient $\mathcal L_\psi(\varphi)$. Since $\lambda\ne0$, $\lambda+w$ is a unit on the strict henselization at $0$. For $n\ge3$ define
\[
\alpha(w)=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+w}(c_2,\dots,c_n)\in\mathbb{G}_{m}^{n-1}.
\]
The equation of the $(n-1)$-variable constrained family with parameter $\alpha(w)$ becomes, after multiplication by the unit $(\lambda+w)/\lambda$, exactly the equation of $Y'_w$, while the phase $\varphi$ is unchanged. Thus $\mathcal F$ is the pullback of the lisse $(n-1)$-variable cohomology sheaf supplied by Theorem~\ref{thm:self-cohomology-package}; it is therefore lisse at $w=0$. If $n=2$, the unique solution is $u_2=-(\lambda+w)/c_2$ and the coefficient is $\mathcal L_\psi(-c_2/(\lambda+w))$, visibly lisse near $0$. Hence $N_{(\infty)}$ has only slope $0$ and $\mathrm{Swan}_\infty(N)=0$.

The local module $N_{(\infty)}$ lies in the slope-$0$ subcategory, so Theorem~\ref{thm:laumon-local-special} applies with $s=0$.  The stationary-phase decomposition of the global Fourier transform identifies the resulting $(\infty,0')$ local transform with the local monodromy of $\mathcal H_n|_{\ell_c}$ at $h_1=0$.  Hence $\mathrm{Swan}_0(\mathcal H_n|_{\ell_c})=0$. Finally $\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c}$ is a subquotient of the mixed cohomology sheaf $\mathcal H_n|_{\ell_c}$ by the weight filtration of Theorem~\ref{thm:self-cohomology-package}; Swan conductors are nonnegative and additive in short exact sequences, so its Swan conductor at $0$ is also zero.
<!-- end proof-87 -->
<!-- lemma-28: body_md -->
\label{lem:conv-identification}
Let $n\ge2$, $p>\max(2,n)$, and fix $c=(c_2,\dots,c_n)$. Put
\[
\mathcal M:=\Big(\bigotimes_{i=2}^{n}m_{c_i}^*\mathrm{Kl}_2\Big)\otimes\mathcal{L}_\psi(\lambda t)\quad\text{on }\mathbb{G}_{m,t},
\]
and let $\iota$ be the inversion $t\mapsto t^{-1}$. Then, as lisse sheaves on $\mathbb{G}_{m,h_1}$,
\[
H^1_c\big(\mathbb{G}_{m,t},\mathcal N_n|_{\ell_c}\big)\;\cong\;\mathrm{Kl}_2\ *_!\ \iota^*\mathcal M ,
\]
the multiplicative convolution $R^1\pi_!$ along $\pi:\mathbb{G}_{m}\times\mathbb{G}_{m}\to\mathbb{G}_{m}$, $\pi(u,v)=uv$.
<!-- end lemma-28 -->
<!-- proof-88: body_md -->
By definition $\mathcal N_n|_{\ell_c}=m_{h_1}^*\mathrm{Kl}_2\otimes\mathcal M$ on $\mathbb{G}_{m,t}$, so its $H^1_c$ has stalk $H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_{m,t},\mathrm{Kl}_2(h_1t)\otimes\mathcal M(t))$ at $h_1$. Substituting $u=h_1t$, an isomorphism $\mathbb{G}_{m,t}\to\mathbb{G}_{m,u}$ for each fixed $h_1\in\mathbb{G}_{m}$, this becomes $H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_{m,u},\mathrm{Kl}_2(u)\otimes\mathcal M(u/h_1))$. The stalk of $\mathrm{Kl}_2*_!\mathcal L$ at $h_1$ is $H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_{m,u},\mathrm{Kl}_2(u)\otimes\mathcal L(h_1/u))$, so the two agree with $\mathcal L=\iota^*\mathcal M$.
<!-- end proof-88 -->
<!-- lemma-29: body_md -->
\label{lem:conv-admissible}
Both $\mathrm{Kl}_2[1]$ and $(\iota^*\mathcal M)[1]$ are pure perverse middle-extension objects on $\mathbb{G}_{m}$, defined over a finite field after enlarging the ground field if necessary, and neither has a Kummer subobject, a Kummer quotient, or a Kummer geometric constituent.
<!-- end lemma-29 -->
<!-- proof-89: body_md -->
Theorem~\ref{thm:kl2-local-internal} gives purity of $\mathrm{Kl}_2$.  The sheaf $\mathcal M$ is a tensor product of pure sheaves with the weight-zero Artin--Schreier sheaf, hence is pure, and inversion preserves purity.  A lisse sheaf on $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ shifted by $[1]$ is perverse, and its extension from $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ to itself is already a middle extension.

A Kummer sheaf is tame at both $0$ and $\infty$. Let $P$ be wild inertia at the relevant boundary point. The $P$-action factors through a finite $p$-group, and over a characteristic-zero coefficient field its representation category is semisimple. Thus a representation with no $P$-invariants has neither a subrepresentation nor a quotient on which $P$ acts trivially. Theorem~\ref{thm:kl2-local-internal} says that $\mathrm{Kl}_2$ is totally wild at $\infty$, so it has no Kummer subobject, quotient, or geometric constituent. For $\mathcal M$, the factor $\mathcal{L}_\psi(\lambda t)$ has break $1$ at $\infty$, whereas every $m_{c_i}^*\mathrm{Kl}_2$ has break $1/2$ there. By Lemma~\ref{lem:self-unequal-break}, every break of $\mathcal M$ at $\infty$ is therefore $1$. Hence $\mathcal M$ is totally wild at $\infty$, and $\iota^*\mathcal M$ is totally wild at $0$. The same argument excludes Kummer subobjects, quotients, and geometric constituents.  After replacing the finite ground field by a finite extension, all objects and tame characters under discussion descend to that field, which is the arithmetic setting required in Theorem~\ref{thm:rojas-product}.
<!-- end proof-89 -->
<!-- theorem-21: body_md -->
\label{thm:rojas-product}
Let $K$ and $L$ be pure perverse middle-extension objects on $\mathbb{G}_{m}$, defined over a finite field, with no Kummer geometric constituent, subobject, or quotient. For a tame character $\chi$ over a finite extension, define
\[
P_{M,\chi}(T)=\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z}a_iT^i
\]
by letting $a_i$ for $i>0$ count the unipotent Jordan blocks of size $i$ in the tame part of $\mathcal L_{\bar\chi}\otimes M$ at $\infty$, letting $a_i$ for $i<0$ count the blocks of size $-i$ at $0$, and choosing $a_0$ so that $P_{M,\chi}(1)=\chi_c(\mathbb{G}_{m},M)$. Then
\[
P_{K*_{\mathrm{mid}}L,\chi}(T)=P_{K,\chi}(T)P_{L,\chi}(T).
\]
<!-- end theorem-21 -->
<!-- proof-90: body_md -->
We reproduce the proof of Rojas--Le\'on, Proposition~6.1, in the normalization used here.  A geometrically constant twist shifts every Frobenius weight by the same integer and does not change any local Jordan block, so we may first twist $K$ and $L$ to weight zero and undo the twist at the end.

For a tame character $\chi$ put
\[
\omega_\chi(M):=H^0\!\left(\mathbb P^1_{\bar k},j_{\infty!}Rj_{0*}(\mathcal L_\chi\otimes M)\right).
\]
For the present product formula no abstract Tannakian formalism is needed.  We use the displayed cohomology group merely as a concrete realization of the Mellin fibre and prove directly the two properties that enter the argument: compatibility with middle convolution and the weight--Jordan dictionary.  This is precisely the portion of the Mellin formalism used in Rojas--Le\'on's proof.

There are two facts to verify.

\emph{Tensor compatibility.}  The middle convolution is the image, in the perverse category, of the forget-supports morphism $R\mu_!(K\boxtimes L)\to R\mu_*(K\boxtimes L)$ for multiplication $\mu:\mathbb{G}_{m}^2\to\mathbb{G}_{m}$.  Twisting by $\mathcal L_\chi$ and using $\mu^*\mathcal L_\chi=\mathcal L_\chi\boxtimes\mathcal L_\chi$, the projection formula identifies the compactly supported Mellin complex with
\[
R\Gamma_c(\mathbb{G}_{m},K\otimes\mathcal L_\chi)\,\overset L\otimes\,
R\Gamma_c(\mathbb{G}_{m},L\otimes\mathcal L_\chi)
\]
by K\"unneth; the same argument without supports gives the ordinary-cohomology complex.  Passing to the image of the compact-to-ordinary map therefore gives a canonical isomorphism
\[
\omega_\chi(K*_{\mathrm{mid}}L)\cong
\omega_\chi(K)\otimes\omega_\chi(L).
\tag{\ref{thm:rojas-product}.1}
\]
The no-Kummer hypothesis has a precise role here: it prevents a punctual or Kummer kernel or cokernel from surviving when the derived convolution is replaced by this middle image.

\emph{The weight--Jordan dictionary.}  For a pure perverse middle extension $M$, apply the nearby-cycle exact sequences at $0$ and $\infty$ to $\mathcal L_\chi\otimes M$.  On a tame unipotent Jordan block of size $j$, the monodromy filtration has one primitive line and successive powers of the nilpotent operator move its weights by two.  In $j_{\infty!}Rj_{0*}$ the primitive line at $\infty$ survives with weight $+j$, while the primitive line of a size-$j$ block at $0$ survives with weight $-j$; the remaining interior contribution is the weight-zero part, whose dimension is fixed by the Euler characteristic.  Consequently $\omega_\chi(M)$ has exactly $a_i$ Frobenius eigenvalues of weight $i$, where the $a_i$ are the coefficients in the definition of $P_{M,\chi}(T)$.  This is the local monodromy-filtration calculation underlying the weight theorem used by Rojas--Le\'on.

Write $P_{K,\chi}=\sum_i a_iT^i$ and $P_{L,\chi}=\sum_j b_jT^j$.  By (\ref{thm:rojas-product}.1), a weight-$i$ eigenvalue from $\omega_\chi(K)$ tensored with a weight-$j$ eigenvalue from $\omega_\chi(L)$ has weight $i+j$.  Hence the multiplicity of weight $r$ in the middle convolution is $\sum_{i+j=r}a_ib_j$, and therefore
\[
P_{K*_{\mathrm{mid}}L,\chi}(T)
=\sum_r\Bigl(\sum_{i+j=r}a_ib_j\Bigr)T^r
=P_{K,\chi}(T)P_{L,\chi}(T).
\]
This is the complete multiplicative argument of Rojas--Le\'on \cite[Prop.~6.1]{RojasLeon-conv}; no further local-convolution formula is invoked below.
<!-- end proof-90 -->
<!-- proposition-36: body_md -->
\label{prop:blocks-at-zero}
Let $n\ge2$ and $p>\max(2,n)$, and write $u$ for a topological generator of the tame quotient of $I_0$ at $h_1=0$. Then the tame local monodromy of the middle convolution $\mathrm{Kl}_2*_{\mathrm{mid}}\iota^*\mathcal M$ at $h_1=0$ is unipotent, with exactly
\[
r(n-1)\;=\;2^{\,n-1}-\binom{n-1}{\lfloor (n-1)/2\rfloor}
\]
Jordan blocks of size $2$, exactly $c_1$ of size $1$ and none of size $\ge3$, where $c_1$ is the number of trivial summands in the Clebsch--Gordan decomposition of $V_2^{\otimes(n-1)}$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:self-cg}; in particular $u-1$ has rank $r(n-1)$ there. Consequently, on the $!$-convolution,
\[
\operatorname{rank}\big((u-1)\,\big|\,H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_{m,t},\mathcal N_n|_{\ell_c})\big)\;\ge\;r(n-1).
\]
<!-- end proposition-36 -->
<!-- proof-91: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:conv-admissible}, the two factors satisfy every hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{thm:rojas-product}. We therefore compute the two polynomials $P_{M,\chi}$ explicitly and multiply them.

\emph{The factor $\mathrm{Kl}_2[1]$.} By Theorem~\ref{thm:kl2-local-internal}, $\mathrm{Kl}_2$ is tame at $0$ with a single unipotent Jordan block of size $2$, and totally wild at $\infty$ with $\mathrm{Swan}_\infty=1$; so $a_{-2}=1$ and $a_i=0$ for $i>0$. Ogg--Shafarevich gives $\chi(\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathrm{Kl}_2)=-\mathrm{Swan}_0-\mathrm{Swan}_\infty=-1$, and for the perverse shift $\chi(\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathrm{Kl}_2[1])=+1$, whence $a_0=0$ and
\[
P_{\mathrm{Kl}_2[1]}(T)=T^{-2}.
\]

\emph{The factor $(\iota^*\mathcal M)[1]$.} Inversion exchanges $0$ and $\infty$. At $0$ the sheaf $\iota^*\mathcal M$ is totally wild, so it has no unipotent tame blocks there and $a_i=0$ for $i<0$. At $\infty$ its tame part is the tame part of $\mathcal M$ at $0$; there $\mathcal{L}_\psi(\lambda t)$ is unramified and each $m_{c_i}^*\mathrm{Kl}_2$ contributes the regular unipotent of $\operatorname{SL}_2$, so the $I_0$-module is $V_2^{\otimes(n-1)}$, whose Jordan blocks are the Clebsch--Gordan blocks of Lemma~\ref{lem:self-cg}: writing $c_j$ for the number of blocks of size $j$,
\[
\sum_j c_j=\binom{n-1}{\lfloor (n-1)/2\rfloor},\qquad \sum_j jc_j=2^{\,n-1}.
\]
Since $\mathrm{Swan}_0(\iota^*\mathcal M)=\mathrm{Swan}_\infty(\mathcal M)=2^{\,n-1}$ and $\mathrm{Swan}_\infty(\iota^*\mathcal M)=\mathrm{Swan}_0(\mathcal M)=0$, Ogg--Shafarevich gives $\chi(\mathbb{G}_{m},\iota^*\mathcal M)=-2^{\,n-1}$ and $\chi(\mathbb{G}_{m},(\iota^*\mathcal M)[1])=+2^{\,n-1}$, so
\[
a_0=2^{\,n-1}-\binom{n-1}{\lfloor (n-1)/2\rfloor}=\sum_j(j-1)c_j=r(n-1),
\]
and
\[
P_{(\iota^*\mathcal M)[1]}(T)=r(n-1)+\sum_{j\ge1}c_jT^j .
\]

\emph{Unipotence.} The same formula applied to a nontrivial tame character $\chi$ gives it. At $0$ the sheaf $\mathrm{Kl}_2$ is tame with unipotent monodromy, so $\mathcal L_{\bar\chi}\otimes\mathrm{Kl}_2$ has all its tame eigenvalues equal to $\bar\chi(\gamma)\ne1$ there and contributes no unipotent block: $a_i=0$ for $i<0$. At $\infty$ it is totally wild, and a tame twist does not change that: $a_i=0$ for $i>0$. Since Swan conductors are unchanged by a tame twist, $\chi(\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathcal L_{\bar\chi}\otimes\mathrm{Kl}_2)=-1$ and $P_{\mathrm{Kl}_2[1],\chi}(T)=1$. The same two observations applied to $\iota^*\mathcal M$ --- totally wild at $0$, and unipotent tame part at $\infty$, which the twist destroys --- give $P_{(\iota^*\mathcal M)[1],\chi}(T)=2^{\,n-1}$. Their product is the constant $2^{\,n-1}$, with no term in a negative power of $T$: the middle convolution has no $\chi$-isotypic tame block at $h_1=0$ for any nontrivial tame character $\chi$ defined over a finite extension. By quasi-unipotence, the semisimple part of tame inertia has finite order prime to $p$; every character of such an order $m$ is realized over some finite extension $\mathbb F_{q^r}$ with $m\mid(q^r-1)$. Hence no nontrivial tame eigencharacter occurs at all, and the tame local monodromy is unipotent.

\emph{The product for $\chi=1$.} Multiplying,
\[
P_{\mathrm{Kl}_2[1]}\cdot P_{(\iota^*\mathcal M)[1]}=T^{-2}\Big(r(n-1)+\sum_{j\ge1}c_jT^j\Big)=r(n-1)\,T^{-2}+\sum_{j\ge1}c_j\,T^{\,j-2}.
\]
The coefficients of negative powers record the unipotent blocks at $0$: the coefficient of $T^{-2}$ is $r(n-1)$ and there is no term $T^{-i}$ with $i\ge3$. A unipotent with $r(n-1)$ blocks of size $2$ and the rest of size $1$ has $\operatorname{rank}(u-1)=r(n-1)$.

\emph{Transfer to the $!$-convolution.} By definition $\mathrm{Kl}_2*_{\mathrm{mid}}\iota^*\mathcal M$ is the image, in the category of perverse sheaves, of the forget-supports map $\mathrm{Kl}_2*_!\iota^*\mathcal M\to\mathrm{Kl}_2*_*\iota^*\mathcal M$; in particular it is a \emph{quotient} of $\mathrm{Kl}_2*_!\iota^*\mathcal M=H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_{m,t},\mathcal N_n|_{\ell_c})$, compatibly with the action of $I_0$. If $V\twoheadrightarrow V/\mathcal K$ is a surjection of $I_0$-modules, the image of $u-1$ on $V/\mathcal K$ is the image of $(u-1)V$, so its dimension is at most $\operatorname{rank}\big((u-1)|_V\big)$. Applying this with $V=H^1_c$ gives the stated inequality. No comparison between the two convolutions is needed: only the inequality in this direction is used below.
<!-- end proof-91 -->
<!-- lemma-30: body_md -->
\label{lem:rank-identity}
For every $n\ge2$, with $c_1$ as in Proposition~\ref{prop:blocks-at-zero},
\[
2\,r(n-1)+c_1=r(n).
\]
<!-- end lemma-30 -->
<!-- proof-92: body_md -->
Since $r(m)=2^m-\binom{m}{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}$, the assertion is that $2\binom{n-1}{\lfloor (n-1)/2\rfloor}-c_1=\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$. If $n=2m$ is even then $n-1$ is odd, $V_2^{\otimes(n-1)}$ has no trivial summand and $c_1=0$, while Pascal's rule gives $\binom{2m}{m}=\binom{2m-1}{m-1}+\binom{2m-1}{m}=2\binom{2m-1}{m-1}$, which is the claim. If $n=2m+1$ is odd then $c_1$ is the multiplicity of the trivial summand in $V_2^{\otimes 2m}$, namely the Catalan number $\binom{2m}{m}-\binom{2m}{m-1}$, and
\[
2\binom{2m}{m}-c_1=\binom{2m}{m}+\binom{2m}{m-1}=\binom{2m+1}{m},
\]
again by Pascal's rule.
<!-- end proof-92 -->
<!-- lemma-31: body_md -->
\label{lem:midconv-pure}
Let $K,L$ be pure perverse sheaves of weights $a,b$ on $\mathbb{G}_{m}$, with no Kummer subobjects or quotients, and let $K*_{\mathrm{mid}}L$ be the image of the forget-supports morphism in the perverse category.  Then $K*_{\mathrm{mid}}L$ is pure of weight $a+b$.
<!-- end lemma-31 -->
<!-- proof-93: body_md -->
The external product $K\boxtimes L$ is pure of weight $a+b$.  Deligne's functorial weight inequalities give weights $\le a+b$ on the perverse cohomology of $R\mu_!(K\boxtimes L)$ and, by Verdier duality, weights $\ge a+b$ on the corresponding perverse cohomology of $R\mu_*(K\boxtimes L)$.  Middle convolution is the image of the natural map between these two perverse objects.  An image is simultaneously a quotient of the source and a subobject of the target; strictness of the weight filtration therefore gives weights $\le a+b$ and $\ge a+b$ on the same object.  Hence all its weights equal $a+b$, which is purity.  The no-Kummer hypothesis is used only to ensure that this middle image is the convolution object in the quotient category and has no discarded Kummer summand.
<!-- end proof-93 -->
<!-- proposition-37: body_md -->
\label{prop:mid-is-W}
Let $n\ge2$ and $p>\max(2,n)$. Then the natural map
\[
\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c}\ \longrightarrow\ \mathrm{Kl}_2*_{\mathrm{mid}}\iota^*\mathcal M
\]
is an isomorphism.
<!-- end proposition-37 -->
<!-- proof-94: body_md -->
\emph{It is surjective.} We spell out the weight convention because a shift is involved. As a lisse sheaf, $\mathrm{Kl}_2$ is pure of weight $1$, so $\mathrm{Kl}_2[1]$ is pure of perverse weight $2$. Likewise $\mathcal M$ is pure of weight $n-1$, so $(\iota^*\mathcal M)[1]$ is pure of perverse weight $n$. Lemma~\ref{lem:midconv-pure} shows that their middle convolution is pure of the sum of the perverse weights; hence its underlying lisse sheaf $\mathrm{Kl}_2*_{\mathrm{mid}}\iota^*\mathcal M$ is pure of weight $n+1$. Lemma~\ref{lem:conv-admissible} supplies the hypotheses. This lisse sheaf is a quotient of $H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_{m,t},\mathcal N_n|_{\ell_c})$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:self-excision} and Theorem~\ref{thm:self-cohomology-package}, the latter is mixed of weights $\le n+1$, its lower part has weights at most $n$, and its weight-$(n+1)$ quotient is $\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c}$. Any image of the lower-weight part inside a pure weight-$(n+1)$ object is zero by strictness of weights. Thus the quotient map factors through $\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c}$.

\emph{It is injective.} By Proposition~\ref{prop:coordinate-zero-tame}, $\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c}$ is tame at $h_1=0$; hence so is its quotient middle convolution. Proposition~\ref{prop:blocks-at-zero} computes that tame inertia representation: it is unipotent with $r(n-1)$ Jordan blocks of size $2$ and $c_1$ blocks of size $1$, and no others. Therefore its rank is
\[
\operatorname{rank}\big(\mathrm{Kl}_2*_{\mathrm{mid}}\iota^*\mathcal M\big)=2\,r(n-1)+c_1=r(n)
\]
by Lemma~\ref{lem:rank-identity}. Since $\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c}$ has rank $r(n)$ as well, the surjection is an isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-94 -->
<!-- theorem-22: body_md -->
\label{thm:swan-total}
Under the hypotheses above,
\[
\mathrm{Swan}_0(\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c})=0,\qquad
\mathrm{Swan}_\infty(\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c})=2^{n-1}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-22 -->
<!-- proof-95: body_md -->
The first equality is Proposition~\ref{prop:coordinate-zero-tame}. Proposition~\ref{prop:mid-is-W} identifies $\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c}[1]$ with the perverse middle convolution. Theorem~\ref{thm:rojas-product}, evaluated at the trivial tame character and at $T=1$, gives
\[
\chi_c(\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c}[1])=P_{\mathrm{Kl}_2[1]}(1)P_{(\iota^*\mathcal M)[1]}(1)=1\cdot2^{n-1}=2^{n-1},
\]
where the two factors were computed in Proposition~\ref{prop:blocks-at-zero}. A shift by $[1]$ changes the Euler-characteristic sign, so $\chi_c(\mathbb{G}_{m},\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c})=-2^{n-1}$. Grothendieck--Ogg--Shafarevich gives
\[
-2^{n-1}=-\mathrm{Swan}_0(\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c})-\mathrm{Swan}_\infty(\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c}).
\]
Using $\mathrm{Swan}_0=0$ yields $\mathrm{Swan}_\infty=2^{n-1}$.
<!-- end proof-95 -->
<!-- proposition-38: body_md -->
\label{prop:boundary-unipotent-infinite}
Let $n\ge2$ and $p>\max(2,n)$. Then $G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)$ contains a nonidentity unipotent element. In particular, $G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)$ is infinite.
<!-- end proposition-38 -->
<!-- proof-96: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:mid-is-W}, the local monodromy of $\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c}$ is the middle-convolution monodromy computed in Proposition~\ref{prop:blocks-at-zero}. It has exactly $r(n-1)$ Jordan blocks of size $2$. Since
\[
r(n-1)=2^{n-1}-\binom{n-1}{\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor}>0,
\]
tame inertia contains a nonidentity unipotent element $u$. Over the characteristic-zero coefficient field such an element has infinite order: if $u=1+N$ with $N\ne0$ nilpotent, then the finite logarithm $\log u=N-N^2/2+\cdots$ is nonzero and $\log(u^m)=m\log u$; hence $u^m\ne1$ for every $m\ge1$. Thus $G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)$ is infinite.
<!-- end proof-96 -->
<!-- proposition-39: body_md -->
\label{prop:finite-det-internal}
For every $n\ge2$ and $p>\max(2,n)$, the geometric determinant character
\[
\delta_n:=\det(\mathcal W_n):\pi_1^{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathbb{G}_{m}^n)\longrightarrow\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell^\times
\]
has finite image. Consequently $G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)\cap\{\text{scalars}\}$ is finite.
<!-- end proposition-39 -->
<!-- proof-97: body_md -->
Choose a finite extension $E/\mathbb Q_\ell$ over which the representation is defined. For each coordinate $h_i$, restrict to a coordinate line on which the remaining coordinates are fixed and nonzero. By symmetry it is enough to take $i=1$. Proposition~\ref{prop:coordinate-zero-tame} shows that wild inertia at $h_1=0$ acts trivially, while Propositions~\ref{prop:mid-is-W} and~\ref{prop:blocks-at-zero} show that tame inertia acts unipotently. Hence the determinant is $1$ on each standard coordinate tame-inertia generator.

Let $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_p$ and $S_k=(\mathbb G_{m,k})^n$. For every integer $m$ prime to $p$, the Kummer sequence
\[
1\to\mu_m\to\mathbb G_m\xrightarrow{(\cdot)^m}\mathbb G_m\to1
\]
and the facts
\[
\operatorname{Pic}(S_k)=0,\qquad
\mathcal O(S_k)^\times=k^\times h_1^{\mathbb Z}\cdots h_n^{\mathbb Z}
\]
give
\[
H^1(S_k,\mu_m)\cong \mathcal O(S_k)^\times/\mathcal O(S_k)^{\times m}
\cong(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z)^n.
\]
Here $k^\times$ contributes nothing because $k$ is algebraically closed, hence $m$-divisible. Under this identification the standard basis classes are the Kummer classes of $h_1,\dots,h_n$, equivalently the characters detected by the $n$ coordinate tame-inertia loops. Passing over all $m$ prime to $p$ shows that the maximal prime-to-$p$ abelian quotient of $\pi_1^{\mathrm{geom}}(S_k)$ is topologically generated by those loops. More explicitly, let $A$ be any finite abelian quotient of $\pi_1^{\mathrm{geom}}(S_k)$ whose order is prime to $p$.  If the image of a coordinate loop were trivial for every coordinate and $A$ were nevertheless nontrivial, then some nontrivial character $A\to\mu_m$ (for $m$ equal to the exponent of $A$) would pull back to a nonzero class of $H^1(S_k,\mu_m)$ that vanished on every standard basis loop.  The displayed Kummer identification makes this impossible.  Hence the coordinate loops generate every such $A$. Since $\delta_n$ is trivial on each of them, every finite prime-to-$p$ quotient of its image is trivial.

The image of $\delta_n$ is compact, so after enlarging $E$ it lies in $\mathcal O_E^\times$. Its remaining image is therefore pro-$p$. Since $p\ne\ell$, the group $\mathcal O_E^\times$ is an extension of a finite group of roots of unity by the pro-$\ell$ group $1+\mathfrak m_E$; every pro-$p$ subgroup is consequently finite. Thus $\delta_n$ has finite image.

Finally, if $zI$ belongs to $G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)$, then $z^{r(n)}=\det(zI)$ belongs to the finite image of $\delta_n$. Hence only finitely many values of $z$ are possible, proving the scalar assertion.
<!-- end proof-97 -->
<!-- lemma-32: body_md -->
\label{lem:gap-n}
For every $n\ge6$,
\[
r(n-1)>\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-32 -->
<!-- proof-98: body_md -->
Set $a_m=\binom{2m}{m}/4^m$. Then
\[
\frac{a_{m+1}}{a_m}=\frac{2m+1}{2m+2}<1,
\]
so $a_m\le a_3=5/16$ for $m\ge3$. If $n=2m$ with $m\ge3$, then
\[
\binom{2m-1}{m-1}=\frac12\binom{2m}{m}\le\frac5{32}2^{2m},
\]
and therefore
\[
r(2m-1)=2^{2m-1}-\binom{2m-1}{m-1}\ge\frac{11}{32}2^{2m}>\frac{10}{32}2^{2m}\ge\binom{2m}{m}.
\]
If $n=2m+1$ with $m\ge3$, then $\binom{2m+1}{m}<2\binom{2m}{m}$ and
\[
r(2m)=2^{2m}-\binom{2m}{m}\ge\frac{11}{16}2^{2m}>\frac{10}{16}2^{2m}\ge2\binom{2m}{m}>\binom{2m+1}{m}.
\]
This proves both parities.
<!-- end proof-98 -->
<!-- theorem-23: body_md -->
\label{thm:ggeom-infinite}
Let $n\ge6$ and $p>\max(2,n)$. Then $G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)$ is infinite, and consequently
\[
G^0_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)=\operatorname{SL}_{r(n)} .
\]
<!-- end theorem-23 -->
<!-- proof-99: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:self-excision}, restricted to the coordinate line, there is a short exact sequence of $I_0$-modules
\[
0\to\mathcal N_n^{I_0}\to H^1_c\big(\mathbb{G}_{m,t},\mathcal N_n|_{\ell_c}\big)\to\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c}\to0,
\]
the sub being of weight $\le n$ of dimension $\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ and the quotient pure of weight $n+1$ of dimension $r(n)$. The weight filtration is by subsheaves, hence stable under the monodromy, so $u$ acts on the sequence.

Suppose $u$ acted trivially on $\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c}$. Then $(u-1)$ would kill the quotient, so its image would lie in the sub, giving
\[
\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}=\dim\mathcal N_n^{I_0}\ \ge\ \operatorname{rank}(u-1)\ \ge\ r(n-1)
\]
by Proposition~\ref{prop:blocks-at-zero}. This contradicts Lemma~\ref{lem:gap-n}, which gives the strict reverse inequality for every $n\ge6$. Hence $u$ acts nontrivially on $\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c}$.

By Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary-fibre-unipotent} and Proposition~\ref{prop:blocks-at-zero}, the action is unipotent. Being unipotent and $\ne1$, $u$ has infinite order: writing $N=u-1\ne0$, nilpotent, one has $u^m=1+mN+\binom m2N^2+\cdots$, and the first nonvanishing term shows $u^m\ne1$ for every $m\ge1$, the coefficient field having characteristic zero. The image of $\pi_1^{\mathrm{geom}}(\ell_c)$ lies in $G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)$, which is therefore infinite.

The infinitude conclusion is the only part needed later. Combining it with Theorem~\ref{thm:fourthmoment-n}, Proposition~\ref{prop:757-general}, and Larsen's alternative gives $G^0_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)=\operatorname{SL}_{r(n)}$, exactly as in the principal proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:monodromy-n}.
<!-- end proof-99 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:all-n}
For every $n\ge4$ and every $p>n$,
\[
G^0_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)=\operatorname{SL}_{r(n)}.
\]
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-100: body_md -->
This is Theorem~\ref{thm:monodromy-n} below. The present corollary is placed here only to emphasize that the boundary argument has no numerical range restriction. No claim about $n=2,3$ is made in this split article.
<!-- end proof-100 -->
<!-- remark-19: body_md -->
\label{rem:boundary-gap}
The middle convolution is a quotient of the $!$-convolution, so the rank of $u-1$ can only decrease on passage to it; this is the direction used in the alternative weight-gap proof. The principal route is stronger: Proposition~\ref{prop:coordinate-zero-tame} supplies tameness, Proposition~\ref{prop:blocks-at-zero} gives the complete tame Jordan structure, and Proposition~\ref{prop:mid-is-W} identifies that middle convolution with $\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c}$ itself. Hence the nonidentity unipotent is present directly on the top-weight sheaf, with no rank-gap inequality and no numerical or Diophantine condition.
<!-- end remark-19 -->
<!-- remark-20: body_md -->
\label{rem:swan-consistency}
The ray calculation in Proposition~\ref{prop:ray-det-p} also supplies an independent conductor check.  For a generic ray all $2^{n-1}$ paired slope-$1/2$ summands of $\mathcal K_a(\infty)$ are nonzero; Theorem~\ref{thm:laumon-local-special} sends each to one rank-one slope-$1$ summand at the Fourier boundary.  Hence the wild part on the ray has total Swan conductor $2^{n-1}$.  This agrees exactly with Theorem~\ref{thm:swan-total}, where the same total is obtained on a coordinate line by an Euler-characteristic calculation.  The two computations use different geometry and therefore provide a useful internal consistency check.
<!-- end remark-20 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{cor:sym-conductor}
With $c$ as above and $r=r(n)$, for every $k\ge1$
\[
\mathrm{Swan}_0\big(\operatorname{Sym}^k\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c}\big)+\mathrm{Swan}_\infty\big(\operatorname{Sym}^k\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c}\big)\;\le\;2^{\,n}\binom{k+r-1}{r-1},
\]
a bound polynomial in $k$ of degree $r-1$.
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proof-101: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:swan-total}, the total Swan conductor on the two boundary points is $2^{n-1}$; hence every individual break at either point is at most $2^{n-1}$. The breaks of a symmetric power are bounded by the largest break of the underlying sheaf, because breaks in a tensor product are at most the maximum of the breaks of its factors; passing to the direct summand $\operatorname{Sym}^k$ cannot increase breaks. Hence each of the $\binom{k+r-1}{r-1}$ breaks of $\operatorname{Sym}^k\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c}$ at either point is at most $2^{n-1}$, and summing over the two points gives the stated bound.
<!-- end proof-101 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{cor:general-lambda-conductor}
Let $n\ge2$, let $\ell_c$ be a coordinate line whose fixed coordinates $c_2,\dots,c_n$ are nonzero, and let $\Lambda$ be any irreducible representation of $\operatorname{SL}_{r(n)}$. Then
\[
\mathrm{Swan}_0\big(\Lambda(\mathcal W_n)|_{\ell_c}\big)+\mathrm{Swan}_\infty\big(\Lambda(\mathcal W_n)|_{\ell_c}\big)\;\le\;2^{\,n}\,\dim\Lambda ,
\]
uniformly in $\Lambda$, in $c$ and in $p$. In particular this gives the coordinate-line conductor estimate normally required in effective equidistribution arguments, with $A=1$ and $C=2^n$ and with dependence on $\Lambda$ that is \emph{linear} rather than merely polynomial.
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- proof-102: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:swan-total}, the total Swan conductor of $\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c}$ over the two points $0$ and $\infty$ is $2^{n-1}$; since Swan conductors are sums of non-negative breaks, every individual break of $\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c}$ at either point is at most $2^{n-1}$.

Let $\Lambda$ be an irreducible representation of $\operatorname{SL}_r$ with $r=r(n)$. Every such $\Lambda$ occurs as a subquotient of some tensor power $V^{\otimes m}$ of the standard representation, $V^{\otimes m}$ decomposing into irreducibles by Schur--Weyl. For tensor products of inertia representations, every break is at most the largest break of the factors; hence every break of that tensor power at $0$ or at $\infty$ is at most the largest break of $\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c}$, hence at most $2^{n-1}$; and breaks can only decrease on passing to a subquotient. Therefore every break of $\Lambda(\mathcal W_n)|_{\ell_c}$ is at most $2^{n-1}$ as well.

The sheaf $\Lambda(\mathcal W_n)$ has rank $\dim\Lambda$, so at each of the two points its Swan conductor, being the sum of $\dim\Lambda$ breaks, is at most $2^{n-1}\dim\Lambda$. Summing over $0$ and $\infty$ gives the assertion. Nothing in the argument refers to the particular shape of $\Lambda$, so the bound is uniform in $\Lambda$; and nothing in the argument depends on the chosen nonzero $c_i$ beyond Theorem~\ref{thm:swan-total}.
<!-- end proof-102 -->
<!-- remark-21: body_md -->
\label{rem:sym-special-case}
Taking $\Lambda=\operatorname{Sym}^k$, whose dimension is $\binom{k+r-1}{r-1}$, recovers Corollary~\ref{cor:sym-conductor}. The point of the more general statement is not the extra generality for its own sake but the observation that the argument never used any property of $\operatorname{Sym}^k$ beyond its being a subquotient of a tensor power, which is true of every irreducible $\Lambda$.
<!-- end remark-21 -->
<!-- remark-22: body_md -->
\label{rem:effective-partial}
Proposition~\ref{prop:boundary-degen} shows that the mixed sheaf $\mathcal G=R^5\pi_!\mathcal{L}_\psi(F_4)$ drops rank along $\{h_1=0\}$; that fact alone does not distinguish tame from wild ramification. The required conductor information is instead supplied internally by Theorem~\ref{thm:swan-total}:
\[
\mathrm{Swan}_0\big(\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c}\big)=0,
\qquad
\mathrm{Swan}_\infty\big(\mathcal W_n|_{\ell_c}\big)=2^{\,n-1}.
\]
Corollary~\ref{cor:sym-conductor} then gives a conductor bound for $\operatorname{Sym}^k\mathcal W_n$ that is polynomial in $k$. This is precisely the type of conductor input required by standard effective-equidistribution arguments. No analytic application of that machinery is used in the proof of the present article.
<!-- end remark-22 -->
<!-- lemma-33: body_md -->
\label{lem:projective-ray}
For every integer $k\ge0$,
\[
\left|\sum_{t\in G}\psi(L(t))a_t^k\right|\le 7\cdot2^k q^{3+k/2}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-33 -->
<!-- proof-103: body_md -->
The set $G$ is stable under scalar multiplication and $C_{ct}=C_t$, hence $a_{ct}=a_t$. Writing $\bar G$ for the projectivisation and summing first along each ray,
\[
\sum_{c\ne0}\psi(L(ct))=\begin{cases}q-1,&L(t)=0,\\-1,&L(t)\ne0.\end{cases}
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_{t\in G}\psi(L(t))a_t^k
=q\sum_{[t]\in\bar G\cap\{L=0\}}a_{[t]}^k-\sum_{[t]\in\bar G}a_{[t]}^k.
\]
The projective hyperplane $L=0$ has at most $q^2+q+1\le3q^2$ points and $\mathbb P^3(\mathbb F_q)$ at most $4q^3$ points. Lemma~\ref{lem:ninelines-bound}(i) gives $|a_t|\le2q^{1/2}$ on $G$. Hence the absolute value is at most
\[
q(3q^2)(2q^{1/2})^k+(4q^3)(2q^{1/2})^k\le7\cdot2^kq^{3+k/2}.
\]
<!-- end proof-103 -->
<!-- proposition-40: body_md -->
\label{prop:generic-ray}
For every fixed $n\ge3$,
\[
\sum_{t\in G}\psi(L(t))V(t)^n=O_n\big(q^{(5n+6)/2}\big).
\]
<!-- end proposition-40 -->
<!-- proof-104: body_md -->
Lemma~\ref{lem:sigma0-planecubic} gives $V(t)=-q^2(a_t+2+3/q)$ on $G$. Thus
\[
V(t)^n=(-1)^nq^{2n}\sum_{k=0}^n\binom{n}{k}(2+3/q)^{n-k}a_t^k.
\]
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:projective-ray} term by term. The largest exponent occurs at $k=n$ and equals $2n+3+n/2=(5n+6)/2$.
<!-- end proof-104 -->
<!-- lemma-34: body_md -->
\label{lem:decouple}
For every $n\ge1$, every finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ of odd characteristic, and every $\lambda\ne0$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
q^4\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q^n}|\Sigma_n(h)|^4&=\sum_{t\in\mathbb{F}_q^4}\psi(L(t))\,V(t)^n,\\
V(t)&:=\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q}\prod_{j=1}^4K(t_jh),\qquad L(t):=\lambda(t_1+t_2-t_3-t_4).
\end{aligned}
\]
where $V$ is the \emph{same} function of $t\in\mathbb{F}_q^4$ as in Section~\ref{sec:monodromy} --- built solely from the classical one-variable Kloosterman sum $K$, with no reference to $n$.
<!-- end lemma-34 -->
<!-- proof-105: body_md -->
By additive orthogonality, exactly as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:711},
\[
\Sigma_n(h)=\frac1q\sum_{t\in\mathbb{F}_q}\psi(t\lambda)\prod_{i=1}^nK(th_i)
\qquad(h\in\mathbb{F}_q^n).
\]
Since $K$ is real, $|\Sigma_n(h)|^4=\Sigma_n(h)\Sigma_n(h)\overline{\Sigma_n(h)}\overline{\Sigma_n(h)}$; assign dilation variables $t_1,t_2$ to the two unconjugated factors and $t_3,t_4$ to the two conjugated factors. Conjugation sends $\psi(t\lambda)$ to $\psi(-t\lambda)$ while leaving $K$ unchanged, so the resulting phase is precisely $L(t)=\lambda(t_1+t_2-t_3-t_4)$. Thus
\[
q^4|\Sigma_n(h)|^4=\sum_{t\in\mathbb{F}_q^4}\psi(L(t))\prod_{i=1}^n\Big[K(t_1h_i)K(t_2h_i)K(t_3h_i)K(t_4h_i)\Big].
\]
Summing over $h\in\mathbb{F}_q^n$, the $n$ coordinates are independent, so the product over $i$ factors as $\big[\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q}K(t_1h)K(t_2h)K(t_3h)K(t_4h)\big]^n=V(t)^n$. Two features of this step carry the general-$n$ argument. The phase $\psi(L(t))$ carries no $h$, so it passes outside the $h$-sum untouched; and each coordinate $h_i$ occurs in exactly one bracket, so the sum over $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ separates into $n$ identical copies of a sum over $\mathbb{F}_q$. Consequently $n$ enters the right-hand side only as the number of those copies, that is, only as an exponent: the variable $t$ ranges over $\mathbb{F}_q^4$ whatever $n$ may be, the $4$ recording the degree of the moment and not the dimension of the family. This is why the four-variable moment geometry, computed once, serves every $n$: the stratification and the estimates on it live on the same four-dimensional parameter space for all $n$. It is the moment geometry that propagates, not the $n$-variable sheaf geometry, which was established internally in Theorem~\ref{thm:self-cohomology-package}.
<!-- end proof-105 -->
<!-- lemma-35: body_md -->
\label{lem:zero-general}
For every fixed integer $n\ge2$,
\[
\sum_{t\in Z}\psi(L(t))V(t)^n=O_n(q^{2n+3}).
\]
<!-- end lemma-35 -->
<!-- proof-106: body_md -->
Let $r$ be the number of nonzero coordinates of $t$. The estimates in Theorem~\ref{thm:721} come before taking the fourth power and therefore apply directly to $V(t)$ itself. If $r=0$, then $V=q$ and there is one tuple. If $r=1$, then $V=0$. If $r=2$ and the two nonzero entries coincide, $|V|\ll q^2$ and there are $O(q)$ such tuples; if they are distinct, $|V|\ll q^{3/2}$ and there are $O(q^2)$ tuples. If $r=3$, then $|V|\ll q^2$ and there are $O(q^3)$ tuples. Thus the four contributions to $\sum_{t\in Z}|V(t)|^n$ are respectively
\[
O(q^n),\quad 0,\quad O_n(q^{2n+1})+O_n(q^{3n/2+2}),\quad O_n(q^{2n+3}).
\]
For $n\ge2$ each is $O_n(q^{2n+3})$. Since $|\psi(L(t))|=1$, the same bound holds for the twisted sum.
<!-- end proof-106 -->
<!-- theorem-24: body_md -->
\label{thm:fourthmoment-n}
For every fixed $n\ge3$ and every finite field $\mathbb F_q$ of characteristic $p>\max(2,n)$,
\[
\sum_{h\in\mathbb F_q^n}|\Sigma_n(h)|^4
=2q^{3n-2}+O_n\big(q^{3n-2-\delta(n)}\big),
\qquad
\delta(n)=\min\left(1,\frac{n-2}{2}\right).
\]
<!-- end theorem-24 -->
<!-- proof-107: body_md -->
Lemma~\ref{lem:decouple} gives
\[
q^4\sum_h|\Sigma_n(h)|^4=\sum_{t\in\mathbb F_q^4}\psi(L(t))V(t)^n.
\]
On $D$, Lemma~\ref{lem:diagonal-coefficient} gives $2q^{3n+2}+O_n(q^{3n+1})$. On $P$, Lemma~\ref{lem:pair-general} gives $O_n(q^{3n+1})$. On $Z$, Lemma~\ref{lem:zero-general} gives $O_n(q^{2n+3})$, which is $O_n(q^{3n+1})$ for $n\ge2$. Finally Proposition~\ref{prop:generic-ray} gives $O_n(q^{(5n+6)/2})$ on $G$. Hence
\[
q^4\sum_h|\Sigma_n(h)|^4
=2q^{3n+2}+O_n(q^{3n+1})+O_n(q^{(5n+6)/2}).
\]
Since
\[
3n+2-\frac{5n+6}{2}=\frac{n-2}{2},
\]
the saving before division by $q^4$ is $\delta(n)=\min(1,(n-2)/2)$. Dividing by $q^4$ proves the result.
<!-- end proof-107 -->
<!-- remark-23: body_md -->
\label{rem:normalisation}
The sheaf $\mathcal W_n$ is pure of weight $n+1$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:self-cohomology-package}, whereas $\Sigma_n(h)$ has natural size $q^{(n-1)/2}$. There is no discrepancy: the top-weight trace is $q\Sigma_n(h)$ up to the explicitly bounded lower-weight contribution. We therefore normalize only the scalar Frobenius trace,
\[
A_q^{(0)}(h):=q^{-(n+1)/2}A_q(h),
\]
where $A_q(h)$ is the geometric Frobenius trace on $\mathcal W_n$. No half-integral Tate twist of the sheaf is introduced. Theorem~\ref{thm:fourthmoment-n} and the lower-weight bound in Theorem~\ref{thm:self-cohomology-package} give
\[
q^{-n}\sum_{h\in\mathbb{G}_{m}^n(\mathbb F_q)}|A_q^{(0)}(h)|^4=2+o(1).
\]
The scalar normalization does not change the invariant space $W_n^{\otimes2}\otimes(W_n^\vee)^{\otimes2}$, so Katz's moment theorem identifies the limiting value with $M_4(G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n),W_n)$.
<!-- end remark-23 -->
<!-- theorem-25: body_md -->
\label{thm:monodromy-n}
Let $n\ge4$ and $p>n$. Then
\[
G^0_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)=\operatorname{SL}_{r(n)}.
\]
The proof is independent of the Guralnick--Tiep classification and of every finite computation in Appendix~\ref{app:computations}.
<!-- end theorem-25 -->
<!-- proof-108: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:fourthmoment-n}, Remark~\ref{rem:normalisation}, and Katz's moment theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:751}),
\[
M_4\bigl(G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n),W_n\bigr)=2.
\]
Proposition~\ref{prop:757-general} gives reductivity, Proposition~\ref{prop:finite-det-internal} gives finiteness of the scalar intersection and of the determinant image, and Proposition~\ref{prop:boundary-unipotent-infinite} gives a nonidentity unipotent element, so $G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)$ is infinite. Larsen's alternative, Theorem~\ref{thm:753}, says that a reductive group with $M_4=2$ either contains $\operatorname{SL}_{r(n)}$ or has finite projective image. Because the scalar intersection is finite, the latter branch would make the whole group finite, contradicting the boundary unipotent. Hence
\[
\operatorname{SL}_{r(n)}\subseteqG_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n).
\]
On the other hand the determinant has finite image by Proposition~\ref{prop:finite-det-internal}; therefore the connected determinant is trivial and $G^0_{\mathrm{geom}}\subseteq\operatorname{SL}_{r(n)}$. The two inclusions give equality.
<!-- end proof-108 -->
<!-- remark-24: body_md -->
\label{rem:n23-obstruction}
The present split article states its connected-monodromy theorem only for $n\ge4$. The fourth-moment estimate itself is proved here for every $n\ge3$, and the boundary-unipotent construction works for every $n\ge2$; nevertheless the low ranks are kept outside the stated scope so that this article does not import their separate case analyses. The longer manuscript \cite{EbadiFull} contains those low-rank arguments. Nothing in Theorem~\ref{thm:monodromy-n} depends on them.
<!-- end remark-24 -->
